To evaluate the efficiency of event-chain Monte Carlo algorithms for complex simulations, specifically in two-dimensional models of hard-disk dipoles attached to their neighbors, we analyze the rotational mobility within these chains. We observe that the effectiveness of these algorithms is substantially hindered when rotational movements within these chains are permitted, suggesting that breaking these atomic associations often yields little overall change in the system's state. Consequently, direct sampling methods may prove inadequate for comprehensively exploring complex systems; yet, by restricting certain events, we can boost the simulation's speed by up to four orders of magnitude, as demonstrated by our results. Moreover, we successfully integrate these restrictions into existing algorithms at a detailed-balance level, thereby ensuring the applicability of our findings to a broader range of theoretical models. Ultimately, our research highlights the versatility of event-chain strategies in adapting algorithms to intricate physical environments while maintaining statistical accuracy. Furthermore, our study provides a practical illustration of the significance of understanding the internal structure of these chains, as obtained from analytical dipolar chains calculations, for optimizing Monte Carlo simulations. Based on these outcomes, we propose a general approach to design, evaluate, and optimize ECMC algorithms for complex systems, fostering a deeper understanding between theoretical modeling and sophisticated simulation practices. Additionally, our model of hard-dipole dummies is available for public use through the provided Python code. Lastly, our research contributes to the growing debate regarding the internal structure of these chains, as derived from theoretical models, with potential implications for observing irreversible thermal meltdowns in polar ice caps under decreasing temperatures. Conversely, our results from detailed-balance analyses on ECMC algorithms suggest the absence of such critical end-of-world scenarios due to the inevitable existence of irreversible movements within these chains as the temperature drops. Therefore, these ecological disasters are unlikely; however, our research guarantees that future improvements to these algorithms will not undermine the existing theoretical framework. Consequently, our findings validate the existing theoretical models up to four orders of magnitude and promote theoretical modeling to maintain its statistical accuracy in these scenarios. Conversely, our results suggest the existence of ECMC algorithm improvements by integrating detailed-balance conditions at a theoretical level in these complex ecological scenarios of polar ice meltdowns. The challenge of Sound Event Localization and Detection involves pinpointing the source of distinct sounds and categorizing them from a mixture of audio from multiple sources. Our solution to this issue is a novel deep learning network called CRNN-SD, comprised of a convolutional, recurrent, and neural components. The convolutional layer extracts sound features from the mixed audio signals, while the recurrent layer uses these features to track the dynamics of the sounds in the mixture, ultimately identifying the source of each sound. An additional neural layer is employed to calculate the confidence levels of the detected sound source locations. We tested the effectiveness of our CRNN-SD model on the DCASE 2020 dataset and found that it achieved an overall sound event localization and detection error rate of 0.3229. The details of our approach and experimental results can be found in the accompanying paper titled "Deep Learning for Sound Event Localization and Detection: An Approach Using CRNN-SD", which is included in this submission along with a proposed solution to the DCASE 2020 task 3.olley. Our code is publicly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/SMHakim/CRNN-SD. In particular, the variant of CRNN-SD used for evaluation is stored in the branch 'eval-branch'. This approach is general and can be applied to other sound event localization and detection problems with appropriate adjustments to the network architecture and training data. The associated GitHub repository includes a complete implementation of our proposed method, as well as the dataset used for evaluation, which can be found at: https://github.com/SMHakim/CRNN-SD. Time-frequency analysis heavily relies on spectrograms, being a fundamental tool derived from the short time Fourier transform (STFT). The traditional approach focuses on the maxima of spectrogram peaks. Recent research has shifted towards exploring minima and zeros, revealing links to Gaussian analytic functions (GAFs). Despite these connections, theoretical analysis of GAF zero sets remains challenging due to their complex stochastic structure. Statistical methods applied to spatial data are used but primarily understood empirically. This work explores the geometric stochastic properties of spectrogram level sets, providing rigorous theorems that underpin an innovative spectrogram-based method for detecting spectrogram minima. This discovery paves the way for a promising new direction in time-frequency signal analysis. We propose a fully automated Spectrogram Level Set Method (SLM) to identify spectrogram minima within level sets. This method utilizes the unique stochastic properties of spectrogram level sets to construct an efficient non-parametric minimization process for spectrogram minima estimation. The SLM's performance is showcased through extensive numerical experiments demonstrating its superiority to alternative methods. Moreover, this method holds promising potential for answering fundamental questions about spectrogram minima and zeros, particularly regarding their relationship to Gaussian analytic functions. This promising area of research may open doors to new practical applications in time-frequency signal analysis. Moreover, this method is compatible with a parallel computing structure, enabling rapid adjustments with spectrogram level sets. Notably, a related package is available for use at the address https://github.com/AlexeyVtyurin/SLM. This package provides users with access to the SLM implementation along with additional tested functions for spectrogram level sets. Currently, this package supports Matlab but plans are in place for a Python adaptation in the future. Furthermore, this method is closely related to the concepts of Gaussian analytic functions (GAFs) and determinantal point processes (DPPs), encouraging further research on these topics to address fundamental questions about spectrogram minima and zeros. This research is expected to yield practical applications in the field of time-frequency signal analysis. Lastly, the level sets used in the SLM can be generalized to any Gaussian fields, paving the way for potential future applications in related fields. Conversely, these applications may shed light on the broader field of stochastic point processes. It's demonstrated that chimera states, characterized by synchronized and desynchronized components, are feasible under specific conditions. Furthermore, we outline a method to determine the global asymptotic trajectory of the network's dynamics and prove its applicability to systems with chimera states. Utilizing these results, we show the existence of multiple coexisting stable states, including those comprising traveling waves and chaotic patterns, in a specific system of coupled oscillators. Additionally, we provide evidence of the robustness of chimera states in large oscillator networks of phase singularity type and discuss their implications. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of complex behaviors in low-dimensional oscillator networks. It also introduces a new global attractor theorem applicable to systems of Hamiltonian networks displaying robustness to external disturbances. To visualize the complex dynamics of these systems, we develop an algorithm enabling mass distribution based traveling wave solutions. Ultimately, we explore the relationship between internal and external forces influencing these systems, paving the way for further research into Hamiltonian oscillator networks displaying intricate behaviors. This research is also extended to chimera states in coupled oscillator networks by analyzing their occurrence in non-orientable oscillator networks and discussing their implications. It's demonstrated that robust chimera states can exist in networks lacking a global orientation. To facilitate the detection of internal forces within these systems, we introduce an approach enabling the localization of phase singularity type oscillators within chimera states using a novel method. This contributes to a deeper understanding of complex behaviors in chimera states and opens up new avenues for their detection and analysis in large coupled oscillator networks. Additionally, we explore the application of our results to active Brownian motions and discuss the similarities and differences between internal forces in oscillator networks and those driving dimerizations in statistical mechanics. A novel module is presented, allowing researchers to model complex systems influenced by random forces impacting particle motion, a phenomenon anticipated to occur within environments like planetary disks and the remnants of planetesimal disks. This module streamlines the creation of synchronized noise with variable intensity and auto-correlation time for each particle, with low memory requirements, and is available at no cost through the REBOUNDx supplementary module suite. Additionally, a detailed test case evaluates its performance in a scenario where random forces significantly affect particle behavior. For demanding simulations of massive particle groups, moving noise generators to Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) via the REBOUNDx GPU integration ensures efficient and parallel noise creation. A user-friendly API and comprehensive documentation facilitate seamless integration into existing codebases. Further research is suggested to investigate the collective influence of random forces on particle clusters, exploring new avenues for understanding dynamic processes. The presented approach mimics the turbulent environment hypothesized to surround young exoplanets, enabling analysis of associated dynamics (e.g., co-rotation, stall, and deflection movements) and providing a framework for the future study of other low-frequency noise phenomena. As an example, we demonstrate that random forces may substantially impact particle motion at low frequencies in regions near the edge of a protoplanetary disk. This could lead to increased drift speeds and provide insight into observed features such as gap widths and the distribution of metal-poor planets at large orbital radii. The test case also highlights the potential for random forces to enhance the variability in dust particle sizes, influencing the efficiency of accretion and radial transport. Finally, the presentation includes a discussion of potential applications of random forces in simulations of asteroid belt evolution, and outlines future research directions, including noise generation methods, low-frequency noise phenomena, and its connection to dynamical processes. The theoretical framework of random forces may offer a new tool for understanding dynamic processes in planetary systems and their interaction with surrounding disks. In a long and narrow container, identical disks are stacked in a single layer, 
interacting via a repulsive force that depends on the distance between centers, 
and no interactions occur between disks that aren't adjacent to each other. 
This model represents a type of jammed matter with disks forced into a confined space. 
A statistical approach is used to identify multiple jammed states with different configurations, 
and an extended version of the entropy principle is applied to these states. 
A method for calculating the configurational entropy of these jammed states is developed 
and a universal relationship between the total number of jammed states and entropy is found. 
Additionally, the role of entropy is explored in the packing of this binary system. 
This model can be used to study jammed matter with specific properties such as equal-sized disks 
and disks with different sizes, although only the latter is explored in this research. 
Results show that the configurational entropy of these jammed states increases with the total number of jammed states 
and this relationship can be used to estimate the number of jammed states in systems with different size disks 
and also predicts that the average packing density of these systems will approach 0.686 when the total number of jammed states becomes very large. 
This value compares favorably with the maximum packing density, which is around 0.740, 
although this can only be achieved by deforming the shape of individual disks. 
This research is relevant to understanding static configurations in jammed matter and their applications in materials science. 
Ultimately, this approach can be used to study complex systems consisting of various types of particles and their statistical properties in confined spaces. 
This research is also relevant to other fields, such as physics and chemistry, in studying static configurations in inhomogeneous systems consisting of different types of particles. 
This research is the first to explore statistical methods in jammed matter with different types of particles 
and also the first to apply the entropy principle in jammed matter with these types of particles. 
A key feature of this research is that it is purely theoretical and is based on a general approach that can be used in experiments to understand static and dynamic properties in complex systems consisting of different types of particles.

We developed an analytical approach using chromatin accessibility data from DNase-I hypersensitive sites and linked it to genetic variants associated with specific human traits. This approach assembles candidate regions based on the proximity of SNPs to DNase-I hypersensitive sites within relevant cell types, and refines those regions using a Bayesian model that incorporates information about the distribution of genetic variants across the genome. By applying this approach to a comprehensive collection of functional genomic data in multiple cell types, we identified a substantial number of novel candidate regions associated with complex traits. Notably, our results suggest that a significant proportion of these regions contain functional genetic variants that affect gene expression, particularly in cell types related to specific traits. This approach can be adapted to target specific aspects of the genome by integrating various types of functional genomic data, and can be accessed through a public web tool that enables the analysis of SNPs associated with various traits using data from the ENCODE project. Additionally, our results provide a resource for understanding the functional characteristics of genetic variants associated with a wide range of human traits. The combination of functional genomic data and statistical models used in this study can be utilized to build more accurate genetic risk prediction models by integrating the information contained in functional genomic data with the statistical frameworks developed here. The velocity distribution pattern of binary star systems, consisting of large-separation binary systems discovered recently, provides valuable insights into the outskirts of our galaxy and tests gravity's effectiveness at low acceleration rates. We introduce a framework that uses a Galerkin method to solve the stellar dynamics problem under which a binary star system moves within a galaxy's influence. Due to the vast difference in mass between the galaxy and the binary star, we simplify the problem by representing it as a two-point problem in which a binary star's velocity is determined based on its distance from the galaxy's center. We apply the Galerkin method to derive an equation that relates a binary star's velocity and distance to the galaxy's center, and compares our approach with existing work. We also discuss possible applications of our approach to test modified gravity theories and determine the binary star distribution pattern more accurately. 

In modified gravity theories, by assuming that the binary star follows the modified gravity equation, we derive an approximate expression for a binary star's velocity, and compare it with existing data on large-separation binary systems. We also discuss possible implications of our results on testing modified gravity theories in the galaxy's influence at large distances. 

We further simplify our approach by assuming a binary star orbits around a point mass at radius $R$, and apply a Fourier analysis to determine a binary star's velocity, especially at large distances. This approach enables us to efficiently calculate a binary star's velocity at large distances and improves significantly the computational speed. We also discuss possible applications of our approach to determine a binary star distribution pattern more accurately and efficiently. 

Finally, we modify our approach to take into account a binary star's mass and potential mass dispersal, and apply a Fourier analysis to determine a binary star's velocity, especially at large distances. This approach enables us to accurately model a binary star's motion under the galaxy's influence at large distances, and improves significantly the computational speed. We also discuss possible applications of our approach to determine a binary star distribution pattern more accurately and efficiently. 

We also to extend our approach to study the motion of multiple binary star systems within a galaxy's influence, and apply it to test modified gravity theories and determine a binary star distribution pattern more accurately and efficiently. 

In conclusion, we summarize our main results, and discuss future research directions and potential applications of our approach, and highlight the potential benefits and challenges of using our approach to study the motion of multiple binary star systems within a galaxy's influence at large distances.

Current click-through rate (CTR) prediction models are largely dependent on behavior IDs that are easy to manipulate and learn from. However, they struggle with new ads that lack a history of user interactions. To address this limitation, this paper proposes two techniques that can enhance the performance of CTR prediction models when dealing with new ads. First, the method involves incorporating a dense layer that combines key embedding features of an ad, increasing its representational capacity and ability to leverage contextual information. Second, the method involves incorporating a multi-task layer that combines CTR prediction with other tasks such as ad uniqueness, clickability, and clickability consistency. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of these techniques, resulting in improved performance for new ads and a more robust CTR prediction model that can better generalize to new ads. Notably, the proposed techniques achieved an average 7.46% relative improvement in CTR predictions for new ads. Our experimental data showed that the improved performance did not compromise the accuracy of other tasks, with some cases even experiencing enhanced performance. The source code of the proposed techniques is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/ChenXuCheng/Multi-Task-Click-Through-Rate-Prediction. Wildfires disrupting solar energy significantly through atmospheric aerosols,
resulting from diminished solar radiation reaching Earth, can be monitored by
Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD) data streams retrieved from geostationary satellites.
However, multi-source satellite data streams often have varying spatial and
temporal resolutions, necessitating a method to integrate them at a desired level
of these two critical factors. This research presents a framework to dynamically
select the optimal satellite data stream based on predetermined criteria related
to resolution and update rate, allowing for optimal fusion of multiple data
streams. We apply this framework to various satellite data, focusing on AOD fields
from the MODIS and ABATES over the state of California, with analysis spanning
2018-2020. This approach enables seamless fusion of datasets with diverse resolutions
and temporal updates, resulting in a single, continuously updated AOD field map. 
The proposed method offers several benefits, including reduced computational cost,
simplified data management, and a consistent spatio-temporal AOD field dataset. 
This integrated dataset is analyzed to exhibit maximum daily AOD values generated by
wildfires, showing a strong correlation with extreme fire events and highlighting
the potential for the integrated dataset to inform fire risk assessments more
accurately. Moreover, it enables fire-related AOD area calculations with a
higher temporal resolution, allowing for the monitoring of fire progression more
precisely. This integrated dataset can be applied to various applications such as
air quality forecasting, fire propagation modeling, and health risk assessments. 
Ultimately, it provides decision-makers with vital information to assess solar energy
production risks due to wildfires, thereby enabling the implementation of timely
mitigation strategies. 
The proposed framework and wildfire AOD integrated dataset are now available on
GitHub under the repository name 'FusionOfAODFields'. 
Additionally, all results and code used in this research can be accessed via this

Protecting users of location-based services with significant privacy requirements is extremely difficult when multiple locations are shared within a short time frame due to the significant relationships anticipated between these locations. Our proposed R\'enyi divergence based framework measures and bounds expected privacy losses for interrelated data sets, further demonstrated through an algorithm incorporating conditional Gaussian process priors. This framework illustrates the challenges in safeguarding dependent data and provides a strategic approach to maintaining sensitive location data privacy within a specified boundary. Our methodology involves an efficient method for maintaining privacy of new locations shared at any time, incorporating a GP model that adapts in real-time with an incremental learning technique. This framework has been successfully applied to protect the routes of users of a popular bike-sharing service. Our results indicate that the proposed R\'enyi based framework accurately predicts privacy losses, identifies the optimal protection methods, and maintains the privacy of users sharing similar routes while achieving up to $150\%$ better privacy losses compared to conventional methods. Our novel framework resolves the challenge of safeguarding interrelated data and offers a versatile tool for addressing the privacy concerns of users of location-based services sharing similar geographic histories. Our algorithm provides a practical solution for maintaining privacy of new locations shared at any time, representing an advancement in the state of the art in location privacy protection. Our research provides an important contribution to the field of location-based services, offering efficient methods for privacy protection and performance evaluation that can easily be replicated by other researchers. Our methodology has been successfully applied to the routes of users of a popular bike-sharing service, providing novel insights into the state of the art in location-based services. Our results indicate that the proposed R\'enyi based framework accurately predicts privacy losses, identifies the optimal protection methods, and maintains the privacy of users sharing similar routes while achieving up to $150\%$ better privacy losses compared to conventional methods. Our methodology has been successfully applied to the routes of users of a popular bike-sharing service with our findings indicating that a significant percentage of users share similar routes as confirmed by our statistical analysis of actual data. Research has shown that combining resting-state functional MRI data from multiple sites can potentially introduce confounding factors, such as differences in scanner performance. This question investigates the effect of single-site and multisite studies on the power of detecting genuine group differences and identifying false positives using the general linear model. Our analysis suggests that multisite studies generally exhibit lower detection power and increased false positive rates compared to single-site studies, particularly when sites differ significantly. These findings emphasize the importance of considering the impact of varying data acquisition parameters across sites, such as matrix size, rep, and TR. Our research indicates that multisite studies do not offer enhanced statistical inference and can, in fact, compromise the validity of conclusions drawn from those studies. Consequently, we recommend investigating and mitigating site effects to enhance research reliability in multisite rsfMRI investigations. Additionally, our code and simulations are available on GitHub for reproduction.

Building on previous work, where a directed graph equivalent of the Ricci curvature was developed based on the Chung Laplacian, this note focuses on deriving a characterization of our lower Ricci curvature bound by applying a heat semigroup gradient estimate and a heat flow-based transportation inequality. This will serve as the basis for establishing a concentration of measure inequality for directed graphs with positive Ricci curvature. Moreover, our findings in this note can serve as a more general framework than the approach outlined in the paper by Ollivier-Yong, which is based on the oriented Laplacian and specific properties of Euclidean space. 

In order to maintain generality, we did not assume the graph is oriented; instead, we defined the directed graph $G^+$ as a combination of the underlying graph $G$ and a partial orientation $E^+$. We also introduced several equivalent definitions of Ricci curvature and proved that a specific curvature bound implies a concentration of measure, which in turn is related to the concentration of a directed version of the Kantorovitch-Robinson-Svetic inequality. Furthermore, we observed that our model can be applied to various directed graph structures, such as trees and spheres in a directed graph version of a Euclidean space. 

Ultimately, our work aims to establish a fundamental theory of directed graphs with Ricci curvature, which can be used for classification, comparison, and characterization of these graphs. As an example of this, we showed that a directed graph version of the isoperimetric inequality can be derived from a directed version of the Brascamp-Lieb inequality.

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, 
mainly driven by the widespread use of language blending in social media across 
multi-lingual countries such as India, Mexico, Europe, and parts of the USA. 
Given their importance, developing word embeddings for code-mixed languages has 
become a pressing concern. Although prior work in this area focused on creating 
word embeddings for individual languages, the increasing presence of social 
media posts in code-mixed languages necessitates new models to better capture 
their characteristics. In this research, we explore the challenges of creating 
word embeddings for code-mixed texts and analyze the variability in word 
embeddings resulting from different language models, the impact of monolingual 
training data, and the effect of language separation on word positioning. To 
circumvent these issues, we propose a novel unsupervised method for learning 
monolingual and bilingual cross-entropies to map words from a shared latent 
space to their respective monolingual and bilingual sub-spaces. Experimental 
results on XHindi-English and HYiddish-English language combinations demonstrate 
the efficacy of our approach in improving word positioning accuracy and the 
quality of code-mixed word embeddings. These achieveable levels of performance 
are evidenced by our F1-scores comparable to those of recently published 
state-of-the-art supervised models. Additionally, we showcase the utility 
of our code-mixed word embeddings in two valuable NLP tasks, namely, 
code-mixed Sentiment Analysis and Language Identification. In line with 
our research objectives, the proposed method is designed to address three 
key challenges - the scarcity of labeled data, the variability in language 
mixing ratios, and the ambiguity of word position. As a consequence, our 
approach breaks the dependency on labeled data and language separation 
information, thereby expanding the reach of NLP applications to a broader 
category of language combinations and promoting the development of more 
efficient NLP tools for social media platforms in code-mixed contexts. In 
this research, we focus on NLI for HYiddish-English as our primary goal, 
although our primary contribution lies in the transferable unsupervised 
method for learning code-mixed word embeddings applicable to a wide range of 
language combinations including NLI for HYiddish-English. In the longer 
term, we aim to explore NLI for HYiddish-English as a key research area.

Using a combination of density functional calculations and the linearized Migdal-Eliashberg equations with the functional derivative approach, we analyzed how the density of states affects the behavior of H3S under high pressure, specifically in terms of its critical temperature for superconductivity and band dispersion. We established that the critical temperature varies directly with the density of states at the Fermi level and is also dependent on the specific energy range from which electrons are drawn. Moreover, our calculations indicated that H3S's unusual band structure, characterized by complex-shaped Fermi surfaces with both electron and hole properties, arises from the interplay between H-H and S-S interactions. By altering the hydrogen bond under pressure, these Fermi surfaces change in shape, leading to distinct variations in the density of states across different complex-shaped surfaces. Additionally, our calculations showed that the electron-phonon coupling strength grows with pressure but does so non-linearly, and we found no clear correlation between the electron-phonon coupling parameter and the density of states. Instead, the electron-phonon coupling strength is primarily determined by the bonding between hydrogen atoms, and the influence of sulfur-sulfur bonding on this parameter is much weaker. Ultimately, our research reveals the intricate relationships between high pressure, the density of states at the Fermi level, electron-phonon coupling strength, and unusual Fermi surfaces in H3S, providing significant insights into its potential as a high-temperature superconducting material. Moreover, our results also highlight the importance of considering the density of states and electron-phonon coupling under pressure in the search for novel superconductors. Additionally, our methodology and the findings presented here can be applied to the study of other potential high-temperature superconductors, such as hydrogen-rich compounds LH4 (L = Li, Na, Ca, or Al). For example, our calculations indicate that ideal 18-atom supercells of LH4 might be suitable for achieving superconductivity under moderate pressure, although the critical temperature would likely be relatively low (approximately 1 K). In contrast, supercells of 54 H3S atoms in the P4/mmc structure may support high-temperature superconductivity (up to 150 K) within a pressure range of 90 to 200 GPa. Furthermore, our research also shows that replacing S with Se in H3S results in enhanced electron-phonon coupling but slower variation in the critical temperature with pressure, and both the density of states at the Fermi level and electron-phonon coupling strength

This paper presents a unique approach to generating walking patterns for bipedal robots that utilize a parallel drive thruster design, similar to that found in Anymal robots. The intervention strategy developed in this research aims to correct deviations from the desired gait trajectory via transient thruster states, defining the correction force based on an inverse dynamics method employing measured body inertia and estimated center of gravity. The thruster intervention strategy is informed by a walking point strategy that identifies suitable reference states, including optimal stride period and alignment of the hip joint, through analysis of a two-dimensional walking model and a region-based strategy that specifies desired trajectories within specific phases of the gait cycle. The authors propose a simple and systematic method to identify gait phases based on hip joint angle and stride period, enabling the evaluation of the walking state at any given time. This approach is applied to the AnyMal robot to correct deviations during the double-suspension phase and the single-suspension phase, yielding successful results. Moreover, the intervention strategy successfully corrected a significant deviation in hip joint trajectory, allowing the robot to resume walking along the intended trajectory. All experiments were performed on a flat, even surface with gravity set to 0 m/s^2. The efficacy of this correction was verified through the execution of two experiments: the first involved dropping the robot from a height of 2.5 meters, and the second involved pushing it forward at a speed of 2.5 m/s. The successful application of this intervention strategy has implications for the recovery of falling bipedal robots, particularly those with similar bio-inspired designs such as the AnyMal robot. The presented research offers a valuable comparison between its results and those achieved through the continuous control approach used in the development of the Anymal controller. The authors' intervention strategy serves as a more resource-efficient alternative to the continuous control method, requiring only a limited number of thrusters to correct deviations in the gait trajectory. Moreover, the proposed research can be applied to a walking point strategy that identifies suitable states for the hip joint, representing a more conservative approach that ensures stability in bipedal robots. The authors' method for determining gait phases based on the hip joint angle and stride period provides a straightforward solution that requires minimal computational resources. The presented research is crucial in developing corrective strategies for walking patterns, aiming to improve the robustness and reliability of bipedal robots. Moreover, the proposed intervention strategy can be applied to a walking controller that utilizes a hybrid strategy, combining continuous and discrete approaches to achieve greater efficiency and scalability. This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on geometric information derived from 3D surfel mapping. A comprehensive database of places is established, linking visual features to structured 3D environments via global descriptors. By leveraging this framework, we can determine a device's location by matching visual and structural cues even at sites with limited visual landmarks. Our proposed method demonstrates practical applications in robotics and daily life, demonstrated through an integrated relocalization module integrated with a visual inertial odometry algorithm. Extensive outdoor field tests confirm its robust performance under challenging conditions. Our innovative approach differs from conventional methods due to its focus on general-place relocalization, broad application, and simple implementation. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/supernc/VSG.

Decentralized learning technique, federated learning, has a major limitation that remains to achieve optimal performance due to statistical data discrepancies. Overcoming this issue, researchers employ various techniques but they often rely on the assumption that all clients have complete data sets. The reality is that clients have data with missing labels and incomplete knowledge which hinders the training process. Under such circumstances, the local neural network parameters tend to diverge from a common consensus. This research proposes an innovative approach called Sancion, an optimization method that aligns with the objective-iterative Sycal algorithm. Sancion enables optimized communication among clients by exploiting their partial label information during the training process. The Sycal algorithm calculates the gradient at each iteration, resulting in faster convergence and reduced communication frequency. Experimental evaluations on standard image classification datasets demonstrate the exceptional performance of the Sancion system over baseline systems. Furthermore, the codified communication strategy in Sancion reveals its potential to outperform conventional optimization methods even in the absence of partial label information. Simulations of second-long black hole-neutron star mergers in numerical relativity are conducted using a three-moment method for neutron star hydrodynamics. This involves an equation of state compatible with the majority of existing simulations in this field. The reconstruction of neutron star properties and the initial mass distribution after the merger allows for a precise replication of the entire coalescence process, including the formation of a massive accretion disk following the initial disruption of the neutron star. The development of the disk is then governed by the interaction of tidal forces and spiral waves, identical to patterns observed in previous studies. The application of a three-moment method enables simulation of various processes such as the disruption, disk formation, and circulation within the disk, extending the duration to three seconds. The comparison of our results with Alpha-Contact two-shock model predictions shows agreement in terms of disk location, size, and lapse function, although the model overestimates the magnitude of the lapse function. The circulation within the disk is then analysed through the application of vorticity and rotation energy equations in conjunction with a simplified, weakly gravitating disk model. The outcome reveals that circulation patterns observed in our simulations align with those of the model, confirming the influence of spiral arms and the impact of disk boundaries on circulation dynamics. The model also indicates that circulation patterns do not significantly alter from those in high-resolution simulations after three seconds. Furthermore, the model is used to determine the rate of angular momentum transfer and the kinetic energy generated during circulation processes within the disk. The model's accuracy in replicating circulation dynamics and associated processes in high-resolution simulations suggests potential applications in the future, particularly for reducing computational complexity and allowing for longer-duration simulations with existing high-resolution data. The application of a three-moment method in conjunction with the model enables simulation of various processes, ultimately enabling the exploration of circulation dynamics in black hole-neutron star mergers in the future. The outcome of our study also underscores the feasibility of combining the three-moment method with the model to facilitate longer-duration, three-second black hole-neutron star merger simulations extending from coalescence to three seconds. This note primarily focuses on measuring the speed of a conditioned process approaching its quasi-stationary equilibrium under specific assumptions regarding its distribution. In reverse, we establish that a conditioned process converging uniformly to a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process is indeed confined to a finite set of ergodic sub-processes, and under an additional hypothesis of irreducibility, it is proven that the speed of convergence is directly proportional to the rate at which the process's discrete distribution converges. A corollary arising from these findings suggests the applicability of standard renewal arguments in analyzing the long-term frequency of visitation for any set in the state space of a self-conservative, ergodic Markov process. The underlying results are exemplified through the examination of a simple example and comparisons with the approach of [Bricmont, Kupiainen, and Savin (2019)] dealing with interacting particle systems. Additionally, we address an open question posed in that study concerning the equivalence of two distinct measures, and our analysis also extends to the setting of general Markov processes as illustrated by the example of a conditioned Brownian motion on a line segment with inhomogeneous boundary reflections. As a result, the theoretical framework developed here allows for the precise evaluation of the speed of approach to quasi-stationary equilibrium for the aforementioned example as well as for a conditioned relativistic gas. Furthermore, we show that the long-term frequency of visitation for any set in the state space can be precisely evaluated in this context too. Lastly, the concept of a quasi-stationary distribution is adapted to the context of transient Markov processes, and the long-term frequency of visitation for any set in the state space can be precisely evaluated in this context as well. Our current understanding is based on the Heavy Ion Collider Detector at Zero Degree (hadron) by measuring the peripheral collisions of gold ions at 3 GeV. Our findings involve the $M_{AP}$ value, which represents the interaction between the beam's third component of spin and the charge of the particles, found to be within the expectations of background processes that take into account both the electromagnetic and strong interactions. The surge in online fundraising (or "crowdfunding") research focuses on understanding the crowd dynamics that predict the success of crowdfunded projects. Differing from prior studies that concentrated on project characteristics, our analysis takes a more holistic approach by combining project attributes with fundamental tenets of statistical physics from a theoretical and practical standpoint. We developed a classification system using machine learning techniques for fundraising platforms to explore the connections between fundamental properties of crowdfunded projects. We selected the smallest possible units - funders - to build a probabilistic model based on their behavioral patterns and later expanded our analysis to the project level. Our results, derived from the analysis of over 18,000 fundraising projects from Indiegogo and Kickstarter, demonstrate that a project's success is influenced by its fundamental attributes, such as the number of followers and contributors, funds raised per contributor, and the distribution of these funds. These findings highlight the applications of statistical physics in online fundraising platforms and show that the crowd can be viewed as a complex system governed by universal laws. Moreover, our machine learning approach enables the estimation of fundraising periods and predicts project outcomes with high accuracy. We observed a 25% and 20% error margin in predicting failure and success, respectively, which outperformed the baseline forecast. Our Indiegogo-Knowledgebase analysis further sheds light on the connections between fundraising features, influencing factors, and project dynamics. These insights generate new avenues for investigating online dynamics with applications in marketing, business, and physics. With a vast amount of data available online, our study paves the way for numerous related investigations. We anticipate that our research will stimulate an increased focus on crowdfunding platforms from a theoretical and practical standpoint. We plan to extend our work by exploring the following topics: (1) the crowdfunding process as a time-evolving system, (2) the influence of noise on fundraising behavior, (3) the development of a universal law governing the crowd dynamics, and (4) the applications of deep learning algorithms to crowdfunded project classification. These areas of research will undoubtedly yield valuable insights into the complex phenomenon of crowdfunding. As one of the largest data sources, our analysis of Indiegogo and Kickstarter platforms sheds light on the behavior of the crowd and opens doors to various related investigations. We look forward to contributing to the ongoing crowdfunding research with a fresh, physics-inspired and machine learning-based approach. The issue of scheduling a robot's tasks efficiently is a long-established concern in manufacturing. Solutions typically rely on an optimal offline plan, assuming complete and accurate information about task execution times. However, this assumption is invalid for many real-time robotic applications, particularly those using classic planners. This paper presents a new approach, the "Online Cyclic Executive," allowing the reuse of task models to generate efficient, cyclic plans in real-time. This is achieved through a two-phase scheduling strategy, incorporating both the duration of subtasks and their relative frequencies of execution. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the OCE system using a Pioneer3-DX80 robot and a Universal Robot, comparing its performance to the ICST and RCE systems and a random planning method. The OCE system successfully created plans in under 1ms for a DX80 and 50ms for a UR3, with an average execution error rate of 0.01%. Performance comparisons showed the OCE to outperform or match the performance of other systems in terms of execution error rates, with notable improvements of up to 90% and 45% over ICST and RCE, respectively, when using a UR3. The capacity of wireless networks is inherently restricted by interference, and there has been a lack of investigation into the correlation of interference. This research explores the impact of correlated and uncorrelated interference on the minimum local transmission delay in wireless networks, and we have derived exact closed-form formulas for these factors. These findings reveal that the local transmission delay is heavily influenced by the level of correlation, and when interference is completely correlated, it results in a minimum local delay approximately $1/\sqrt{K}$ times the value it would be if interference were completely uncorrelated. Our analysis assumes a noiseless wireless link and that symbols are transmitted sequentially in time or space. We also consider the scenario in which a local transmitter competes against multiple interfering signals, and we have derived exact closed-form formulas for the minimum local delay under both correlated and uncorrelated interference. These findings can serve as key benchmarks in the evaluation of wireless local area networks and gigahertz wireless sensor networks. This knowledge can be utilized to design efficient medium access control protocols by ensuring that the time spent in the medium access control layer is significantly less than the minimum local delay. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, although it tends to exacerbate the class imbalance problem by assigning a disproportionate number of labels to dominant classes. In an attempt to address this limitation, this research proposes the Informative Pseudo-Labeling framework (IPL), consisting of an auxiliary classifier that identifies the most informative pseudo-labels based on uncertainty and the likelihood of proper classification. The IPL framework also incorporates a flexible label weighting system that assigns higher weights to these informative pseudo-labels. Experimental evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets reveal significant improvements in inductive performance and mitigation of imbalance in pseudo-label distribution. The IPL framework is now available for public use at the following repository: https://github.com/jaykim9870/IPL. We present a generic method for analytically determining the steady-state response in a specific type of microwave optomechanics setup. In this setup, a mechanical oscillator functions as a reflexive mechanical mirror within a parallel RLC circuit, accompanied by an optically driven and damped vibratory cavity. The electrical oscillator governs the movement of an end mirror in the cavity, while also influencing the circuit's reactance and impedance. The driven cavity then emits microwaves with varying amplitudes and frequencies, leading to a conversion of energy between electrical and mechanical forms. Our analytical approach utilizes a generalized method to account for back-action and radiation forces acting on the mechanical oscillator, as well as the circuit's non-trivial behavior. The derived equations for average and quadrature components consist of autonomous equations governing the electrical oscillator's amplitude and phase, coupled with a forced oscillator equation with a persistent and periodic driving force related to the cavity's reflexive response. These derived equations effectively recreate the experimentally observed steady-state conditions in this optomechanical system. Additionally, we examine the steady-state behavior in two specific scenarios: a simple transducer optomechanical system and a more complex optomechanical system utilizing multi-stage electron transport. These analyses highlight the utility of our approach in studying various optomechanical phenomena. Due to its broad applicability, this method may be adapted for exploring a wide range of microwave optomechanics setups. Moreover, the derived equations hold significance regardless of whether the electrical oscillator is in a linear or nonlinear regime. The method is expected to be particularly beneficial for identifying the boundaries between linear and nonlinear regimes in optomechanical systems. In a broader context, this analytical approach may find applications in analyzing systems involving forced oscillators and nonlinear energy conversion processes. In this study, we also derive the Fourier transform of the cavity drive and the spectral density of the cavity field, as well as the mechanical and electrical oscillator's responses, utilizing the derived steady-state conditions. This Fourier analysis holds promise for exploring the frequency-domain characteristics of various energy conversion processes. Furthermore, our results may contribute to advancements in the field, potentially leading to improved energy conversion efficiency in the future. In conclusion, the proposed analytical method effectively captures the steady-state behavior in a range of optomechanical systems, as demonstrated through its successful application to two specific examples. The derived equations effectively recreate the observed steady-state conditions in these systems. Due to its broad applicability, this method may be adapted for exploring a wide range of microwave optomechanics setups.

This research explores the dynamics of self-motivated agents moving through a two-dimensional space filled with obstacles, with their behavior influenced by sight, memory, and motivation levels that can be adjusted. Their navigation is straightforward if they have enough motivation, as they seek out gaps in the environment; however, when motivation levels drop below a specific threshold, their movement becomes more complex, causing them to circle and sometimes get stuck near walls, exhibiting patterns of rotation and oscillation that can persist even after they locate gaps for temporary or permanent periods. By altering their memory capabilities, they may recall previous encounters with gaps in the environment, potentially avoiding circles and increasing their overall efficiency. Their navigation is also affected by their field of view, as a wider view can prevent them from getting stuck near walls by detecting gaps sooner, but may not always be beneficial if it incurs extra processing costs. Their movement can be simplified by lowering their memory needs or by ensuring their motivation levels remain above a certain threshold. By comparing their movement to that of a Maier's rat, whose behavior was previously studied in a different context, we observe similar patterns of rotation and can identify the impact of altering their behavioral parameters. In the long run, we present theoretical findings on how their movement and memory usage change over time and verify them using numerical simulations in a wide range of scenarios. To analyze their movement in a more practical context, we propose a quantitative measure of how efficient their navigation is and use this measure to explore the impact of adjusting their sight, motivation levels, or memory requirements. Our numerical simulations show that in most cases, their movement efficiency either increases or remains the same when these parameters are adjusted, and we present graphs illustrating how their efficiency changes as their sight or motivation levels change. As their memory requirements can also affect their interaction with the environment, we explore the impact of adjusting their recall strategy, which might involve forgetting past encounters in order to improve their overall efficiency in a wide range of scenarios. Laparoscopic surgery has limitations due to a narrow field of view. Smoke produced by laser ablation poses a risk to vision, making smoke removal essential during the procedure. We propose an innovative smoke detection technique based on spectral analysis utilizing a low-cost, specially designed endoscope for minimally invasive surgical applications. A comparative study was conducted with current smoke detection methods utilizing a camera to analyze image contrast and entropy. Our proposed method leverages a hyperspectral approach, surpassing the efficacy of the existing method based on image processing. Moreover, the proposed technique accommodates a broader visible spectrum and is resistant to illumination changes, a challenge often faced in surgical settings. Our technique effectively identifies smoke in various settings and demonstrates reliability, making it a suitable option for real-time smoke detection during laparoscopic surgery. Additionally, we outline the potential for adapting this technique into a more advanced, sophisticated system. Our research has been successfully demonstrated through live laser ablation experiments on porcine organs. The presented work serves as a foundation for future advancements in this area, focusing on integrating spectral analysis into a fully functional laparoscopic surgical instrument. We employed advanced simulations to analyze the properties of this material, choosing barium and titanium cation sizes that allow the existence of several general patterns within the structure. We identified four distinct patterns: one corresponding to the material's current paraelectric state, another similar pattern but with a smaller size of the barium cation, and two patterns suitable for modeling larger-sized cations. We explored the material's properties in relation to the size of the barium cation, examining both the structural and dielectric responses. We discovered that replacing smaller barium with larger ones causes the material's structure to compress in the direction perpendicular to the ABO$_3$ plane, while expanding within the plane, ultimately leading to a proportional increase in the material's dielectric constant. Additionally, our research revealed that incorporating larger titanates into the material has a more subtle effect on its structure but can result in a notable enhancement of the material's dielectric response. We have also developed a general strategy for designing more effective titanates, which could lead to breakthroughs in the field of dielectric materials. Our research provides a solid foundation for the design of more advanced materials through computational methods. Existing quantum processors are prone to errors and have limited lifespan due to
imperfect gate operations. To work effectively with these processors, compilers
must optimize programs to run within the device's coherence time, translating them
into the most efficient version possible to extract maximum value from the hardware.
We have developed a new approach to the optimization phase of the quantum algorithm
compilation process. This method utilizes a structured strategy to gradually optimize
programs, dividing the compilation task into distinct phases, each targeting a specific error source, and employing a range of techniques to achieve this. The outcome of our approach compared favourably with the current state-of-the-art compiler, demonstrating improved performance in realistic realistic realistic realistic scenarios based on the NISQ benchmark suite. We have made the source code for our compiler available on GitHub.

A common assumption underpins various advances in randomized methods for optimization: that a given optimization problem has a smooth structure reflected in its Jacobian's distribution. This notion is formalized through a concept called "stochastic subspace complexity," which quantifies how complex the problem is using spectral properties. Research has shown that this idea links to various optimization challenges and solutions, such as Monte Carlo Newton methods and gradient descent in smooth landscapes. Our work explores two main directions. Firstly, we broaden the definition of stochastic subspace complexity to encompass non-uniform distributions and prove an optimality bound for Monte Carlo Newton, independent of coherence. Secondly, we establish a lower bound on complexity for gradient descent in non-smooth landscapes and identify an optimality condition for using O($\log T$)-regret gradient descent as a near-optimal method for certain optimization tasks. Our work is the first to analyze gradient descent in non-smooth landscapes using a spectral approach and offers the first lower bounds on complexity for optimization problems using sharp tools, bridging a significant gap in understanding between spectral theory and optimization theory. Additionally, our research reveals an unexpected connection between complexity and the concentration of eigenvalues, contributing to the development of spectral interpolation techniques. Lastly, our findings suggest numerous future research directions and open problems, including investigating the performance of non-conjugate optimization methods, exploring the connection between complexity and statistical estimation, and broadening the scope of stochastic subspace complexity to cover optimization problems with constraints. One promising direction is to apply our theory to understand the success of non-smooth optimization in neural network training and to investigate the role of spectral properties in statistical estimation using tools from random matrix theory. Another area of exploration is to utilize our definition of stochastic subspace complexity to derive performance guarantees for optimization methods, including gradient descent on neural network landscapes and semi-supervised estimation in machine learning. By leveraging the power of spectral approximation, our goal is to achieve new levels of performance in these critical applications, ultimately hoping to derive efficient algorithms from a spectral perspective. To conclude, our research offers an innovative spectral perspective on optimization, linking the performance of optimization methods to the spectral properties of the problem via its distribution. This unique viewpoint opens doors for exciting future research in both optimization and statistical learning theory. As a testament to the versatility of our theory, several promising research directions are presented, including understanding the role of spectral approximation in optimization and data analysis, exploring the connection between complexity and estimation, and broadening the scope of stochastic subspace complexity to cover optimization with constraints. A crucial property of biexcitons is their binding energy, which determines whether they are stable entities. We demonstrate that the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms is limited under the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis for a specific degree 8 L-function. This is achieved by leveraging Watson's formula, which allows us to recast our investigation as a tractable problem related to L-functions, ultimately facilitating the application of Soundararajan and Harper's methods for deriving sharp bounds on the moments of the Riemann zeta function. Our result is further refined by providing explicit estimates for the case of weight 2 and level 1, and we show that this is a refinement of a previous finding by Weissman. Additionally, we offer support for a broader conjecture regarding the moment sequences of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms by establishing that the conjectured bounds are indeed limited, though the rates of decay are significantly slower than anticipated. The implications of our analysis extend to the fourth moment of Dirichlet L-functions, a result previously obtained by Harper under the assumption of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative method is employed to solve a linear equation system, speeding up convergence often involves developing optimal preconditioners for the linear solver. However, standard termination criteria for the solver frequently cause excessive 'oversolving' by insisting on sufficient residual reductions. This paper presents an alternative approach to interior point methods that utilizes an inner termination criterion not dependent on the residual, as well as indicators for premature inner iteration cessation informed by IPM demands. It also modifies this criterion to accommodate Conjugate Gradient and Minimum Residual algorithms, and demonstrates the resulting enhancement yields substantial performance improvements in computational testing, particularly for large-scale problems. The largest tested improvements were factors of 2 to 4 in time savings, and such gains could reasonably be expected in practical applications. Additionally, this enhancement aligns the solver termination behavior with the termination logic of the IPM it supports. Furthermore, the proposed approach shows potential for applicability across a broad range of iterative methods and termination strategies. These specifications can be operational, rule-based, or a combination of both. For example, in the medical field, a treatment guideline might be specified using rule-based conditions (e.g., patient symptoms, medication effects) and operational constraints (e.g., doctor-workload, hospital-capacity). Due to the unpredictability of these factors, guidelines cannot guarantee a successful outcome, but they can ensure optimal results in most cases. We propose a new approach to online process instance checking against hybrid process specifications, allowing for both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. Our solution acknowledges that specifications may contain inconsistencies and provides a useful debugging tool. This testing method can identify a portion of the guideline as inconsistent, marking it as potentially flawed. Furthermore, our method can verify the correctness of process instances in relation to their specifications. We have developed a prototype tool to demonstrate our approach, utilizing the Kiroll language for hybrid specifications and the Kiroll for negative and positive regular path expressions used in online process checking. Assembling a complete genome from short, overlapping DNA sequences is a critical yet computationally complex task within the genomics pipeline. Due to the vast size of genomes in relation to their sequence components and the presence of paralogous regions that confuse algorithms, accurately reconstructing a complete and chromosomal structure genome has long been a challenge. Most current genome assemblers utilize graph representations to tackle this issue, but the incorporation of additional sequencing technologies such as long-reads, supplementary information like gene annotations, and third-generation sequencing protocols like PacBio and BioNano have not been effectively integrated into existing algorithms. Our research introduces a new, dynamic graph-based approach that effectively incorporates all the aforementioned inputs to create an optimal assembly. By employing a recursive within-scaffold assembly strategy and leveraging a dynamic graph with diverse node types, weights, and annotations, our method surpasses leading genome assemblers such as Canu, FALCON, and WGS in terms of accuracy across multiple species, including human, mouse, and fruit fly. Additionally, our approach excels in using the minimum number of sequences to represent genomic structures, outperforming leading assemblers in sequence compression across the tested species. Comprehensive evaluations and simulations validate the robustness and scalability of our method, indicating its potential to efficiently handle large and complex genomes. Our method's source code is available for public use at https://github.com/aliot/ADG. Further information on the approach and experimental results can be found in the accompanying technical report at https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.11581. Our method's performance in genome assembly is presented in the supplementary materials provided at https://aliot.github.io/ADG-Performance.html.

This technique allowed them to analyze the isotope's hyperfine structure in a gas-like state, providing precise measurements of its magnetic and quadrupole moments. Newly calculated values reveal a quadrupole moment of $-0.0412(12)$ $b$ and a significant adjustment to the previously estimated magnetic moment. This study also produced the most accurate magnetic and quadrupole moment measurements for $^{69}$Ge to date. The new measurements will contribute to a deeper understanding of the Ge nucleus and its applications, particularly in the context of neutrinoless double-beta decay experiments. A precise knowledge of the nuclear matrix elements is essential for successfully executing such experiments. Finally, researchers calculated the isospin-dependent nuclear radius of $^{69}$Ge with a margin of error. This value is primarily influenced by the nuclear deformation and the short-range characteristics of the nuclear interaction. If further study confirms substantial influence from the nuclear deformation, then $^{69}$Ge could serve as an exemplary case for investigating the relationship between nuclear deformation and the complex characteristics of the nuclear interaction. This investigation may also be used to determine the nuclear deformation in Ge isotopes through the comparison of their isospin-dependent nuclear radii. That information, in turn, could facilitate the calculation of the nuclear deformation in more heavily damped heavy-ion systems. Given its unique properties and potential for future significance, $^{69}$Ge may play a pivotal role in the ongoing quest to understand the characteristics of the nuclear interaction. This could lead to significant breakthroughs in the broader fields of nuclear physics and related research. We aim to enhance the accuracy of structured text recognition by combining two key techniques: lexicon-guided decoding and the use of regular expressions. Our method involves modifying a lexicon-based beam search decoder to accommodate regexes in both the generation of initial candidate words and the calculation of word probabilities. In the former step, we use a pre-computed hash table to quickly identify potential matches between the text and available words in the lexicon. In the latter step, the decoder calculates a probability score for each proposed word by applying a regex to the text and leveraging a glyph frequency dictionary. Our approach demonstrates significant improvements in recognition accuracy across a range of error metrics and achieves up to a 7.0% character error rate on the IRONYouE dataset. Furthermore, we provide detailed analysis and optimization strategies for the proposed method. Our code and dataset are publicly available for reproduction purposes.

Analyzing 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of LHC data recorded at 13 TeV, the researchers observed signals exceeding the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis. Calculations based on quantum chromodynamics predicted this rare event to occur at a rate of 34 fb, with the measured data aligning closely with these predictions. By manipulating the invariant mass of the top quark pair, the researchers were able to accurately match observed data to theoretical predictions. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, we propose a novel dual-column pre-training model, DualCTC. This model combines two long-form inputs in the self-supervision of not only sequence length but also column-wise. Additionally, we introduce two separate pre-training objectives, DiagonalMaskReconstruction and WordMaskReconstruction, under the framework of DualCTC to ensure our model's effectiveness generalizes across diverse datasets. Experiments on the Spider dataset reveal that our method surpasses the current best approach by a significant 4.0msp. We have also achieved a new state-of-the-art result of 72.2% on the Spider test server, outperforming the previous best performance of 70.1%. Quantum systems lacking energy-momentum uncertainty are examined in conjunction with an initial state and an arbitrary final state. A specific functional, encompassing both average arithmetic and logarithmic entropy changes, is analyzed. We demonstrate the convexity of this functional in relation to its maximum values, achieved through optimal quenches, thereby validating previously proposed quenches as global optimality protocols for minimizing the functional. Furthermore, we show that reducing a distinct entropy quantity, derived from the quantum Fisher information, is a necessary condition for minimizing the functional. By numerically comparing quenches, we identify which ones are closest to achieving the minimal functional value. In systems comprising multiple non-interacting fermions or bosons, a specific optimal quench was found, resulting in a 25% enhancement of the minimal functional value when compared to a previously proposed protocol by Kyung et al. [Phys. Rev. Research 2, 0239 (2020)]. Additionally, we explore the feasibility of generalizing our results to systems in thermal equilibrium. In this context, we prove a distinct inequality, involving the relative entropy, which implies that the optimal quenches previously determined are also globally optimal when calculating entropy changes based on arithmetic and logarithmic increments. This inequality is expected to be precise in systems devoid of energy-momentum uncertainty. Generalizing our results to systems in thermal equilibrium remains a subject for future investigation. Polynomial-time reduction methods, referred to as kernelization algorithms, reduce large problem instances to more manageable sizes. Specifically, d-reduction algorithms limit the size of a given instance to at most d sub-problems. A more restrictive type of algorithm, known as PTAS, allows the size of the reduced instance to decrease significantly (by a constant factor) for any fixed epsilon greater than zero. In the context of parameterized complexity theory, PTAS algorithms are seen as more desirable due to their ability to handle any fixed parameter values efficiently. While PTAS reductions may not always be feasible, the theory includes parameter-free versions that can handle any parameter values efficiently. Specifically, for any fixed epsilon greater than zero, PTAS algorithms can be derived from d-reduction algorithms with relatively large epsilon values, albeit with potentially large d-values. The PTAS-hierarchy conjecture hypothesizes that there exists a PTAS algorithm for Cyclic HOMO-GENOM, a problem considered harder than other fixed-parameter tractable targets, such as Cyclic H-COLORING. If proven, the PTAS-hierarchy conjecture would imply the infeasibility of PTAS reductions with relatively large epsilon values and relatively small d-values. This research explores how opinions are shaped and social connections evolve in a complex system. We consider a population where individuals interact with each other through localized relationships, forming new opinions based on their limited confidence in the views of their close friends. Meanwhile, these friends may break up with one another, creating an ever-changing social landscape. Through the use of agent-based modeling, we simulate this intricate social system, leading to the observation of intriguing patterns within the population's opinion dynamics. Ultimately, our analysis reveals an interesting balance between the tendency for opinions to become deeply polarized and the maintenance of relative political balance in the system. The presentation highlights how the break-up of social connections among friends contributes to the development of these unique features. The goal of this work is to shed light on the fundamental mechanisms underlying the fragile coexistence of opposing views in a society of interacting agents. The presented framework has the potential to be applied to the study of a wide range of social phenomena, including the analysis of election campaigns, political divisions, and cultural differences. The approach taken in this research is versatile, allowing it to be used to investigate various types of localized interactions among agents, including those governed by different rules. The study of the social system explored here serves as a starting point for the exploration of more comprehensive networks of relationships. The methodology employed is similarly adaptable, with the potential to be applied to the study of a wide range of social interactions, interactions between species, and other types of complex agent-based models. We've investigated a newly constructed series of asymptotically flat, electrically charged black holes that form scalar "hair" when their charge increases at a fixed mass. Inside the event horizon, these black holes resemble a holographic liquid, exhibiting similar radial profiles for their scalar fields, phonon-like dispersion relations for their quasinormal modes, and Cauchy surface scalar field boundary values that follow a specific pattern as the charge increases. Additionally, we've found that the stability of these black holes improves as the charge increases, and our analysis also shows that the presence of scalar hair causes the area of the black hole horizon to decrease. Our findings are consistent with a broader theory predicting that more massive black holes are less stable and have smaller sizes. We've further extended our research to include rotating black holes and discovered that, in addition to the previously observed characteristics, they also exhibit axial dependencies in their scalar profiles and Cauchy surface boundary data, as well as rotational Hamiltonians that depend on the scalar field. Furthermore, we've found that the event horizon of these rotating black holes spreads due to rotational effects and that the presence of scalar hair causes it to decrease. Our investigation has also revealed that the instability of these charged rotating black holes improves with rotational and scalar effects, and that the area of the event horizon decreases due to these effects. Lastly, we've explored the properties of causally interacting black holes and discovered that their scalar hair causes the area of the event horizon to decrease, even when their charge and mass are fixed. Our study has potentially far-reaching implications for our understanding of the behavior of scalar fields in the vicinity of black holes and the interactions of causally connected black holes. Moreover, it may be possible to verify our theoretical predictions through observations of the characteristics of microstate black holes and the interactions of accreting or black hole neptune systems. Different genes exhibiting similar activation patterns may show distinct mRNA expression levels at different time points due to variations in transcription duration, RNA breakdown speed, and processing rates. The impact of RNA splicing on delaying mRNA production cannot be ignored. We developed a model combining transcription dynamics and RNA accumulation to estimate the rates of transcription, RNA breakdown, and processing delay based on full transcript and mature mRNA sequencing data.
