Chiral SU(N) gauge theories, consisting of Weyl fermions and additional fermions that allow for fermion-fermion gauge boson couplings, can't be fully understood using lattice Monte Carlo simulations due to sign problems that arise from these interactions. However, theories with Weyl fermions have unique properties that allow for comparing lattice simulations to theoretical predictions. We've derived lattice formulations for SU(N) theories with an odd number of Weyl fermions and calculated chiral and mixed 't Hooft anomalies. These results demonstrate that anomaly matching can be used to determine if lattice simulations in lower dimensions accurately represent the behavior in higher dimensional space-time. We applied this to an SU(N) theory with three Weyl fermions in two dimensions and found that lattice simulations with an even number of fermions in a specific channel doesn't consistently match the theoretical predictions. However, theory predicts that anomalies can be matched by introducing an infrared fermion bilinear that breaks chiral symmetry, indicating that this is a necessary condition for our 't Hooft anomalies matching to hold. We also discovered that the mixed gauge and chiral 't Hooft anomalies can be matched by introducing a specific density-density correlation interaction on the lattice. As a result, this theory can be formulated using a local lattice model that doesn't exhibit sign problems in the far infrared and has the same degeneracy pattern as the continuum theory. Our findings suggest the potential use of density-density interactions to remove sign problems in lattice Monte Carlo simulations of chiral SU(N) gauge theories. We've also explored this approach in the SU(N) theory with three Weyl fermions in two dimensions and simulated it using a local lattice model that doesn't have sign problems. This allowed us to study the interplay between gauge bosons and Weyl fermions as they form composite fermions and eventually switch from one phase of matter to another. We've examined the distribution of carmenic in the interphase and found it to be symmetrical. Our research on this subject is ongoing and will be reported elsewhere. To our knowledge, this is the first time anyone has successfully removed sign problems in lattice Monte Carlo simulations of chiral SU(N) gauge theories using a local lattice model. We believe our findings will contribute to the ongoing debate in the field and may lead to breakthroughs in our understanding of Yang-Mills theories and gauge-mediated supersymmetry breaking. A linear complementary pair of group codes $(C, D)$ is formed when the direct sum of $C$ and $D$ results in the entire group algebra $R[G]$, given a finite principal ideal ring $R$ and a finite group $G$. We identify a required and confirming criterion for pairs of group codes $(C, D)$ in group algebra $R[G]$ to be a linear complementary pair, subsequently proving the equivalence in terms of permutations between codes $C$ and the dual code $D^{\perp}$. Under specific conditions, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for group codes $(C, D)$ to be a linear complementary pair, providing a constructive approach that can be applied when codes $C$ and $D$ share a common dimension. Additionally, we extend the concept of linear complementary pairs to group codes over stochastic group algebra $\mathbb{Q}[G]$ and develop corresponding criteria. Our study further explores examples of linear complementary pairs achieved through specific code constructions for different combinations of groups $G$ and principal ideal rings $R$. The ability to find objects visually or auditorily in a 3D space is a critical capability that underpins many real-world applications, such as search and rescue operations, navigation assistance, and robotic object detection. In this research paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages a wave propagation simulation to efficiently model acoustic propagation and object reflection. This method allows for precise mapping of sound waves in three dimensions and identifies the source location based on the pattern of these waves. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach is effective in locating objects visually and auditorily within a complex environment. We achieve an average error of less than 2 cm when the distance between the source and the sensor is less than 1.5 meters. Moreover, our approach has a significantly faster runtime compared to traditional optimization-based methods. While these methods take around 180 milliseconds to accurate object localization, our approach can do so in as little as 20 milliseconds. This research offers a foundation for developing more effective multisensory systems that integrate visual and auditory cues to enhance object localization in complex 3D environments. of light. We achieve this through the application of a suitable 'pre-non-
relativistic' geometrical parametrization, thereby facilitating an
analytical $1/c^2$ expansion of general relativity. Ultimately, this method
permits an in-depth examination of the Einstein-Hilbert action expansion up to
its next-to-next-to-leading order. Additionally, we briefly illustrate how
this expansion can be applied in the context of branes. Furthermore, we derive
a non-relativistic Hamiltonian from the action, demonstrating how the $1/c^2$
expansion contributes to the formation of solitonic black holes. Lastly, we
investigate how the $1/c^2$ expansion influences gravitational waves and their impact on the conservation of the energy-momentum four-vector; interestingly, this effect can be observed at large distances, potentially even exceeding the reach of current telescopes. This research proposes a unique framework that leverages the concept of odd-spaces from 3D geometry to develop image features that can't be easily reversed. The framework relies on the robustness of its image descriptors to arbitrary distortions found in 3D objects, providing a reliable basis for common image recognition tasks such as registration, filtering, and matching. The framework's performance was tested in a practical 3D classification scenario, demonstrating its capability to produce reliable results even with minimal and noisy data. The developed image features exhibit a natural invariance to pose and distance distortions, ultimately leading to improved data efficiency and image filtering performance. Moreover, we present a novel application where our image descriptors help maintain the integrity of a classifier's accuracy even when the data is subjected to significant shape deformations due to split-merge operations. The proposed framework significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving a 5-10% gain in accuracy using filtered point clouds that are automatically generated from noisy 3D data. Moreover, we validate our approach by demonstrating its robustness against a wide range of shape deformations through the manipulation of input geometry. As an extension to this work, we present an innovative 3D reidentification method that employs our image features to identify and distinguish shape fragments. These observations confirm an 89-day eclipse cycle, which is equivalent to the binary's orbital period. In numerous machine learning applications, the adoption of global pooling (GP) units has been witnessed within multiple deep learning architectures. These units summarize the data fed into them by aggregating the information from every position within the input data structure, such as images, and producing a single output vector that represents the overall characteristics of the input data. This summary is then used to generate output predictions during the training process. We have delved into the theoretical underpinnings of GP units and discovered that their ability to make accurate predictions relies heavily on the characteristics of the training data rather than the architecture of the model. Additionally, the effectiveness of GP units is hindered by the inclusion of spatial convolutional layers in the architecture, and we have found that replacing them with GP units does not yield improved performance. However, replacing GP units with spatial convolutional layers does yield improved performance in certain scenarios. Our experimental framework consists of three different datasets, including the CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and MNIST datasets, and our results validate the consistency of our findings across the various datasets. Our research suggests that the decision to use GP units or spatial convolutional layers should be based on the nature of the data rather than a predetermined assumption. We propose an alternative method called the GP-CNN, also referred to as the Mungan architecture, in which GP units are combined with spatial convolutional layers in a way that allows the model to make accurate predictions of the output class without referencing spatial information. Our experiments have shown that the Mungan architecture outperforms the baseline CNN in classification tasks, and our analysis has shed light on the benefits of combining GP units with spatial convolutional layers in deep learning models. The primary objective of this research is to examine the optical properties of Type 1 Seyfert galaxies. In total, 39 Type 1 Seyfert galaxies were identified within a $1.5^{\circ}$ radius of 19 extragalactic narrow-line emitters observed by the ZTF survey, and a subset of 17 of these were found to have matching optical spectra. Analysis of their spectral features and broad-band optical colors reveal specific patterns for these active galaxies, and our data show that elliptical galaxies cannot account for the narrow-line emitters' spectral data. Instead, our results indicate that Type 1 Seyfert galaxies are more likely to be found in spiral or irregular galaxies. Furthermore, by utilizing the 2MASS, Pan-STARRS1, and Gaia DR3 data, we were able to analyze the morphological characteristics of these active galaxies and explore their scaling relations. Notably, our study finds that the mass-metallicity relation of these active galaxies matches that of non-active galaxies, but with a distinct shift towards higher masses. Additionally, our data suggest that the relationship between black hole mass and bulge mass for these active galaxies aligns with that of non-active galaxies, and we propose that the broad-line emitters may be associated with the extended mass distribution of these galaxies. Based on these findings, it appears that the broad-line emitters' jet power only plays a significant role in shaping their 1.3 keV X-ray luminosity at very high X-ray luminosity levels. Finally, our data show that there is a significant correlation between the broad-line emitters' radio luminosity and their host galaxy's stellar mass, but with a notable anomaly at higher radio luminosity levels that requires further explanation. Overall, our research suggests that there is a strong connection between the active galaxies in our study and the broader population of active galaxies observed in the local universe. Additionally, our data in the $3.4\mu$m magnitude from Gaia DR3 enable us to monitor the variability of these active galaxies at near-infrared wavelengths, and our findings indicate that there is a positive correlation between near-infrared and soft X-ray variability, and that these active galaxies can be classified into two sub-classes based on their variability characteristics. The positive correlation between near-infrared and soft X-ray variability suggests that these two wavelengths are related through the same physical process, and that variability in the near-infrared can serve as an effective alternative to monitoring the active galaxies in the soft X-ray band. Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires extensive ground truth data and can be labor-intensive. Previous research showed promising results by using unsupervised learning from video data to obtain effective prior knowledge for the segmentation task. In this study, we explore the effectiveness of unsupervised learned representations by leveraging only video data for pre-training and demonstrate improved performance on several benchmark datasets. Notably, our findings reveal that incorporating depth estimation alongside unsupervised contrastive learning leads to enhanced performance in semantic segmentation, surpassing the performance of conventional supervised segmentation methods. We attribute this improvement to the unique challenge of predicting depth and object categories simultaneously, resulting in more robust video prior knowledge that can be transferred to the segmentation task. Our code and pre-trained models are publicly available on GitHub. Experimental results on multiple datasets indicate that our method consistently outperforms other state-of-the-art methods, with a notable enhancement of almost 5% mIoU on the ADE20K dataset. Our method is particularly effective when only a few labeled samples are available for the segmentation task. Moreover, its efficacy extends to segmentation tasks involving video sequences, demonstrating improved performance over other leading approaches. In addition to improving segmentation performance, our method is versatile and can be adapted to other low-level vision tasks. We thoroughly analyzed the unsupervised representations learned by our method and found that they effectively capture geometric and shape information, contributing to their effectiveness. Our method is an innovative approach to exploiting video data for segmentation purposes, underscoring the significance of unsupervised learning in automated image and video understanding. Moreover, its applicability to a wide range of tasks, including depth estimation, makes it an invaluable resource for image and video enhancement applications. Based on these findings, we propose potential research directions focusing on improving segmentation using geometric information, transferring unsupervised learned representations across domains, and exploring new applications of depth estimation, shape estimation, and semantic segmentation. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the rapid advancement of image and video understanding through unsupervised learning. To this end, our method is an important milestone, paving the way for the automated acquisition of prior knowledge for image and video interpretation. As a consequence, we anticipate that our method will facilitate a shift from labor-intensive image annotation to efficient, automated video analysis prior to the segmentations, making it more viable. The ability to create complex, engaging stories about the characteristics and behaviors of time-series data is highly valuable in fields like geology, meteorology, epidemiology, finance, stock market analysis, and sales forecasting. Current approaches to time-series narration often rely on descriptive narratives, using simple comparisons and basic logic to draw from a limited knowledge base about the characteristics of the data. We introduce TCube, an innovative framework for time-series narration that leverages a rich set of context-specific rules to dynamically create stories about the data properties. The rules in TCube are based on a thorough examination of the time domains in which the time series are set, and they are derived from a comprehensive understanding of the domain-specific attributes and events. We illustrate the effectiveness of TCube by applying it to scenarios in the fields of geology and meteorology, and we show that TCube's stories about the data are significantly more detailed and nuanced than what would be possible with simply labeling the time periods in which the data are set. Furthermore, the stories generated by TCube are an order of magnitude longer than those produced by other methods, and they offer a level of depth and complexity that current approaches to time-series narration simply can't match. On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation. These measures have explicable connections to the previously discovered 'double-circle' probability amplitudes found in the quantum Ising model. We also establish a relationship between our findings of periodic measures and the set of periodic Gibbs measures observed in the quantum Ising model on the same graph. Notably, this set is empty when the model is parameterized in a specific way, yet our analysis reveals the discovery of unique'semicircle' probability amplitudes. Finally, we extend our analysis to the context of spin lattices by examining the Ising model on a specific type of graph known as the 'flower graph'. The results obtained from this analysis are then discussed.

This study explores the long-term behavior of solutions to strictly hyperbolic equations, where the coefficients exhibit a mild blow-up near the origin. We demonstrate that in this scenario, solutions display an attractive equilibrium in a specific polynomial space, along with an attractive manifold defined by a logarithmic blow-up near the origin. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between the growth rate of coefficients and the properties of solutions, as the main blow-up time approaches the age of the universe. Additionally, we incorporate an approach utilizing the Lippmann-Schwinger type of integral equations to analyze the high-frequency asymptotic behavior of solutions. This investigation is particularly relevant to the high-frequency linear scalar hyperbolic type equations. Crucially, our findings apply to a wide range of functions that may not be smooth near the origin. The key to our success lies in the application of the Redheffer differentiation property and the construction of a suitable Green function for the associated model problem. Upon completion of the current research, it became evident that the constructed Green function possesses an intrinsic value and could likely be applied to various other problems, potentially including nonlinear equations. However, an in-depth exploration of its implications and applications remains a subject for future research. As an extension of the current study, we also explore and implement an iterative method for corresponding nonlinear equations, leveraging the unique behavior observed in the strictly hyperbolic equation context. This approach appears to be novel and pure, and as such, it requires further mathematical analysis to assess its convergence and effectiveness. Ultimately, our findings suggest that solutions to the given equation may be more smooth than initially assumed, potentially up to a degree equivalent to the negative of the dimension multiplied by 0.5. This research introduces a novel application of the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to tackle the challenging task of Japanese word segmentation. Building on previous breakthroughs in Chinese word segmentation using LSTM and GRU, this study tackles the more complex task of Japanese word segmentation which involves various character types such as hiragana, katakana, and kanji. These characters lead to significant orthographic variations and increase the difficulty of accurately segmenting Japanese words. To address this complexity, this study proposes an LSTM-based model for Japanese word segmentation, taking into consideration the essential global context. Experimental outcomes confirm that the proposed model attains exceptional accuracy when evaluated across different Japanese corpora. Furthermore, this study also explores various pre-training strategies utilizing the widely-used Wikipedia dataset. Interestingly, these pre-training experiments yield substantial enhancements in segmentation performance, highlighting the valuable contribution of unsupervised data in enhancing Japanese word segmentation capabilities. Moreover, this study delves into the critical role of character embeddings in Japanese word segmentation, investigating how different designs of character representations affect the overall performance of the model. Furthermore, this study also applies the proposed Japanese word segmentation model to related tasks like Japanese part-of-speech tagging, thereby doubling the utility of this powerful tool. Experiment outcomes confirm the efficacy of this tool across both single-word and multi-word scenarios. Lastly, this study implements and distributes a publicly accessible code base for the proposed Japanese word segmentation model, catering to the needs of researchers and practitioners working in the area of Natural Language Processing for the Japanese language. On the Stack Overflow platform, users utilize 11,926,354 external connections to share relevant off-site information, augmenting the existing knowledge base. This collaborative effort enables improved question answering, yet raises concerns regarding the potential for malicious intent, such as spamming. To determine a user's likelihood of engaging in undesirable activities, we employ a supervised machine learning approach, applying a comprehensive set of features to classify users based on their link sharing behavior. Our findings reveal that a significant majority, 99.9%, of external links shared on Stack Overflow originate from a limited set of popular websites. We develop a classification system combining user and question characteristics to predict the probability of a user engaging in spamming, duplicate answering, or other undesirable activities. In contrast to existing research focusing solely on user features, we incorporate question metadata as key performance indicators to mitigate classification bias. Our proposed framework yields impressive classification accuracy for spamming (94%), duplicate answering (88%), and off-topic content (85%), using ten times more positive samples than negative samples. This approach provides a versatile framework for detecting undesirable activities within knowledge-sharing platforms. In addition, our research highlights several takeaways for informing policy decisions, empowering moderators to effectively identify and block harmful content. Finally, our analysis offers actionable insights for improving user engagement through targeted engagement campaigns. Galactic rotation curves show a range of varying inner slopes. We compare two cosmological models, one with cold dark matter and another featuring self-interacting dark matter, to their respective predictions based on observations of rotation curves and baryonic feedback processes such as supernovae and stellar winds. For a self-interacting dark matter model, we utilize data from the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope's predicted photometry, to assess its cross-section between 0.1 and 10 GeV. The findings indicate that a self-interacting dark matter model is more sensitive to baryonic feedback than its cold dark matter counterpart, with a cross-section ranging from 0.01 to 0.1 cm^2/kg, assuming a trust radius of 10 kiloparsecs. Moreover, a self-interacting dark matter model is capable of accommodating a range of dark matter densities, from 0.2 to 0.8 times the critical value, without conflict. In contrast, a cold dark matter model is primarily limited by the density within the innermost 10% of a galaxy, particularly for more luminous galaxies. Ultimately, a self-interacting dark matter model offers a more comprehensive solution to galactic dark matter, one that is compatible with observations of small-scale structures and galaxy rotations, as well as theoretical limitations on baryonic feedback. Additionally, such a model is consistent with nucleosynthesis constraints on dark matter, leaving room for additional non-thermal production mechanisms. Finally, a self-interacting dark matter model remains a viable candidate for addressing cosmological and astrophysical dark matter, one that may be further validated by future observations of galaxy surveys, stellar dynamics, and direct dark matter detection experiments.

Clinical symptoms recorded in unstructured doctor's notes are inaccessible for further use.
This problem can be resolved by using information extraction techniques capable of adapting to different medical settings and professionals. 
In this research, we address the issue of extracting symptoms by using pre-trained and fine-tuned models, trained on diverse patient data, medical institutions, and specific conditions. 
Our models utilize pre-trained transformer architectures, including RoBERTa and BERT, and evaluate various data augmentation methods to enhance model performance and adaptability. 
The models are evaluated on a multi-center dataset containing over 50,000 patient records from three different hospitals, and our results indicate that pre-training and dataset-specific fine-tuning yield superior outcomes compared to other training and evaluation methods. 
Furthermore, our experiments reveal that a specific augmentation technique and method of adapting models to new data can effectively recognize known symptoms and discover new ones. 
This research offers insights on effectively using pre-trained models for extracting symptoms from clinical notes in diverse settings and promotes the use of informed thresholds to determine model reliability.

In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, necessitating novel approaches for mitigation. Recent proposals, rooted in concepts such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption, often come at a cost of significant computational overhead, rendering them unsuitable for practical application. This work presents an alternative solution by harnessing the capabilities of Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard data and model interactions, specifically introducing Flatee: an efficient federated learning framework across these environments, that substantially minimizes both communication and computation burdens. Flatee relies on TEEs to safeguard data and relies on differential privacy to strictly limit potential information leaks, resulting in a substantial reduction in overhead compared to existing solutions. Flatee's performance evaluation demonstrates substantial improvements over state-of-the-art solutions, achieving an average speedup of 10 times in communication cost and 20 times in computational cost. Experimentation with the framework, involving training a convolutional neural network for CIFAR-10 classification, shows its suitability for real-world applications, including federated learning in mobile privacy and with image recognition tasks. This paper introduces Timeloops, an execution environment monitor specifically designed to boost the performance of microservices applications. Timeloops complements traditional static analysis methods, which are prone to errors and miss necessary system calls due to the difficulty in identifying all possible program paths during analysis. In contrast, Timeloops learns a reliable filter for system calls on the fly as it runs in real-time, making it ideal for complex microservices applications. Our research involves creating a suitable training protocol for Timeloops' machine learning-based system call filter, and our results demonstrate that Timeloops surpasses static analysis methods in system call filtering efficiency, particularly for complex microservices applications. Additionally, Timeloops provides transparent system call access, allowing for easy development and testing of system calls, as well as the integration of third-party APIs. Furthermore, the training protocol for Timeloops determines the optimal training duration, training frequency, and training window size, which significantly impact performance; and our investigation into the effects of noisy training data reveals strategies for mitigating its influence on filtering performance. As a bonus, our research into the effects of noisy training data offers a valuable reference for other microservice architecture studies. This paper bridges the gap between compressed sensing and statistical learning, leveraging sparsity and structure to minimize computational burden in learning tasks. We demonstrate how to derive efficient, compressive algorithms within the framework of stochastic gradient descent by capitalizing on the sparse nature of signals and structured matrices, thereby obtaining faster convergence rates. Our findings encompass situations involving correlated data, structured bases, and matrix completion with entries drawn from a low-dispersion distribution. To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes random species assignment at each lattice site and a rule for species competition that favors one species over another in occupied sites. Focusing on the torus, we demonstrate that the von Neumann algebras generated by three or two fusion operators of higher rank have infinite type $II$ and non-hyperfinite, respectively. It's proven that the uniqueness of the ground state in abelian quantum double models is preserved under local operations, providing the region's boundary is sufficiently smooth. This is shown for the torus and a finite rectangular planar area with an aspect ratio greater than or equal to three. Frustration-free ground states in abelian quantum double models, defined on a convex area surrounded by smooth curves, can be found through periodic boundary conditions. This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need while simultaneously transmitting energy to those with energy requirements. In return, users with energy needs, positioned as reflectors within the environment, redirect part of the transmitted energy back to the hub. This two-way communication and energy transfer process is modeled through a stochastic differential equation that incorporates both data and energy transmission rates. This stochastic differential equation is then utilized to develop a differential game involving players that represent the hub and potential energy-seeking D2D users. The core challenge lies in finding a Nash equilibrium that accounts for both long-term revenue optimization and energy-efficient data transmission. This issue is addressed by establishing an integral part of the Nash equilibrium that accounts for both the hub's and D2D users' strategies. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that any Nash equilibrium is stable and provides a degree of protection against malicious actions from D2D users. This finding serves as the groundwork for evaluating various strategies, such as a safeguard strategy that involves tracking a stochastic process to deter D2D users from engaging in unfair behavior. In addition, our analysis reveals the link between a reliable transmission mechanism and a reliable energy supply, highlighting potential challenges that may arise in environments with limited energy supplies. Finally, our study explores the connection between incomplete data requirements and network topology, indicating that any Nash equilibrium remains unaffected by minor changes in network connectivity. However, significant alterations in network connectivity do impact the Nash equilibrium and requires readjustment. This ground has been laid for evaluating various strategies, such as a strategy that involves tracking a stochastic process to optimize the hub's strategy in response to changes in network connectivity. In contrast, our study reveals that an unlimited energy supply enables efficient data transmission. In cases where the energy supply is constrained, our analysis shows that the hub can prioritize data transmission over energy supply by adjusting the energy supply rate. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through computational and 
experimental analysis, we investigate the potential for a phase plate to be 
programmed for specific purposes. Our research indicates that phase plates can be 
optimized for specific conditions such as electron energy and objective lens 
focusing to achieve desired diffraction patterns. Additionally, we find that 
typical STEM imaging conditions can be improved by using a phase plate with a 
limited number of programmable zones. A maximum of 7 zones in our model and 15 
zones in our experimental implementation can correct spherical aberration to a 
significant extent. These findings suggest that a phase plate with a modest number 
of zones is capable of effectively correcting spherical aberration for TEMs. 
Lastly, our research explores the feasibility of phase plate designs with ferroelectric 
materials like Bismuth Ferite and Ferroelectric Barium Stannate. Our experimental 
results confirm the potential of these materials for phase plate implementation. 
However, further investigation into the phase plate structure and performance is 
required to fully capitalize on the advantages of these materials. Our study 
contributes to the ongoing development and optimization of phase plates for TEMs, 
suggesting a range of innovative designs to mitigate spherical aberration. 
Moreover, our research paves the way for a new generation of phase plates with 
advanced features and improved performance. Our research ultimately aims to 
reinvigorate the programmatic capabilities of phase plates and stimulate further 
innovations in this field. Our findings serve as a foundation for the 
redevelopment/optimization of existing phase plates as well as the creation of 
novel, feature-rich designs. Our research is a crucial step towards unlocking the 
full potential of phase plates for TEMs. Our research aims to revive and 
contribute to the ongoing efforts in this field and stimulate further 
innovations/optimizations in this domain. Our research explores the phase plate 
designs, performance, and materials, serving as a crucial reference for future 
developments in this area. Our research primarily focuses on the phase plate 
programmability for a specific application, a distinctive feature that sets our 
work apart from other contributions in this field. Our research is unique in

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. Masked Speech Synthesis addresses this concern by masking crucial context components during speech generation. An encoder processes the masked speech along with the remaining contextual segments to identify the missing features. We introduce a contextual loss function that encourages the generated speech to incorporate the masked elements, resulting in a more accurate reconstruction. This approach was incorporated into a state-of-the-art speech synthesis system based on Transformer, and our experiments using the WikiText2 speech dataset revealed a notable improvement in speech quality when all contextual sentences were used, and a moderate boost when only the sentence preceding the current one was employed. An additional assessment using human evaluators confirmed these findings. Furthermore, using pre-trained contextualized word embeddings led to enhanced performance in both speech quality and its naturalness. Our novel strategy for speech synthesis outperformed existing methods, surpassing a 1.0 MOS point in comparison to the baseline system. The proposed architecture and methods have potential for applications in other sequence-to-sequence tasks that involve handling long-term contextual information. The code and data used in this research can be accessed at!oscar-ui.github.io/MSS.html. We've enhanced projection predictive inference by enabling efficient selection of variables and structures in models beyond those in the exponential family. By projecting predictive variables into a latent space, we have created a generalized framework that: 1) maintains the original model's integrity while performing variable selection, 2) accurately detects relevant structures and retains posterior uncertainties, and 3) extends its applicability to non-Gaussian models within the exponential family. We've rigorously evaluated our approach by comparing it to established methods on various datasets, and the results demonstrate its superior performance in accurately selecting variables and recovering relevant structures. Notably, this has been particularly evident in scenarios involving partial network connectivity and variable ranking challenges. The associated R code is available on GitHub under the repository name 'proj-pred-inference'.

Recent research has demonstrated that Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to adversarial attacks, which can be exacerbated by the data labeling process. The reliance of machine learning models on human annotation has driven the development of methods exploiting common labeling errors, such as the utilization of labeled data with reversed labels in Binary Classification. However, the existing techniques primarily focus on synchronous attacks and do attacks on larger datasets compared to the attack on a single instance. This research aims to tackle a more complex problem - attacking a instance with significantly more features than the model. Moreover, we propose an innovative approach that incorporates an intrinsic aspect of the data labeling process by utilizing the labeled data in a way that exploits inconsistencies in the annotation process. The proposed method, "Label Manipulation for Binary Classification attacks through data transformation," involves transforming data into the opponent's domain using a pre-trained model, then adjusting it to induce a reversal of labels. Our approach can be applied to various data types and we provide empirical evidence of its effectiveness through experiments on two real-world datasets. The outcomes demonstrate that our proposed method achieves higher accuracy rates compared to current techniques. Climate change communication is complicated by the proliferation of conspiracy theories regarding climate change issues, particularly prevalent on social media where they gain traction quickly. This paper proposes a novel, multi-task deep learning model that simultaneously handles image segmentation and image denoising/deblocking. The segmentation pathway of the network employs a compact, efficient design utilizing a combined skip-connected EfficientNet module, while its image restoration pathway leverages a lightweight, efficient transposed convolution layer. The fusion of these pathways through a 1×1 convolution bridge and efficient residual connection enables the seamless integration of the two tasks. Due to the distinct requirements of the two tasks, a novel multi-task optimizer is developed to adaptively adjust the loss weights in proportion to the network's depth, promoting balanced convergence and accurate results for both tasks. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated on the Sintel dataset, outperforming other models in image denoising/deblocking while achieving comparable segmentation results to state-of-the-art segmentation models. Moreover, the model successfully transfers to other datasets, delivering impressive performance on Aachen DB, BSDS, and SegThor. Notably, the source code and pre-trained models will be made available for public use.

Active galactic nuclei, which harbor rapidly rotating black holes, allow us to study the mass and spin of black holes across vast distances. By analyzing the electromagnetic spectra produced by matter accreting onto the black holes, researchers can infer the mass and spin of the black holes. This is done by comparing their observations to detailed physical models, which are often based on simplified ideas of how black holes interact with accreting matter. One such concept is the Blandford-Znajek process, which proposes that black holes extract energy from their spins via interactions with magnetic fields, thereby driving the emitted spectra. Due to the intricacies involved, researchers often rely on simplified assumptions when exploring the connection between black hole spins and the observed spectra. In our work, we eliminate the need for such approximations by directly linking the characteristics of black holes to the properties of the observed spectra using neural network-based inference. By training and testing a neural network on simulated data, we've found that it accurately relates black hole parameters to electromagnetic spectra without referencing physical models, and achieves precision within 10% for mass estimates and 20% for spin estimates. This breakthrough enables rapid exploration of the phase space of black holes, and paves the way for similar applications in other astrophysical contexts. Given its potential for contributing to our understanding of black holes, we've made the relevant code publicly available for further modification and development. A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. These storms exhibit significant intensity fluctuations in very short time frames, on the order of minutes. The exact mechanisms behind these fluctuations are still debated among researchers, with theories pointing to either intermittent particle beams or sudden changes in the electromagnetic interactions within the coronal mass ejections.

We observed a type-I noise storm associated with a microflare in real-time data from the GOES-16 satellite. The energy released in this event caused the intensity of the noise storm to increase by a factor of 20 in about 2 minutes, followed by another sudden drop of the same scale 5 minutes later. The parameters of the noise storm changed in distinct phases, first showing rapid increases in both frequency and flux, before shifting into a phase where the frequency remained relatively stable while the flux continued to rise, eventually giving way to a phase where the flux remained steady while the frequency varied. The storm's spectral density was best explained by two components with different variations, one associated with the beam plasma interaction and another possibly linked to the plasma coalescence.

The coalescence component dominated the spectrum during periods of stable flux and increasing frequency, while the beam component was more prominent in phases of rising flux and stable frequency. The relative strengths of these components determined the observed shape of the storm's spectrum, with varying proportions of curved and straight lines. The two component model was able to explain both the smooth and sharp transitions between phases, as well as the overall shape of the storm's spectrum, making this understanding a crucial step towards diagnosing the underlying physical processes at play in type-I noise storms. The successful application of this model to other storms could potentially yield important insights into the storm dynamics. The model could also be used in conjunction with other radio wave generation mechanisms to explain more complex phenomena. Moreover, we observed that the storm duration was primarily determined by the relative strengths of its low frequency component and the local plasma environment. The combination of these two factors could potentially predict the storm's behavior and shape, giving the phenomenon its characteristic appearance. A recent study using the VLA4 survey at 6 cm wavelength found that the central region of the Galaxy contains a significant number of radio-loud stars, primarily located in or near large star clusters such as Pegasus and Perseus. These clusters, hosting massive O-type stars, possess massive interstellar clusters and vast amounts of dust. Outside of these regions, fewer stars with strong radio emission were detected. Researchers speculate that hot, low-density clusters, such as those in the vicinity of Pegasus and NGc 531, may be home to stars emitting radio signals. It's theorized that these clusters, rich in new star formations, could alter the ambient conditions, affecting the movement of stars within the Galactic plane and their interaction with surrounding gas. These findings suggest an association between star clusters and the formation of stars that emit radio signals, though more extensive observations are needed to confirm this link and explore the dynamics of star cluster formations. 

Our investigation focuses on a region in the Galactic plane containing multiple star clusters, including those associated with the massive star clusters CCs 33 and 37. Both clusters reside near the direction of the star gamma Centauri (M42) and are located outside of a region previously surveyed (Matthews et al. 2018). This new survey, conducted using the VLA4 at a wavelength of 6 cm, allowed us to identify compact radio sources within a region approximately 30 minutes in diameter, and our data show 114 of these sources have optical counterparts, primarily consisting of main sequence stars or those already documented in the Galaxy's stellar population catalog. 

However, our survey also reveals 14 stars emitting strong radio signals within a region associated with a small, open cluster (CCs 33/37) and 11 more in its surroundings. These stars, emitting intense radio signals, are likely to be massive (early-type), hot stars (greater than 20 solar masses), and are associated with the star cluster (CCs 33/37), though not as heavily as earlier surveys suggested. These radio-emitting stars reside near a region of low stellar density and are thought to be moving rapidly in random directions. 

These findings are consistent with the idea that massive, hot stars (greater than 20 solar masses) are not confined to dense star clusters and can be found in less crowded areas, and that their association with gas in these regions can create new star clusters. Also, these stars are thought to be relatively rare compared to cooler, less massive stars emitting radio signals.

This paper investigates the normalized ground state solution to the given biharmonic Choquard type equation under specific constraints on the parameter $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in a given context. In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable channel estimation crucial for optimal system performance, yet the conventional method used in pilot-based channel estimation may be inadequate for mobile vehicles due to its low pilot allocation efficiency. This has motivated the development of a novel pilot allocation scheme known as pseudo-pilot sequence (PPS), designed to enhance channel tracking for moving vehicles by utilizing known symbols within regularly spaced frames. We investigate the effectiveness of the PPS in assisting channel tracking for D2D communication, particularly in scenarios where vehicle mobility is present, and analyze the impact of PPS on system performance in terms of loss rate and throughput. Simulation results indicate that PPS can significantly mitigate the adverse effects of channel fading on D2D communication, yielding improved loss rates and higher average throughputs compared to traditional methods. Notably, the PPS exhibits superior performance in diverse channel conditions, with improved results that can reach nearly 100% in severe channel environments. This research suggests PPS as a viable solution for reliable D2D communication in the presence of vehicle mobility, outperforming traditional methods by a margin of around 50% in medium to severe channel conditions. Specifically, PPS outperforms traditional methods by approximately 30% in moderate channel conditions, with even better performance possible in scenarios involving high vehicle speeds and dense vehicle populations. With the potential to greatly improve D2D communication performance in a wide range of scenarios, the proposed PPS represents an innovative approach to reliable D2D communication in vehicular environments. In particular, PPS offers several key advantages, including the ability to efficiently utilize pilot resources in sparse networks, and improved resistance to large-scale interference resulting from the localized nature of vehicle deployments. Furthermore, the structural simplicity of PPS enables the use of conventional detectors for reliable decoding, with the potential for the development of more advanced and optimized PPS schemes in the future. Although the proposed PPS scheme has been designed for D2D communication in vehicular environments, the underlying principles of pseudo-pilot sequence optimization are applicable to a much broader range of problems in channel estimation, including the optimization of existing pilot schemes and the development of new schemes for specific problems. As such, the proposed scheme represents an important contribution to the field of D2D communication, with the potential for the improvement of existing pilot schemes and the development of new schemes tailored to specific needs. The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community. Despite advancements, the task poses significant challenges due to an immense color space, varied visual contexts, and the need for semantic segmentation. To overcome these obstacles, this research proposes a pioneering approach called SpecColorize, which utilizes spectral characteristics derived from visible spectroscopy to obtain underlying color attributes. These attributes serve as a foundation for generating colored images, which are further refined using a learned multi-scale color reconstruction network. Evaluations on synthetic datasets and real-world photographs demonstrate the superior performance of SpecColorize compared to existing methods. Notably, this technique demonstrates robustness in low-light conditions and its potential applications extend to image color enhancement and colorization. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/IndigoTeam/SpecColorize. Additionally, a live demo is available at https://speccolorize.org.

Deep Artificial Neural Networks are exemplified by expressing their approximation properties using polynomials, which are subsequently analyzed through the perspective of Minimal Networks, facilitating weight computation by Newton's iterative method, whose convergence is guaranteed by the Weierstrass Theorem. This theorem justifies a numerical scheme for computing weights by leveraging an implicit function, whose convergence is ensured by the Implicit Function Theorem. Our study replaces the smoothness assumptions typically required by this theorem with bounded activation functions, thereby allowing the use of Deep Neural Networks to solve nonlinear equations. Additionally, our scheme is versatile, accommodating both fully connected and convolutional architectures, as well as any activation function. A key advantage of our method is its efficiency, allowing the computation of weights in a single pass through the dataset. Experimentally, we demonstrate its efficacy, particularly in scenarios involving small datasets and for hyperbolic CNNs, where traditional optimization methods struggle. Our code is available for reproduction of these results. Furthermore, we examine the connection between Artificial Neural Networks and Artificial Algebraic Networks, revealing a common basis in Artificial Neural Models, and utilizing this linkage to enhance the solution of nonlinear equations. Specifically, we analyze and compare two specialized Algebraic Networks, the Homogeneous and the Gaussian Type, both of which are capable of approximating any continuous function within a specified error margin. However, they differ in the manner in which they utilize additional variables, either homogeneously or randomly, respectively, in proportion to the dimensionality of the input variables. Consequently, Deep Homogeneous Neural Networks require fewer additional variables than Deep Gaussian Neural Networks, as confirmed by numerical evaluations. Moreover, we establish a relationship between Artificial Neural Networks and Artificial Algebraic Networks of Homogeneous Type, resulting in the latter being able to approximate any continuous function on a compact domain. Notably, the width of the Algebraic Network no longer needs to scale with the size of the domain, unlike standard Neural Networks, as illustrated in our numerical demonstrations. Building upon these discoveries, we propose an innovative two-step strategy for training Deep Neural Networks based on Artificial Algebraic Networks of Homogeneous Type. First, we utilize the Implicit Function Theorem, allowing the computation of weights by Newton's method, and offering a more efficient alternative to backpropagation. Subsequently, we leverage the expressiveness of Deep Homogeneous Neural Networks to enhance the solution of nonlinear equations, and improve the regression and classification performance in various benchmark datasets. Our code is available for reproduction of these results. Moreover, we successfully applied this two-step strategy to the development of Hyperbolic Convolution

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, cooperated with ECFA by offering input and insights, and introduced several projects focused on comprehending and addressing the varied needs of young researchers. This report outlines the details of the panel's formation and operations as well as its engagement with numerous activities during its first two years of operation. It particularly highlights the panel's creation of a Young Researchers Working Group, consisting of representatives from FLARE and various sub-panels of ECFA, that is committed to addressing the unique requirements of early career researchers. This report also summarizes the panel's participation in key events such as the ECFA site visit to Grenoble, the ECFA workshop on Future Electron-Positron Colliders, and the ECFA workshop on FLARE activities. Furthermore, the report documents the panel's presentations at ECFA meetings where various topics including research funding, career development programs, mental health and well-being, and the needs of young researchers were discussed. Lastly, the report highlights upcoming tasks and projects for the panel in the upcoming years.

This study develops mathematical formulas describing line wave propagation and also identifies specific conditions under propagation that can lead to complete signal confinement. Furthermore, it's shown that line waves are semi-reversible and explains how these waves can be effectively used in the study of signal transmission between two metasurfaces through an external medium that changes periodically. This capability enables the detection of changes occurring at the interface through a measurable effect that appears as a shift in frequency. This finding also extends to situations where one of the interfaces is missing. The condition for detecting this frequency shift becomes the basis for a new mathematical concept called impedance phase mismatch. This concept provides a critical measure of how a surface interacts with external fields and also serves as the foundation for developing new technologies that can control and manipulate energy transmission between two surfaces in proximity. Moreover, this idea can be applied to a wide range of fields including acoustic waves and electron behavior. Currently available technologies that exploit similar phenomena are limited to those that involve electron behavior and periodic patterns that affect the way electrons behave. However, the concept of line waves offers a more comprehensive and versatile approach to controlling energy transmission and has the potential to be more widely applicable. Nonetheless, realizing this potential will require innovative designs for dual electromagnetic interfaces that work together to control signal transmission and also separate interfaces that work independently. Developing such structures is a significant challenge, particularly since most available technologies that exploit electromagnetic and dual electromagnetic phenomena rely on designs that require precise alignment of multiple components to work together effectively. However, recent breakthroughs in the design of electromagnetic metasurfaces that work together and separately have paved the way for novel and innovative approaches to controlling energy transmission and have created new possibilities for discovering and exploiting new phenomena such as line waves. The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-task
approach, training existing relation extraction models alongside knowledge graph
link prediction to ultimately boost the models' overall performance and achieve
predictable gains in accuracy. The evidence from our experiments, conducted on
the Stanford Clinical Questions dataset, suggests this approach yields substantial
improvements in that domain, with particular success in situations involving
multi-token objects where previous models would struggle to accurately recognize
the object and its related subject. Notably, our results indicate this method
canpects a significant boost in F1 score, increasing from 75 to 83.3. The code
supporting this research is available at https://github.com/alecgrout/grout-2022-kge.

Our study focused on the magnetic arrangements within the crystals of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 using neutron-diffraction experiments. In Tb3RuO7, neighboring ruthenium atoms created a chain pattern, with some being ordered magnetically and others remaining randomly aligned. This unique combination resulted in an intermediate disordered state, with the two ruthenium types exhibiting similar yet distinct behaviors. In Nd3RuO7, the magnetic patterns were uniform and independent for the two ruthenium species, with both being ordered at temperatures below 17.5 K. We attribute the disordered state in Tb3RuO7 primarily to the magnetic frustration caused by the distinct properties of its two ruthenium components, particularly their response to magnetic fields, which led to a unique coexistence of ordered and random magnetic patterns. This behavior offers a unique analogy to systems in physics known as the "monolayer Weyl semimetal," where the presence of a particular crystal structure leads to a disordered magnetic state. Additionally, our experiment discovered that applying a magnetic field could alter the disordered state in Tb3RuO7, leading to a uniform ordered state, an effect that can be attributed to the magnetic field's impact on the two ruthenium species's response to magnetic fields, which led to a uniform ordered state. Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, which can be achieved through the
application of an Autoencoder. In our research, we adapt a novel dual neural
network architecture, consisting of an image-based convolutional neural network
block paired with a modalities-agnostic, shape-shifting block featuring multiple
dense layers. This innovative approach allows our model to efficiently process
both single images and sequential video frames. Additionally, its modularity
enables the substitution of any section with an alternative dual or single-point
model, enhancing the potential for future exploration and generalization. We
successfully demonstrated the efficacy of our model through the application of
a specific reduced representation, called ShapeMlp, to the domain of 3D shape
reconstruction and category-agnostic 3D shape representation for images and
videos. Specifically, our model was utilized in a 3D shape prediction task from
depth maps in the MPI-INF 3DOPEN dataset, resulting in a 70.6% Acc@1 rating when
tested on the test set, outperforming the baseline model by 15%. Further details
on our dataset, model, and experiment settings can be found in our research paper.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features, and then proceed with a classifier trained on labelled data. We explore a more efficient approach that simultaneously learns adaptation and supervised learning on the available data. Specifically, we develop a novel objective function that combines both tasks, and can be optimized using either importance weights or domain-invariant features, and we further demonstrate the effectiveness of combining semi-supervised learning with importance weights or domain-invariant features results in better performance compared to using either method alone. The proposed method achieves superior results on diverse covariate-shift adaptation scenarios, and also performs competitively on semi-supervised learning benchmarks. Ultimately, the advantage of this approach lies in the potential for higher accuracy and reduced need for unlabelled data. To reinforce the value of this methodology, we provide theoretical justifications and several successful applications of the method in video classification and medical image analysis. Furthermore, we introduce a new benchmark for covariate-shift adaptation using the StagLeMon framework and make available our implementation through an open-source repository. Lastly, we emphasize the domain-invariant representations learned through this method are highly interpretable due to the simplicity of the objective function and the characteristics of domain-invariant features. The potential applications of this methodology extend to various areas such as text classification, speech recognition, and more. Finally, we outline potential future research directions including the incorporation of generative models and reinforcement learning. We also present two previously unpublished articles that have arisen from this work. The first article delves into the details of semi-supervised learning adaptation, while the second article explores an alternative formulation using generative models. Within this context, we map the geometric structures of convolutional neural networks, residual networks, recursive neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and the equilibrium propagation framework. Furthermore, this geometric framework enables us to explore the relationships between geometric structures and the performance of different neural networks, thereby guiding the design of deep learning architectures at an algorithmic level. Additionally, our study also sheds light on the optimal training processes for deep learning systems at an algorithmic level. Our work is an effort to bridge the gap between deep learning and fundamental theoretical concepts in mathematics and physics. It is also hoped that this geometric model of deep learning systems will facilitate the development of new and efficient deep learning architectures. In future, this model may further contribute to a deeper understanding of the inner workings of deep learning systems and potentially open up new avenues for future research in both machine learning and theoretical physics. Furthermore, our study also provides a method for evaluating the geometric structure of a deep learning architecture based on its functionality, thereby potentially guiding the design of deep learning architectures with desired performance characteristics. We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\zeta_3)/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $d$ is a positive cube-free integer. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in the cubic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ arising from the prime factorization of $d$ in relation to generators of ambiguous principal ideals. Specifically, we investigate the occurrence of generators of such ideals among the lattice minima and explain their impact on the principal factorization type of the cubic field and its associated field extension when applying Voronoi's algorithm. Our research provides a strategy for determining the field extension's principal ideal factorization type based on the lattice minima and their geometric relationships. Ultimately, we showcase our method in several non-CM fields of degree $6$ to manually calculate the field extension's principal ideal factorization type. Furthermore, we have developed a program in MAGMA to capitalize on the outcomes of our theoretical analysis and automate this calculation for any given field extension of the aforementioned form. This program is accessible at https://xgmc.github.io/cubicambiquous/index.html. Our computational results are also documented in the file output.txt available at the same URL. Additionally, our proof combines elementary methods with a geometric interpretation of the lattice minima, aligning with the techniques employed in the paper by Harborth and Nierstrasz about the maximum number of layers in lattice minima. Our work can be extended to other number fields, but the associated generalizations are more complex and less effective than our method, which is specifically tailored to this particular type of field extension. To our knowledge, no existing literature directly addresses the behavior of lattice minima in the context of this field extension. However, the underlying methods in our work are reminiscent of those applied in the calculation of the maximal unipotent orbit in the work of Hirzebruch, Claudon, and Kahn. Specifically, our geometric analysis of the lattice minima is closely related to their respective lattices. Moreover, the concept of a middle layer in our lattice minima is a direct analogue to the intermediate representation in the work of Hirzebruch, Claudon, and Kahn. A research framework is introduced to uncover and analyze decision-making processes from deep neural network classifiers in jet substructure tagging techniques. The method relies on the utilization of relevant 'expert' variables, constructed through a multivariate analysis, that complement and enhance DNN performance. By incorporating these specialized variables into the DNN architecture as additional input channels, titled an Extended DNN, the underlying architecture is dissected and explained. The research finds that each DNN layer plays a distinct role in the classification process and that the Extended DNN surpasses its standard DNN counterpart in performance, particularly for complex tagging challenges involving low-mass $W$-boson decays in jet substructure. Furthermore, the study highlights the achievements of each DNN layer in categorizing jet substructure regions and illustrates the explanation mechanisms underlying the DNN decisions. The proposed method can be applied to a broad range of DNN-powered tagging strategies and is expected to accelerate the development of more efficient jet substructure tagging methods. Moreover, this method can be adapted for use in self-supervised and unsupervised learning methods by explaining and understanding decision-making processes after training. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Furthermore, the same architecture can be adapted to tackle the fermion sign problem in lattice quantum field theories. Our code is available open-source on GitHub at the specified URL. Our team has successfully simulated a (1+1)-dimensional quantum field theory incorporating 4 fermion interactions with up to 96 fermion species, a task previously impractical due to an overwhelming sign problem. We have extracted key physical insights under extreme conditions of density and temperature. Moreover, this approach has enabled us to study the thermal properties of a fermionic lattice gas with up to 1024 spatial sites and various temperatures, an equally intractable case only a few months ago. Our simulations have provided detailed insights into its equation of state, free energy, and specific heat. This innovative method can be applied to a broad range of challenging sign problem instances in (1+1)-dimensional quantum field theories, offering a promising pathway for first-principles calculations of physical properties. Moreover, the same architecture can be adapted to tackle the fermion sign problem in (2+1)-dimensional quantum field theories, an ongoing area of research in our team. Additionally, our method holds potential for a future transition to quantum computers, where the sign problem remains a persistent challenge. Our research demonstrates that there is no fundamental reason why the sign problem cannot be solved; instead, the difficulties arise from previous algorithmic shortcomings. Consequently, we anticipate that the FeXNet algorithm will facilitate groundbreaking advancements in the computational methods for quantum many-body physics. Moreover, the adaptable nature of this algorithm ensures that it can be applied in various contexts, as exemplified by our successful simulation of a fermionic lattice gas and potential future applications in (2+1)-dimensional quantum field theories. In conclusion, our FeXNet algorithm represents a significant breakthrough in tackling the sign problem through an efficient and scalable solution. As a result, this method enables the computational study of quantum many-body systems under extreme conditions of density and temperature that were previously inaccessible. Moreover

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence and then applying various predictive models to successfully employ VPPMs in malicious contexts. Specifically, we focus on a scenario where an attacker uses a VPPM to coerce a victim into visiting a specific physical location. Our key contribution is in developing and testing an optimization algorithm that maximizes the effectiveness of VPPMs, thereby boosting attack success rates. Our findings indicate that VPPMs posing minor discomfort can yield high attack success rates, while those causing significant discomfort still achieve substantial results. Moreover, we observed that VPPMs have a more significant impact when utilizing haptic VPPMs. Ultimately, our research highlights the potential for VPPMs to be utilized in heinous crimes, emphasizing the need for developers to implement safeguards within VR applications to prevent such manipulations. This work marks a first in optimizing VPPMs for malicious purposes, fostering significant discussion around the ethical implications of these interactions. To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains. Moreover, it explores the potential of utilizing partially or fully zero-shot techniques for model adaptation, highlighting their efficacy and efficiency. Our findings indicate that a combination of shared and task-specific weights for adapting to new languages offers a satisfactory balance between performance and computational requirements. Specifically, zero-shot adaptations yield satisfactory results with minimal training data, while fine-tuning this adaptation towards our base model yields more optimal outcomes, although it necessitates more training data. Ultimately, a hybrid approach combining shared and task-specific weights proves most effective, yielding a 14% gain in performance with only a 2% increase in computational requirements compared to the initial model. Our research suggests that integrating novel languages with minimal training can be achievable using a more streamlined and computationally efficient protocol. Recent high-resolution observations using VLA4 and VLA5 frequencies have revealed binary systems within protostars. Researchers have proposed that binary formation occurs through core fragmentation. However, it's unclear how binary mass fraction (in terms of total mass) relates to the core mass. We addressed this by simulating core fragmentation using numerical codes for various core masses. As a result, we found that binary fragment mass ranges from 0.01 to 0.1 times the core mass. Our findings are consistent with observational data and suggest a binary formation method through core fragmentation. We also discovered either equal-mass or nearly equal-mass binary systems or wide binary systems with a massive companion. These outcomes are a natural consequence of core fragmentation. We propose that binary systems with masses less than 0.01 times the core mass may be generated through disk fragmentation. Therefore, the mass ratio distribution of binary systems could be explained by combining core and disk fragmentation methods. Core fragmentation might primarily produce equal or near-equal mass binary systems, while wide binary systems are mostly produced by high-mass core fragmentation. Conversely, disk fragmentation could primarily produce unequal-mass binary systems, explaining the peak at 0.01. These predictions can be verified by future observations using the VLA. Social media platforms host an immense volume of content, encompassing a broad array of views on society. Despite the numerous opinions expressed, verifying their accuracy can be challenging due to their subjective nature. To address this, we aim to condense these posts into distinct narratives, thereby isolating the core assertions. By gaining insight into and visualizing the various narratives surrounding a particular topic, individuals can more effectively understand and grasp the different perspectives circulating on social media. To achieve this, we have developed a system known as SiNCHRO, which leverages a neural network-based approach to discover underlying narratives within a given set of posts. By utilizing a limited number of labeled narratives as guidance, SiNCHRO can uncover hidden narratives within social media discourse with remarkable accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that SiNCHRO outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches, further, we provide qualitative insight into its effectiveness, showcasing its capacity to uncover intricate narratives. To facilitate reproducibility, we have made our code available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/adinf/adinf-sinchro/tree/main/sinchro. We have also created a dedicated webpage to showcase the results obtained from our approach: https://adinf.github.io/sinchro/. Identifying trending social media events in real-time is crucial for numerous applications such as disaster response, sports analysis, and public transportation scheduling. The dynamic nature of social media data streams makes it essential to track them in real-time, yet detecting occurrences like natural disasters or sports events simultaneously poses a challenge. Our proposed approach utilizes social media posts related to distinct events by considering both popular hashtags and post densities over time. In our experiments using data from Twitter and HashtagTracker, we evaluated different combinations of features and found that using event-specific hashtags coupled with a threshold-based approach for detecting density anomalies yields the best results. Our proposed method outperforms existing solutions by accurately identifying multiple events in a single data stream while minimizing false positives. The proposed framework demonstrates high precision and recall rates, specifically 94% and 92%, respectively. The generated models using different social media events can be applied to new, unknown events with minimal manual configuration required. Furthermore, our technique can be adapted for use with other data streams such as Instagram, HashtagCloud, and Geotagging platforms. Our method comprises an open-source implementation accessible through GitHub and an accompanying tutorial for reproducibility also available on GitHub. To facilitate practical applications, we also provide a simplified version of our approach suitable for smaller-scale operations and resource constraints in Section 7. In addition, HashtagEventDetector is compatible with Windows, Linux, and macOS operating systems. Experimental outcomes are presented in Section 8, and future research directions and potential extensions explored in Section 9. Finally, conclusions and future work outlined in Section 10.
