It is recommended to utilize at least these specifications for real-world applications. Though the presented experiments focused on detecting two, three, and four events simultaneously, our approach can theoretically detect any number of occurrences in a single data stream. Nevertheless, this may result in decreased precision values. In the future, we aim to enhance the technique's scalability for detecting large numbers of events by possibly introducing a hierarchical event structure. Moreover, this idea warrants further investigation and validation. In terms of potential limitations, our approach relies on the availability of social media data during event creation, which may not always be the case

New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurements and tomographic galaxy surveys in the upcoming years will enable more efficient cross-correlation analysis. We examine the usefulness of the weighted skew-spectrum as an efficient tool for extracting information about cosmic structures and parameters, utilizing angular momentum and non-linear bias properties. We develop a comprehensive framework for calculating the weighted skew-spectrum of galaxy counts and conduct thorough analyses on the scalability of computation. Our results show that the weighted skew-spectrum can effectively identify key information about cosmological parameters, particularly when combined with the power spectrum, allowing us to gain a more precise understanding of $A_s$, $n_s$, and $\Omega_m$. With future data sets, we anticipate gaining precise new constraints on the parameters related to the properties of dark matter and deriving significant limitations on the properties of sterile neutrinos. The analytical calculation of spectroscopic and bispectral clustering coefficients facilitates a comprehensive evaluation of the scalability of the weighted skew-spectrum computation. Based on the expected data in the Haloscope Pathfinder Experiment (HiPACT), we anticipate that the weighted skew-spectrum will become computationally expensive, reaching the practical limitations of current computational capabilities with future data in the Large Scale Structure Survey (SSurvey). Nonetheless, our findings suggest the potential for the weighted skew-spectrum to become a vital information source in the forthcoming decade of cosmology and dark energy. By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training, we developed a rigorous framework for training robust Neural Networks (NNs). This framework utilizes posterior sampling to select weights that excel in worst-case scenarios, resulting in highly resilient BNNs capable of withstanding various attacks. The advantages of BNNs lie in their capacity to accurately represent weight uncertainty and generate robust counterfeits during the training phase, thereby enhancing adversarial robustness. The framework's advantages are manifested in the robustness-accuracy tradeoff; specifically, BNNs exhibit improved robustness compared to conventional BNNs and rival methods within the same domain. This framework's efficacy has been validated across diverse scenarios, including real-world applications in image classification and generative tasks involving latent space exploration. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/krkthecoder/BNN-AT.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety and fear of disease contagion. Under such a chaotic social environment, the dissemination of online rumors gained further momentum. Research into the dynamics of rumor propagation is crucial for mitigating the spread of misinformation, a challenge particularly acute during public health crises when trust in authorities is compromised. This study analyzed the temporal and spatial patterns of SARS-CoV-2 rumor propagation in China using Google Trends data, focusing on how weather, holidays, case reports, and mortality rates influenced the spread and persistence of such rumors. Our findings showed that rumors related to coronavirus infection via weather, food, and physical contact generally persisted, with some propagating as far as 150 days. Our results also indicated that rumors are more likely to spread during holidays and in areas experiencing recent case reports or deaths, with certain viral patterns potentially linked to weather patterns. These findings highlight the significance of combining data from various sources when investigating the dynamics of social phenomena. Furthermore, our study's approach can be adapted for anticipating and preventing the propagation of other social hazards. A detailed analysis of the implications of our research is presented in the conclusion. This research explores the impact of reducing hyperspectral image dimensions on pixel classification accuracy through methods like pixel-wise compression, CPIC, CPIC with spatial correlation, SCPIC, and CPIC combined with a Bayesian approach, BCPIEC. We compared these methods to traditional dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA, ICA, and a Bayesian approach, and found that pixel compression resulted in higher classification accuracies across various hyperspectral datasets, especially at higher compression rates. Furthermore, our research highlights that pixel classification accuracy is largely influenced by the amount of data noise and the number of classes in a dataset. We also evaluated the effectiveness of these methods on pixel-wise prediction, and found that some methods performed better than others in noisy environments. Our work culminated in the creation of an open-source R package, cpic, which utilizes these compression methods for hyperspectral image analysis. This package has been successfully applied to real-world scenarios, as demonstrated in our analysis of the sub-pixel classification problem in two hyperspectral images, where we employed CPIC to classify vegetation cover types with a high compression rate of 97%. Our research has also been utilized in various application domains such as remote sensing, astrophysics, and biomedical imaging, where large multi-dimensional image datasets often pose a challenge to classification tasks due to memory and computational constraints. Our research addresses these challenges through efficient compression of hyperspectral images, enabling precise pixel-wise classification while conserving computational resources and disk space. Ultimately, our goal is to facilitate the use of these methods in real-world hyperspectral image analysis, as exemplified by our case studies on pixel-wise prediction in hyperspectral images. The potential applications of this research extend to domains such as remote sensing, astrophysics, and biomedical imaging, where precise pixel classification is essential but often hindered by data dimensionality and computational constraints. Our R package, cpic, offers a practical solution to these challenges via efficient hyperspectral image compression, enabling precise pixel classification while conserving computational resources and disk space. Our research focuses on discovering such a minimal sub-network model (quantization) for neural networks without accessing the original full network, utilizing an alternate approach based on the evolution of neural networks (ENE) can efficiently achieve this goal. The ENE can now be used to find minimal, trainable sub-network models efficiently. The integration of the ENE with a decoder is responsible for the creation of a minimal, trainable sub-network model. A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables the prediction of essential chemical shift characteristics in proteins (specifically, amide proton chemical shifts) based on a predicted protein structure, taking into account the effects of multiple conformations associated with chemical shift variations. This approach differs from other prediction tools, instead opting for a more realistic representation of protein structures where regions exhibit conformational flexibility. A large-scale assessment of the ProCS method demonstrated its accuracy, with results indicating a significant correlation between predicted and actual chemical shifts for a comprehensive test dataset. A significant number of well-predicted residues (approximately 29%) exhibited errors less than 0.5 ppm. A comparison of ProCS with other prediction tools revealed it outperforms CASP evaluation rounds 72-74, with ProCS exhibiting more consistent results across various assessment categories. A statistical analysis of key ProCS parameters, related to energy, allowed for the identification of specific factors influencing proton chemical shift variability. This research highlights the potential for using molecular dynamics simulations to gain insights into protein dynamics, specifically through the analysis of amide proton chemical shifts. A simplified version of the ProCS method, referred to as ProCS-harmonic, was also developed, aiming to improve prediction accuracy and efficiency. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate the effect of loss function on the generalization performance of deep neural networks. Our findings reveal that certain, previously undiscovered loss functions, including the cross-entropy loss, exhibit superior generalization capabilities compared to other, more complex loss function alternatives on standard datasets. Furthermore, we highlight the inherent regularization properties of a standardized subset of loss functions, potentially providing insight into their effectiveness in enhancing generalization. To facilitate reproducibility, we provide open-source code enabling the replication of our experiments at: https://github.com/ashishb2003/study-loss-generalization. Additionally, all experimental results have been made available at: https://ashishb2003.github.io/study-loss-generalization/index.html. Based on our findings, we conclude that the traditional reliance on empirical loss function selection may be unnecessary and sometimes misguided; instead, researchers could benefit from exploring the inherent regularization properties of their chosen loss function. Specifically, we recommend continued development of the cross-entropy loss, given its exceptional regularization capabilities and superior generalization performance. Finally, we propose StudLoss, a comprehensive library for deep learning loss functions featuring an automated generalization testing framework, enabling researchers to evaluate the efficacy of novel loss functions on a range of datasets in the future. https://github.com/ashishb2003/studloss.

The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and gives rise to an attractive force that binds electrons and holes together. This binding occurs below a specific critical point known as the Anderson transition, at which a typical semimetal transitions into an excitonic insulator. Our research focuses on examining the existence of an excitonic insulator in two-dimensional semimetals with a trigonal symmetry-driven gap. Using a nonperturbative approach based on bosonic and fermionic action elements, we generate a effective action that incorporates both electron and hole components. At the Anderson transition, the effective action exhibits a phase transition where bosonic fluctuations gain a mass, while fermionic fluctuations remain unaffected. This phenomenon is indicative of the transition from a semimetal to an excitonic insulator. Additionally, our findings demonstrate that in two-dimensional materials with a trigonal symmetry-driven gap, the excitonic insulator phase is realized when the ratio of electron and hole densities falls within a specific range, specifically narrower than a certain critical value. This critical range determines the existence of an excitonic insulator phase in such materials. Our research further reveals that in materials with a trigonal symmetry-driven gap, electron-electron and hole-hole interactions lead to the emergence of a coherence scale that is inversely proportional to the density of carriers. Moreover, our findings show that the coherence scale in such materials is capped at a maximum value determined by the strength of electron-electron and hole-hole interactions. Our research also explores how electron-electlectron and hole-hole interactions influence the behavior of superconductors and excitonic insulators. Our results suggest that a sufficiently strong electron-electron and hole-hole interaction can give rise to a superconducting or excitonic insulating state in a semimetal, provided it is within a specific range of electron or hole densities. Furthermore, our findings imply that a superconducting or excitonic insulating transition in a 2D semimetal with a gap driven by trigonal symmetry may be distinguished from other types of phase transitions only through the use of symmetry-based approaches. In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based reporting platforms that connect users with dispatchers via the internet. These systems enable users to report incidents and receive support and guidance from dispatchers. Users can submit multiple reports, and each incident is assigned a unique ID. Users can track the progress of reported incidents, receiving updates sent to them directly via message. This allows users to gauge the responsiveness of dispatchers and organizations, providing a measurable indicator of response time. To better understand user experience, analysts examine the time it takes for dispatchers to respond to reports, and this has led to the creation of a dataset containing data from the City of Chicago's Community Safety Toolkit. By examining response times, researchers found that messages containing emotional language increased the likelihood of timely responses from dispatchers. Furthermore, users who submitted reports multiple times received faster responses to subsequent incidents. To improve the performance of community safety systems, organizations can utilize these findings to enhance user experience, and this has potential implications for other safety reporting systems. Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. Present techniques either utilize a model's uncertainty or rely on diversity measures, such as clustering or reconstruction, to choose unlabeled examples. However, model uncertainty-based methods are susceptible to outliers and diversity-based methods may overlook key information. To address this, we propose a novel approach that simultaneously considers both uncertainty and diversity in a multi-objective optimization framework, allowing the selection of the most informative samples for labeling. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, outperforming state-of-the-art active learning techniques on both simple and complex data distribution scenarios. Additionally, our approach can be augmented with explainable machine learning to identify key features that contribute to model uncertainty and diversity analysis. This allows for the manual review and modification of the selected samples, potentially expanding the method's applicability to domains with strict data protection regulations. Furthermore, our approach can also be used as a semi-supervised learning technique, demonstrating superior performance compared to traditional active learning and deep supervised learning methods on benchmark datasets. The proposed methodology has been implemented in an open-source repository available at: https://github.com/alegros-lab/madral. Our paper also includes additional information on the methodology, as well as the repository, in the accompanying supplement, available at: https://alegros-lab.github.io/madral/supplement. In the digital age, music has become more varied and accessible than ever before. At the heart of this transformation lies the internet, enabling instant access to an unparalleled breadth of music from around the globe. This has sparked a newfound interest in music research. A key area of study within this realm focuses on quantifying the patterns and trends in song dynamics, thereby uncovering hidden structures within music. In our research, we've analyzed the sound patterns of over a million songs from the MusicNet database to reveal intriguing insights. Contrary to the notion that modern music is increasingly complex, our analysis shows that songs today are actually less complex in terms of volume and overall sound intensity when compared to music from the 1960s. However, this decrease in complexity is largely attributed to changes in the sound patterns specific to that decade. Simultaneously, our results reveal an unexpected correlation between the complexity of songs and their popularity, with more complex music emerging to the forefront in recent years. This may bode well for fans of more intricate audio experiences. Another notable discovery from our analysis concerns the inherent stability of the 12-tone chromatic scale. Our research shows that, when using a detailed analysis of sound patterns, we can identify and measure deviations from this principle with remarkable precision, revealing periodic patterns of discordance tied to musical genres and eras. These patterns of deviation also provided a unique framework for classifying different music genres, with certain patterns uniquely associated with specific styles, such as jazz and classical. Furthermore, we observed that measuring the volatility of these deviations can distinguish between different musical periods, with the Volatility Index as low as 0.05 for the music of the 1960s. Interestingly, our results suggest that, while modern music may not be more dynamic in terms of volume and overall sound intensity, it is becoming increasingly complex in terms of its sound patterns, with a notable decrease in stability since the 1960s. This may imply that, in recent years, musicians have been striving to create more unique and interesting sound patterns. Additionally, our analysis shows that songs with more varied dynamics are generally more engaging for listeners, as measured by chart performance. This relationship holds true across different music genres. At the heart of our research lies the goal of developing an objective framework for classifying music genres. Our analysis shows that, while many patterns of sound and volume can be used to classify different genres, certain patterns are shared across multiple genres, such as the distinctive sound patterns associated with jazz and classical music also appearing in more contemporary music. These groupings, or partitions $\mathcal{P}_t$, split a set of objects $[N]$. A dynamic system governs the evolution of the partitions over time, where elements in $[N]$ either form new groups or join existing ones within a probability framework that is conditional on the current partition. The system's dynamics are driven by a parameter $p$, which represents the probability that an element joins a group when the system is in a state characterized by the partition $\mathcal{P}$. The objective of this study is to derive lower and upper bounds for the mixing time of this process. It is demonstrated through extensive analysis that the mixing time for any fixed $p$ and starting configuration $\mathcal{P}_0$ is on the order of $\log N$. A key component of this study involves developing a framework for comparing the likelihood of system transitions using a non-degenerate random walk on a $d$-dimensional cube. The likelihood of large-scale system changes over time is also explored, and it is shown via a detailed example involving the splitting of integers into random groups that the underlying Markov process exhibits qualitatively distinct behavior when the splitting probability $p$ lies within the interval $(0, 1/2)$. The paper further delves into the challenges associated with analyzing the splitting probability $p$ in a systematic manner and establishes a condition for rapid convergence to the stationary distribution when $p$ is allowed to approach either $0$ or $1$. The study culminates in an in-depth analysis of the splitting probability $1/3$, and it is shown through both theoretical and numerical methods that the mixing time for this value of $p$ lies in a different order of magnitude than the other scenarios explored in the study. The results presented in this paper offer insights into both the qualitative and quantitative dynamics of a novel class of stochastic processes known as reinforcement partitions. The study proves to be particularly significant due to its versatility and the diverse set of related problems it addresses. Given the relatively low risk of airborne transmission compared to close contact, our model suggests the need for improved ventilation rates, rational timetabling for buses, and the effective distribution of face masks to minimize the spread of the virus. These measures are particularly crucial during the initial phase of the pandemic when the risk of airborne transmission is higher than average due to the decreased flow rate of fresh air into the bus. Instead, our results show that the CO2 concentration would decrease over time, primarily due to the influence of external factors such as ventilation rates and the flow dynamics of airflow. Researchers at ILL, Grenoble, recently performed $\beta$-delayed $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy to investigate $\beta$-decay properties related to the transition of $^{137}$Te ($5/2^+$) to $^{137}$I with various final $J$-values. Researchers at RIKEN, Nishina Center, recently performed $\beta$-decay experiments on $^{40}$K ($1^+$) with a 11-MeV beam, also measuring the associated electron and $\gamma$-ray spectra. We conducted a detailed theoretical analysis of these experimentally measured quantities. This paper compares theoretical predictions with recently published experimental results for $\beta$-decay lifetimes, $ft$-values, and $\log ft$-values. Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which mainly focused on handling a single quantity of trade requests. To expand this knowledge, we developed algorithms to support multiple quantity trade requests and allowed for both buy and sell orders to include price ranges. This expansion was done while maintaining the properties of duality, monotonicity, and being allocatable. To assess the performance of our algorithms, we conducted an analysis of the time complexity, and also tested them with real data from the Hanatomy exchange market to compare against the current state-of-the-art technology. Our experiments showed the efficiency and practicality of our algorithms in handling complex trade requests. To further validate the accuracy of our findings, we also gathered feedback from users and tested the stability of our algorithms under different scenarios. Ultimately, our results indicate that these double-sided auction algorithms can be utilized effectively in markets with multiple quantity trade requests, and have the potential to be adopted in real-time systems. Our work, including the code and data used for testing, can be found online. To our knowledge, our research fills a notable gap in the existing literature by addressing the challenging issue of processing complex trade requests in double-sided auctions. By expanding the capabilities of double-sided auctions, our work contributes to the broader field of session types, while maintaining the valuable properties of duality, monotonicity, and allocatability. Our novel session types offer a constructive view, achieved through a introduction of new introduction constructs, and are convertible to the existing types with the help of function and rep introduction. Our work also extends the types by adding a session relabeling semantics, and shows that the types are fully compatible with it. Based on these findings, we propose a type-checking algorithm for the extended types, and demonstrate its efficiency through a complexity analysis. To further validate the accuracy of our method, we tested it with real data from various domains, including chemistry and material science. Our results indicate that the temporal logic used is effective in capturing the semantics of interactive pathways. Michal Szabados initially proposed a theory in his doctoral dissertation. In this current paper, the proposed conjecture is examined by the authors, specifically the Ph.D.'s line conjecture, concerning periodic configurations, $T$, where a metric space, $(X, d)$, is defined with distances between points in $T$ being uniformly bounded. It has been proven that the conjecture holds for spaces of limited size, yet the broader application remains uncertain. A new approach has been developed to analyze the structures within these configurations, offering insights into their shape and providing a framework for future exploration. It has also been discovered that certain generalised nonexpansive lines consist of repeated patterns within the configuration. Alternatively, if no repeated pattern exists, a lower bound has been established for the number of elements in the configuration. Furthermore, a significant finding shows that the Ph.D.'s line conjecture holds for lemmas involving the configuration's 'centre' and 'boundary'. In addition, a lexicographic order has been established, which has enabled the successful resolution of a supporting conjecture. It was also demonstrated that the lexicographic order can be adapted to other bases, and provided a new understanding of the distance between points in a configuration, particularly when the configuration's size is high. Conversely, an example has been found of a configuration that is not perfectly uniform, yet closely resembles one. In another finding, it was discovered that the distance between points in a configuration can be highly varied, and a general lower bound has been established for the distance between points at opposite ends of the configuration. In light of these discoveries, two revised conjectures have been formulated. The first, focusing on the minimum number of elements in the configuration, is less stringent than the original. The second, focusing on the uniformity of the configuration, is more stringent than the original. Both conjectures are evaluated and discussed. In particular, it is considered whether the diversity of distances within a configuration can be minimised, and whether the distance between points in a configuration can always be bounded by a constant, multiplied by the size of the configuration. The answer to both questions is no. Furthermore, a new understanding of the configuration's uniformity has been discovered, and it was found that the distance between points in a configuration can often be approximated by the size of the configuration, multiplied by a constant, representing the diversity of distances within that configuration. This discovery opens the door for further investigation into the relationship between the configuration's size, diversity of distances, and uniformity.

The timeless game of chess has been enjoyed by individuals from all walks of life for centuries, and its analytical depth has made it a favorite among artificial intelligence researchers for decades. One key area of study within chess is the strategic application of openings, which require an extensive understanding of the game and its various strategies. To aid chess players in improving their opening play, we developed a comprehensive network of chess openings, connecting related variations through shared transpositions. This 'chebessa' network is based on a thorough analysis of the Levenfish database, which shows promising results in clustering similar openings and predicting popular choices. Furthermore, we present three methods for generating chess openings, demonstrating the effectiveness of our chebessa network in producing playable and sometimes even top-ranked variations. The chebessa network can be accessed through our website, allowing all chess enthusiasts to explore the various connections within the game. Additionally, we provide a Python package for easy integration of the chebessa network into chess analysis tools, including Stockfish and Levenfish. This initiative aims to enhance chess analysis and play with the inclusion of the chebessa network, making it a valuable resource for the chess community. In the long run, we aspire for the chebessa network to evolve into a collaborative effort, supported by chess players and analysts from around the world. As the largest and most comprehensive network of its kind, our chebessa aims to standardize the analysis and sharing of chess openings, benefiting all players, from club level to Grandmaster. To achieve this vision, we invite the chess community to contribute to the chebessa network, incorporating their expertise and existing knowledge, such as Opening Repertoire books, into the network's structure. By fostering an open environment for discussion and collaboration, we hope to build a thriving chebessa community, working together to create an unparalleled resource for chess analysis and improvement. Finally, the chebessa network has the potential to generate exciting research questions, such as the relationship between chess opening preferences and player skill levels, as well as the influence of cultural factors on opening strategies. As the chebssa network continues to evolve, we look forward to exploring these questions in depth, developing new methodologies, and utilizing the chebssa framework to answer them, and to provide actionable advice to chess players. In the end, the chebssa network aims to become an indispensable tool for chess analysis, making it possible to explore new areas of research within the game, and to provide concrete insights to improve chess play. A method to derive constants of motion beyond local bounds for ODE-based Lagrangian systems is outlined, including a practical example that illustrates its utility for dissipative mechanical systems and its implications on solution existence and behavior under specific assumptions. The framework is further extended to cover Euler-Lagrange equations with order greater than two, yielding new first integrals for particular models, such as the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, paving the way for potential applications in Euler-Lagrange partial differential equations in the future. The analysis demonstrates the emergence of degenerate conservation laws that facilitate analytical estimates in dissipative systems, offering a promising approach to measure theoretical limits in dissipative mechanical systems and potentially influence numerical schemes to optimize convergence rates. The newly derived conserved quantities also offer a geometric interpretation, contributing to a revised understanding of the system's dynamics, as exemplified by the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, whose globally defined first integrals guarantee bounded solutions existing forever in time. The method relies on the degeneracy of constants of motion, making the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator an ideal example, as its high-order constant of motion facilitates analytical estimates, confirming its recently proven non-triviality and zero-energy decay rates. The method provides a universal tool to create constants of motion beyond local bounds, applicable to Euler-Lagrange ODE and partial differential equations, opening up new avenues to investigate theoretical limits in dissipative systems and design conservative numerical schemes. The analysis relies on the global existence of solutions, demonstrated through the Euler-Poisson equations, a generalization of the Euler equations for dissipative inviscid fluids, underscoring the potential for Euler-Poisson equations to model the dynamics of dissipative fluids through conservation of angular momentum, thereby providing new insights into the behavior of fluids and potential applications in Euler-Lagrange partial differential equations in the future. The method offers a promising approach to investigate the theoretical limits in dissipative systems, facilitate analytical estimates, and geometrically reinterpret the system's dynamics, as exemplified by the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, and potentially contribute to the design of efficient numerical schemes with guaranteed convergence rates, along with new applications of Euler-Poisson equations for fluid dynamics and potentially future use in Euler-Lagrange partial differential equations in the future. The method provides a valuable tool to create constants of motion beyond local bounds, applicable to various types of Euler-Lagrange equations, from ODE to partial differential equations, offering new possibilities for analytical estimation and geometric interpretation of the system's behavior, along with potential uses in numerical schemes and partial differential equations

Developing free online collections of 3D shapes has driven research in 3D retrieval. Debates surround the most effective input method, with discussions focusing on the accuracy of sketch-based search. We propose introducing gestural input to the space of free, unstructured human movement, allowing air-drawn gestures in a virtual reality environment to function as both input and output. Our system, 3D Paintbrush, enables users to interact with 3D models through gestural input by measuring the deformation of a virtual brushhead corresponding to the user's VR controller. This measure is used both to search for shapes and to output retrieved models, effectively closing the gap between input and output. Moreover, the distinctive trajectories of these gestures serve as unique identifiers, enabling precise shape classification. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach with retrieval and classification accuracy rates of 0.80 and 0.83 respectively, outperforming previous methods in the field. Our technique also possesses educational and therapeutic applications, particularly in environments that favor immersive experiences. We acknowledge existing limitations, such as the requirement for an external brush influence affecting performance, and highlight potential avenues for further research. HD80606b, a planet that passes in front of its host star, undergoes a significant increase in heat due to its close proximity.
When HD80606b orbits its star at extremely eccentric paths, its surface temperature rises to approximately 2000K, caused by an influx of intense solar radiation.
This unusual temperature fluctuation results in a notable dark spot every 6.9 days in transit data, resulting from the planet's reduced absorption of solar energy due to its cool surface.
A new analysis of 2003-2019 transit data by the Kepler/K2, HATNETS, Microlensing, and other observatories has yielded accurate predictions for upcoming transit events in 2020-2025.
Utilizing a statistical model to analyze data variations and detecting changes in the transit pattern, our research has successfully validated a theoretical framework for predicting future transit times in HD80606b.
This novel approach resolves a long-standing issue of accurately estimating transit periods and reduces computational time from hours to minutes, showcasing its practical applications in predicting transit events in other planets. 
Furthermore, our research has accurately forecast the transit schedule for the next observations by the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) in 2020, as well as upcoming transit events in 2020-2025, which were previously calculated using a complex and computationally demanding method.
Our research has demonstrated that a statistical model can efficiently and accurately predict transit periods in a rapidly growing sample of planets with known transit patterns. 
This approach offers a valuable tool for preparing future transit observations, as anticipated for the James Webb Space Telescope, the Habitable Exoplanet Imaging Mission, and future missions in training neural networks to automate transit prediction. 
In addition, our research has successfully forecast the upcoming transit events in 2020-2025 of K2-97b, a planet whose orbital path was initially believed to be in a stable circular pattern but was discovered to have an irregular shape due to an unknown third object in the system. 
This novel research has successfully utilized a statistical model to analyze data variations and detect changes in the irregular transit pattern of K2-97b, resulting from an unknown third object in the system with a long and complex orbital path. 
This approach offers a valuable tool in detecting objects with long and complex orbital paths in future research.

This leads us to an issue where the equations that govern the collapse become incompatible, which raises questions about the fairness of the outcome. We explore the impact of altering the equation of state, rather than the initial conditions, on the fairness of the outcome and find that using a linear relationship between pressure and density makes the equations completely incompatible. This limits the range of possible equations of state, and we identify a specific class of equations of state for which fairness is possible. This class includes equations of state that are commonly observed in nature (e.g. the perfect fluid equation of state) and ensures the fairness of the collapse for those systems. Additionally, we identify a condition that ensures a fair outcome for any equation of state and demonstrate, for example, that a specific type of radiation collapse is fair. This research identifies a crucial connection between the equation of state and the compatibility of the partial differential equations, leading to a broader understanding of how matter collapse behaves in the presence of gravitational forces. Furthermore, we identify a method to achieve a fair and stable outcome for any equation of state by selecting appropriate initial conditions, even if the equations governing the collapse are not entirely compatible. This reveals an interesting relationship between the stability of the outcome and the compatibility of the equations and may indicate the existence of multiple pathways to a stable and fair outcome, one of which is the case where the equation of state is linearly related to the density. This research also investigates the range of possible densities in the collapsed object and demonstrates that a non-linear equation of state can result in a more extensive range of densities, consistent with the behavior of black holes and fair outcomes. This contrasts with linearly related equation of states, which often result in more limited density ranges. A key goal in reinforcement learning is to invert a target outcome distribution, which can be achieved using end-effect drives to implement goal-oriented motor learning, even without an explicit predictive model. End-effect models utilize a different approach by modeling policy dynamics directly, ignoring the Markovian structure, and are often inapplicable in situations requiring a change in skill level. However, we propose an novel algorithm that combines the benefits of both methods by utilizing a hierarchical variational objective to learn policy dynamics while capturing the distribution of final states. This approach enables the transfer of learned skills and facilitates a range of tasks involving diverse end-effect models. Through our experiments, we demonstrate that existing end-effect models can be incorporated into our framework, and it allows for the execution of complex tasks, such as navigating through multiple environments, even when only a single starting point is available. Additionally, we show that our method enables the seamless combination of exploratory and goal-directed motor learning, and allows for the easy addition of multi-step reward structures. In particular, we observe a significant improvement in performance when navigating through a maze, where our method yields higher success rates than traditional reinforcement learning algorithms. A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour symmetry. This enhanced algebra can serve as a basis for modelling coloured Poincaré gravity and exploring the connection between general relativity and Yang-Mills theory. A potential path to linking the two is through the Dufour and Dubois-Hamza transformation process, which may aid in identifying Yang-Mills sectors within gravity data. Additionally, the new coloured Poincaré algebra provides a foundation for designing non-commutative spacetime geometry, which may offer further insights into the relationship between general relativity and Yang-Mills theory. This paper generalizes the coloured Poincaré algebra previously introduced in D. S. P. Rao et al., "Coloured Poincaré algebra in five dimensions", Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical 49 (10) (2016), utilizing the Dufour and Dubois-Hamza method. The result is a generalized coloured Poincaré algebra that includes three-dimensional, Yang-Mills-like coloured Poincaré bialgebras. These algebras serve as potential foundations for modelling Yang-Mills-like gravity in three dimensions. Alternatively, the Dufour and Dubois-Hamza method can be applied to the base Poincaré algebra, resulting in a coloured Poincaré algebra that incorporates three-dimensional coloured Poincaré bialgebras. These algebras can be distinguished by the inclusion of a colour factor in the generalized algebra. The colour factor, which arises from the Dufour and Dubois-Hamza method, is absent in the coloured Poincaré algebra derived directly from the Poincaré algebra. Instead, the coloured Poincaré algebra obtained via the Dufour and Dubois-Hamza method includes colour symmetry factors in both the coloured Poincaré algebra and the coloured Poincaré bialgebra. The methodology employed in this research can be extended to four-dimensional and five-dimensional coloured Poincaré algebras, which are explored in detail in the associated research papers. The coloured Poincaré algebras developed in this study may find applications in fundamental theories such as Yang-Mills gravity and non-commutative spacetime geometry. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth parameter, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending existing tractability results from undirected graphs to their directed counterparts. This approach also facilitates the derivation of a more efficient XP algorithm for graphs with bounded treewidth. Our results contribute to a deeper understanding of graph layouts and parameterized complexity, providing insight into the interplay between structural graph properties and planar drawings. To achieve these results, we introduced the first parameterized algorithm for identifying upward planar drawings and introduced new techniques and concepts, including SPQR trees and series-parallel graphs. Our SPQR tree-decomposition technique allows us to represent small trees within each recursive step, enabling more efficient recognition of upward planarity in subgraphs. Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem in multiple domains, 
such as robotics and computer vision, and remains an open challenge despite 
various techniques that employ learning from a few examples or purely visual 
approaches. These methods typically rely on temporary memory to track goal 
states but often fail to consider the constant visual context in real-world 
scenarios. Motivated by human memory behavior during goal-oriented tasks, 
we propose the MemoNav system that leverages a similar mechanism. 
MemoNav significantly outperforms existing visual navigation methods by 
maintaining a dynamic short-term memory of environmental cues in a queue. 
It employs a transformer-based observer that efficiently updates queue front 
and rear with relevant cues in every frame, removing less important ones. 
The observer uses a multi-step queue management strategy involving cue age, 
spatial position, and head pose to determine cue retention or replacement. 
Additionally, we introduce the MiniSim algorithm to efficiently train the 
observer using self-supervised learning. MiniSim maximizes navigation 
performance by mimicking the observer's cue selection process. 
Experimental results on the AirSim virtual helicopter platform reveal MemoNav 
achieves superior navigation performance with fewer training examples and at a 
faster pace compared to previous best approaches.

The DTW distance is widely applied in time series analysis across classification, clustering, and similarity search tasks. Nevertheless, conventional DTW is faced with drawbacks including high computational cost, particularly when coupled with complex preprocessing techniques, and its optimal utilization is heavily dependent on the expertise of the analyst. In response to these challenges, we propose the enhanced Pruned DTW (EAPrunedDTW) algorithm. EAPrunedDTW builds upon the pruned DTW, incorporating an advanced early stopping approach that ensures alignment precision and modifies the criteria for initiating and terminating pruned DTW. Furthermore, we introduce a heuristic for selecting the best pruned DTW path, thereby enhancing the algorithm's efficiency while retaining its accuracy. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that EAPrunedDTW significantly outperforms DTW and state-of-the-art approaches in terms of alignment time and accuracy, as well as indexing performance, particularly on modern CPU architectures that feature single-threaded execution. In specific, EAPrunedDTW boasts a speedup of up to 15 times over DTW, up to 7 times over EADTW, and on par with ESDTW, while also offering improved scalability through parallel processing capabilities. The proposed algorithm, along with accompanying experimental data and a demonstrative implementation, is publicly available at https://github.com/alexandremoreira/EAPrinnedDTW. Junction variability analysis across multiple datasets reveals that EAPrinnedDTW accurately captures the underlying time series patterns across most datasets, albeit with some discrepancies on ECG-108, where the pruned DTW path does not entirely reflect the optimal alignment. Nonetheless, the dataset indicates that the optimal DTW path is frequently analogous to the pruned DTW alignment, as identified by the proposed algorithm. To this end, we suggest utilizing the EAPrinnedDTW distance as a viable alternative to DTW for time series analysis, given its enhanced efficiency and accuracy. In addition, we propose this distance measure as a criterion for the definition of the pruned DTW distance itself. Furthermore, the proposed approach effectively addresses two of the major drawbacks associated with DTW, namely its computational intensity and the necessity for expert interpretation. The empirical findings suggest that the EAPrinnedDTW distance effectively captures the underlying patterns of the time series on all tested datasets except ECG-108, as validated by the high correlation between the EAPrinnedDTW distance and the optimal DTW distance. To improve this, we developed an automated testing tool that can encourage the use of testing best practices among programmers by providing personalized recommendations. Our initial research assessed the effectiveness of this tool among 34 senior students who used it in a two-month period while working on personal projects. The results revealed a notable increase in the frequency of using the recommended testing best practices by nearly 50%. To gain a deeper understanding of how to further improve the tool, we conducted in-depth interviews with 13 students, gathering valuable insights on its usability, usefulness, and potential for promoting a testing culture among programmers. In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling the unpredictability of black-box machine learning methods. However, automated techniques for generating explanations often require substantial computational resources and produce explanations that are difficult for humans to understand. This study develops a framework for creating tailored, human-friendly explanations by combining rule-based approaches with the application of principles from cognitive linguistics and psychology to produce explanations that are both accurate and easy to grasp. Our framework takes explanations generated through automated means and reformats them using simpler language to improve their clarity and coherence. This process involves the use of concepts from linguistics and psychology to identify and address complex structures within explanations, allowing them to be rewritten in a more straightforward manner. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a case study involving the need for clear explanations in medical diagnostic decisions made by deep learning algorithms. Specifically, our framework is applied to the problem of providing understandable reasons for a deep learning algorithm's diagnosis that a human physician also finds accurate. We evaluate the quality of our framework by comparing the clarity and coherence of explanations generated before and after being processed, utilizing both automated assessment tools and human evaluators to gauge performance. Results show that our framework significantly improves the clarity and coherence of explanations generated through automated means, leading to improved outcomes in both coherence and coherence-granularity assessments, along with positive feedback from human evaluators. Further research is required to expand the set of linguistic constructs used to assess the structure of explanations and to explore the effective application of our framework across a broader range of domains. Our software implementation and additional resources are publicly available at: https://github.com/jv-hern/xplain. https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.10523

Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to understand the root cause. A thorough examination of the over-smoothing phenomenon and Graph Convolutional Networks is presented in this article, including an estimation of the upper limit for its occurrence. The study sheds light on the pivotal elements contributing to over-smoothing and offers empirical evidence validating various countermeasures to mitigate it. Moreover, this research provides a comprehensive review of the effectiveness of these methods in preventing over-smoothing and promoting more intricate network architectures. Interestingly, our findings indicate that some techniques are not only capable of preventing over-smoothing but also enhance the network's capacity to capture complex patterns. This research aims to stimulate discussion, encourage theoretical advancements in Graph Convolutional Networks, and stimulate the development of more effective methods to mitigate over-smoothing. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/GUoT-EIILABC/Over-Smoothing.git.

This work builds upon the transverse momentum quark model and incorporates the aligned quark spin vector k$_{+}$ in place of the usual momentum $\bar{k}$ in the kernel, thereby retaining its momentum order and allowing the form factor to depend on k$_{+}$. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the efficient creation of highly specialized thin film devices. Yet, there's a critical issue: confirming the occurrence of remote epitaxy. We've developed a new approach using second-order angular resolved photoemission spectroscopy to identify distinct variations in the surface structure of a remote epitaxial film. Our theoretical models and experimental results suggest that rHeusler, a Heusler compound with a remote epitaxy variant, exhibits a lattice distortion different from its bulk counterpart. This difference is reflected in the formation of a quasi 2D film with a specific angle between its lattice and the lattice of a single graphene layer. Furthermore, our calculations show that this particular Heusler compound grows with a particular orientation on graphene, suggesting that rHeusler has a tetragonal structure with a particular dimension. Finally, our calculations and experimental results suggest that the epitaxial film has a specific thickness and growth characteristic, implying that the occurrence of remote epitaxy can be confirmed through the analysis of the epitaxial film's structure. Our findings suggest that the use of advanced techniques, such as ARPS, can facilitate the discovery and understanding of the various growth mechanisms of thin film devices. Our research, therefore, represents an important step in the development of remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene. \end{abstract}

This research proposes a profit-sharing agreement model that allows content providers and internet service providers to split revenues in proportion to their efforts in meeting network congestion and demand requirements. By introducing a spot market for internet service, the model incentivizes providers to invest optimally in network quality and demand management, resulting in improved social welfare and stability. The model is implemented through a two-tier market system where content providers set a baseline price for their content, and internet service providers bid for the right to supply it, leading to the discovery of an equilibrium where each provider's output equals their perceived demand. A numerical example illustrates the benefits of this model, as it outperforms a scenario where the government regulates quality and demand, achieving only half the possible social welfare in the process. Furthermore, the model exhibits pro-social incentives unique to recurring games where all participants maintain their level of effort over time. Specifically, the model exhibits characteristics of a Levitan-Thompson style proof, where content providers and internet service providers engage in a mutual agreement to maintain their current levels of effort in the future, provided all participants agree to do the same. As a result, the phenomenon of multiple equilibria arises naturally in this context, as different groups of providers may agree to maintain their current levels of effort in the future, while agreeing to disagree in the process, ultimately leading to the discovery of an equilibrium where all participants maintain their current levels of effort in the future, provided all possible groups of providers agree to do the same. As an alternative to government regulation, the model presents an unprecedented level of pro-social incentives not seen before in the context of internet congestion, where all participants maintain their current levels of effort over time, ultimately discovering an equilibrium where content providers set a baseline price for their content in proportion to their requirements, while internet service providers bid for the right to supply it in the process, resulting in improved network quality and demand requirements in the long run in the process. The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly equivalent states, as true adjoint invariance does not generally hold for states. This analysis highlights a crucial distinction in understanding the nature of the algebra and its representation when working with general physical states as opposed to compactly supported linear functionals. Specifically, the property of weak containment provides a framework for the characterization of the algebra itself. Furthermore, the failure of true adjoint invariance often indicates that the state is unable to define a representation that is subalgebraic, implying a lack of meaningful physical significance in such instances. We also examine the implications of these findings in the context of standard non-relativistic quantum mechanics. Additionally, these results contribute to a deeper understanding of the structural aspects of the algebra, as these findings are equally applicable to the algebra itself, highlighting certain general properties that are inherent to all C*-algebras. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods are ideal for this purpose.  One such method is cardiac auscultation, which involves listening to the heart sounds produced by the heart's functioning, allowing for the identification of abnormal heart functions. This technique has been used for centuries to diagnose heart conditions.  However, accurately identifying the conditions from these sounds is a difficult task for non-experts and sometimes even experts.  Research in this area focuses on developing techniques to analyze cardiac sounds for diagnosing various heart conditions.  Several studies have been conducted to improve the accuracy of cardiac condition diagnosis using machine learning and deep learning techniques.  This work explores the use of a more efficient deep learning architecture, called DenseNets, for making cardiac condition predictions from heart sound recordings.  Specifically, a DenseNet-based graph is proposed to improve the accuracy of cardiac condition diagnosis.  The DenseNet graph is composed of 10 consecutive segments of 0.75 seconds each of the heart sound recording, and the model uses 40 features derived from spectral characteristics as its nodes.  The model is trained using 724 recordings from the ESC dataset and tested using 192 recordings from the ESC dataset as well as 308 recordings from the Heart Sound and Disease dataset. A twist is utilized as a localized element in the study of topological K-theory. 
Within the framework of equivariant analysis, twists are categorized into four distinct forms, which can be visualized geometrically. 
This paper examines all possible forms of twists for a torus and a Klein bottle, and proves that each is isomorphic to the twisted K-theory of a specific divisor, equivalent to the twisted K-theory of the divisor itself with an added shift. 
As a consequence, the twisted K-theory of a line, both with and without equivariant treatment, is found to be isomorphic to the topological K-theory of the circle, rather than the 2-torus as initially suggested. 
Additionally, the study shows that the twisted K-theory of the torus can be represented by symbols derived from the torus's fundamental group. 
Finally, the findings imply that the twisted K-theory of any manifold that is equivariantly equivalent to the torus or Klein bottle is isomorphic to the topological K-theory of the manifold's divisor. 
Analogously, the twisted homology of any manifold that is equivariantly equivalent to the torus or Klein bottle can be found to be isomorphic to the homology of the manifold's divisor. 
These results extend existing findings in the literature. 
An alternative proof method for the already established result in Eisenbud and Neumann's work on the homology of divisors has been included in this paper.

ADHD is a widely prevalent psychiatric condition that has been challenging to diagnose accurately. The advancement in computational capabilities and machine learning methods has enabled researchers to investigate the use of resting-state fMRI imaging data for classifying ADHD. In contrast to prior studies, which often relied on the entire brain, this research focused on pinpointing the essential regions for utilizing a deep learning-based classification. For this purpose, the data from the ADHD 200 Global Competition were employed, comprising fMRI scans of 82 individuals, including 41 with ADHD and 41 controls. The data were analyzed after extracting the time series from specific brain regions using the Hammersmith Fock Brain Template. A convolutional neural network was designed, trained, and evaluated on the dataset to determine the effectiveness of utilizing a subset of brain regions for classification. The results revealed that using the left default mode network and right frontal areas allowed for 81.95% accuracy in distinguishing ADHD from controls, surpassing the performance achieved with the entire brain. This research facilitated the identification of the most influential brain regions for ADHD diagnosis using machine learning-based classification with a deep learning framework. Moreover, it highlighted the potential of automatically detecting and mapping the essential regions for classification, which could be applied to other tasks in neuroimaging. Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), have been analyzed by recent studies using machine learning techniques to forecast diagnoses based on CTNs, a task known as International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding. Annotating medical data can be particularly labor-intensive due to the time and effort required to read CTNs and understand their context. This study re-examines the value of reading CTNs before annotating, exploring the impact of merely glancing at them on the accuracy of ICD coding. Our research utilized a simple, quick annotation method called 'Eye Catcher' that allowed physicians to spot essential information in CTNs by focusing on key phrases. By implementing this approach, we observed a notable increase in the accuracy of ICD coding, highlighting the significance of briefly reviewing CTNs when annotating medical data. Our findings suggest that merely glancing at CTNs can enhance the quality of annotations, particularly when incorporating clinical expertise. This simple yet effective approach may serve as a model for other medical annotation tasks that involve enhancing the accuracy of annotations when reviewing medical text. Our code is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/serdar-ozturk/eye_catcher. 

Our paper discusses the details of the proposed approach, providing statistical analysis and comparing it to a more time-consuming but accurate annotation method.

Let $R$ be a polynomial ring in $n$ variables over a field $k$. A monomial ideal $I$ within this ring is considered. This paper explores almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes and provides specific classifications for certain types of ideals, including polymatroidal Veronese type and polymatroidal quadratic, based on the Newton pairs/pairs and algebraic Bethe equations, ultimately demonstrating that certain extended polymatroidal square-free divisors meet these criteria. As a result, we can conclude that certain previously defined polymatroidal square-free divisors meet the criteria for almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes. Furthermore, the paper establishes that certain types of monomial ideals whose minimal generators are in combinatorial relationship meet the criteria for almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes. Specifically, it classifies ideal types such as quadratic, Veronese type, and extended Veronese type as almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes. Additionally, it proves that certain types of ideals meet the criteria for almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes, including Gorenstein-regular, strongly Cohen-Macaulay, and power-critical monomial ideals, based on the Newton non-pairs/pairs and algebraic Bethe equations. Critical monomial ideal types, including UPM, QPM, and VM, are shown to meet the criteria for almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that certain types of ideals meet the criteria for almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes, including biquadratic and extended biquadratic ideals. Finally, it is shown that certain types of ideals meet the criteria for almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes, including bi-Veronese type and extended bi-Veronese type ideals. These results generalize previous findings on polymatroidal Newton non-pairs/pairs and algebraic Bethe equations. The study concludes by proposing speculation on Newton non-pairs/pairs and algebraic Bethe equations for arbitrary monomial ideals. The speculation is supported by examples. The paper also includes additional background and a detailed analysis of its results. Additionally, it includes a list of open problems and potential areas of study. These open problems could provide the basis for future research in this field."

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in data is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative way to process data using techniques such as quantum neural networks and variational quantum eigensolvers. An essential aspect of these methods is the comparison of states, typically achieved using trace distance or overlap measurement; however, these approaches are impractical for large-scale problems due to the exponential expansion of resources required. Our proposal for a scalable quantum-based measurement of comparison involves utilizing an ancillary qubit to enhance comparison accuracy, effectively treating trace distance as a probability of measurement outcome. This approach is exemplified through a simple classification task in a binary classification system, where the proposed method surpasses traditional measurement methods in terms of classification efficiency, particularly as the number of data points increases. Furthermore, our idea can be adapted for use in hybrid quantum-classical networks by partitioning the computational task among available qubits. Although our example of binary classification might seem basic, its potential for success suggests the possibility of successful applications of this comparison method in more complex machine learning scenarios, contributing to the evolution of quantum computing as a viable data processing tool. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in addressing image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance optimization efficiency and resist noise. A differentiable two-way communication process is created between the renderer and solver by incorporating this technique. Specifically, the renderer generates synthetic images based on scene parameters, while the solver refines scene parameters using optimization to minimize the discrepancy between predicted and target images. This process employs neural radiance fields as scene representations, and the initial renderer can even be made non-occluding. The researcher then explores three inverse problems - image synthesis, reconstruction, and editing - by leveraging differentiable rendering and optimization. The image synthesis task is considered resolved once the renderer and solver converge to a stable equilibrium, where the generated images exactly match the target image. For image reconstruction, the researcher demonstrates the effectiveness of differentiable rendering on several challenging tasks, such as deblurring, deraining, super-resolution, and occlusion removal. The majority of these experiments rely on a novel self-supervised learning framework. Finally, the researcher applies differentiable rendering to a traditional image inpainting approach, significantly outperforming the baseline on inpainting tasks involving both real-world and synthetic data. The researcher expects this work to inspire future research in this domain and hopes the provided code will facilitate replication and adaptation of these techniques. Our research proposes an innovative framework that integrates Bayesian methods and Markov models to estimate traffic flow, leveraging the longitudinal correlation structure present in sequential traffic sensor data. This approach considers the temporal dynamics and uncertainty associated with each road segment's invasion probability, enabling the quantification of both mean and variance biases in traffic estimates. Our performance benchmarks reveal that this Markov-Bayes method surpasses traditional and state-of-the-art techniques in terms of accuracy and practical applicability, particularly in scenarios involving low sample rates, short sequence lengths, and moderate noise levels. Notably, our results indicate that minimizing variance is just as crucial as achieving precise mean estimates when selecting appropriate traffic sensor samples. This study's findings offer valuable insights for developing effective traffic inference methods, with potential applications in estimating traffic flow, managing traffic patterns, and informing transportation decisions. Our open-source implementation, complete R code, and a related tutorial are available online for reproduction purposes. Moreover, our analysis highlights the practical significance of our work, as successfully yielding a 90%+ classification rate in traffic invasion probability estimation, which can facilitate a 2-4 fold reduction in the number of required samples for future predictions. Our research has significant implications for estimating traffic flow, managing traffic patterns, and intelligent transportation systems, as well as the broader fields of transportation engineering and data analytics. In an array of nonlinear oscillators with random frequencies and purely conserved interactions, global phase coherence is demonstrated to occur within finite networks and further examined as it collapses through the generation of localized periodic waves following a parameter adjustment. The observed phase transition is classified using the concepts of Berezinskii criterion and Landau theory, corresponding to a Berezinskii regime characterized by isolated periodic wave patterns termed phase waves. An analytical model, derived from the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, effectively predicts the phase wave period and amplitude in relation to the system's parameters. The Berezinskii regime can be contrasted with scenarios involving disorder-induced global phase coherence in coupled oscillators and the effects of nonlinearity in the same type of systems. Additionally, we explore the possibility of storing information within the system by adjusting the nonlinearity and find that the resulting patterns exhibit complexity consistent with the concept of information being encoded in the disorder of the system. Lastly, the possibility of utilizing these periodic waves as information carriers is discussed. Due to their localized nature, these phase waves could serve as optimal information carriers despite certain limitations associated with their utilization as information channels. The unique behavior of these phase waves may find practical applications in the storage and transmission of information within localized regions of the system. Moreover, the analytical model developed could be adapted for studying phase transitions in one-dimensional systems exhibiting Berezinskii behavior and applying quantum field theories involving double-well potentials. Conversely, the inherent randomness of the system could be likened to the effects of magnetic disorder in two-dimensional superconductors. Ultimately, the study of these phase transitions may offer insights into the underlying physics of the Bose glass phase and the interplay between disorder and quantum fluctuations. Due to their intricate structure, the study of these phase transitions may also be relevant to exploring the quantum behavior of systems exhibiting Berezinskii behavior and the effects of disorder on quantum field theories. Furthermore, the possibility exists to utilize these phase transitions as a means of exploring the effects of disorder on quantum systems through the manipulation of periodic wave patterns. By adjusting the system's parameters, the study finds that the average energy of these waves can be likened to the behavior of a double-well potential during a quantum phase transition, thereby enabling the examination of disorder-induced phase transitions via numerical simulations of these periodic wave patterns. The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their synergy with additional steps to ensure each step is at least a certain distance from previous ones, generating uniform trees in a smaller subset of the total tree population. While the modified processes retain their quick generation time, the new algorithms guarantee the generated trees fall within a specific subcategory, holding a constant probability relative to the total tree count. By applying these algorithms, this study shows how to efficiently sample a particular subset of trees from a given graph. The research also explores the accuracy of approximate methods that estimate tree properties based on random walks, demonstrating these estimates are accurate but only approach the true value as the graph becomes increasingly complex. These findings are further expanded to understand the properties of trees themselves. The theorems developed to explain these outcomes are independently significant, contributing to our understanding of graph theory. The research concludes by applying its results to volunteer fleets and random networks, using real-world examples to illustrate its impact. One such model demonstrates the potential for manual adjustment of parameters to optimize a particular outcome. Additionally, the paper examines the discrepancy between expected tree properties and those obtained through Wilson's algorithm for regular trees. This investigation reveals an intriguing pattern within these discrepancies. Finally, the research explores alternative methods of approximating tree properties, revealing some instances where these approximations accurately represent the actual value, while others require correction factors to achieve precision. These findings contribute to our understanding, providing straightforward mathematical proof for results previously obtained through numerical methods. Moreover, this research discovers the phase transition behavior in the approximations' accuracy, marking a significant finding in its own right. The computational methods proposed are economically viable, requiring only a relatively low number of steps compared to alternative methods. To illustrate the potential impact, the research estimates that approximating the dominant eigenvalue of a 10,000-node graph could be achieved in under 17 seconds. Conversely, direct computation would take an estimated 1.3 minutes. Similarly, generating a random spanning tree requires around 17 computations, while the direct approach necessitates roughly 10,000 steps. Consequently, this research indicates that the proposed methods are both efficient and feasible. This research introduces a large, multi-modal dataset known as MusicTM-Dataset, comprising a massive collection of 94,812 music videos along with three types of corresponding text modalities: lyrics, song names, and album names. The dataset is uniquely paired with a rich set of metadata, including song duration, genre, and year of release. The aim behind creating MusicTM-Dataset is to address a critical challenge in developing a unified representation for cross-modal learning: the lack of a large, publicly accessible dataset featuring a consistent set of modalities. By building upon the concepts from VideoTM-Dataset and using a similar data processing framework, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 94,812 triplets is established, with each triplet featuring a multi-modal combination of three text modalities and a unifying visual content. The dataset's validity is further reinforced by incorporating a 10-way imbalanced music genre classification task, thereby providing a robust benchmark for evaluating the effectiveness of different cross-modal learning techniques across diverse scenarios. As our first attempt at exploring this dataset, a moment-level multi-modal learning framework is proposed, leading to a notable accuracy rate of 0.896 in the F1-score for music genre classification. The dataset, along with its accompanying code, has been made publicly available for research purposes. One major obstacle when utilizing Linked Data lies in developing intuitive and user-friendly interfaces accessible to individuals who aren't technologically inclined. To address this, Ontodia enables diagrammatic data visualization, illustrated in this study with the Wikidata dataset. We've introduced enhancements to a natural language interface that facilitates the exploration and querying of Linked Data entities. By utilizing distributional semantic models to identify and rank entity properties associated with user input in Ontodia, the method enhances the user experience in navigating the data. The utility of this interface is particularly evident when dealing with entities lacking clear labels or when multiple entities are involved, as is the case during entity disambiguation.
