In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates incident wave patterns with internal distributions within a volume, and previously this correlation was leveraged to increase energy delivered to a target. This study determines a general set of constraints governing the eigenvalues and modes within any such scattering system, and applies these constraints to the specific case of non-propagating modes in a particular type of scattering system, revealing restrictions on the concentration of energy within a defined area just inside a boundary. A fundamental limit was also discovered for the minimum amount of energy that can be confined within a small region near a boundary in a given volume relative to the total energy present in that volume. The minimum energy ratios achieved approach specific limit values as the exterior and interior properties of the scattering system match. Furthermore, the fundamental limit was found to be similar to previously established inverse scattering limits. The properties governing the confinement of energy were also found to be intact when an optically thick layer covered the exterior of the scattering system, and it was observed that optically thick materials with similar properties can be constructed which do not scatter energy at all. The potential to increase the confinement of energy within a small region by intentionally designing a system with similar properties but poor external characteristics was also explored. Our research systematically explores how static strain influences the valley Hall effect in theoretical models of two-dimensional materials. By applying a periodic lateral force, we observe the emergence of a valley Hall response characterized by valley-dependent displacement patterns. To mimic the impact of static strain effectively, we develop a robust and efficient algorithm for solving the strained Bloch wavevector, allowing us to tackle situations with valency and anisotropic elastic properties. Moreover, we examine how this valley Hall effect is affected by strain amplitude and frequency, and our findings reveal distinct responses based on whether the strain is valency-dependent or independent. Additionally, we connect our theoretical model to recent experiments involving strained black phosphorus, and our analysis sheds light on the material parameters that determine the valley Hall effect. Furthermore, our research demonstrates the versatility of our computational approach, and we briefly discuss potential avenues for applying the valley Hall effect in other two-dimensional materials. To facilitate reproducibility, all of our code and the strained Bloch wavevector solver have been made publicly available. Nonetheless, our attempt to share a peer-review compatible version of our code and data has been hindered by the incompatibilities between existing frameworks. As a result, our code and data reside primarily on the repository at https://git.lmpt.uqam.ca/valleyHall/valleyHall/-/tree/v1.0.0, and on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/alexandrecote/valleyHall. In the future, we intend to expand our computational approach to accommodate dynamic strain and electron-electron interactions. Moreover, we plan to explore alternative numerical methods for solving the strained Bloch wavevector, and to apply our computational tool to a diverse range of two-dimensional materials. Ultimately, our ultimate objective is to utilize our computational tool to design materials exhibiting valley Hall effects that are both robust and adaptable. By leveraging our computational framework, we aspire to identify the optimal material parameters that can be achieved through advanced materials design. Furthermore, our research may be extended to other properties and materials by replacing the specific mathematical operators and objects that are unique to two-dimensional materials. Consequently, our computational methodology is versatile and can be adapted to a wide range of situations. Additionally, our code and data are highly customizable and can be utilized in the following areas: calculating the Hall effect in two-dimensional materials under dynamic strain, determining the impact of valency on the Hall effect in two-dimensional materials, simulating the Hall effect in black phosphorus subject to dynamic strain, and exploring the valley Hall effect in two-dimensional materials

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. This approach flexibly accommodates various error types and can be easily extended to support the full fault-tolerant decoding scenario, offering around a hundredfold speedup over the widely used pure state decoding method. Moreover, we discovered that our decoder excelled at situations where noise levels were low but unexpected spikes in error rates occurred, outperforming traditional methods in such scenarios. In contrast, a proposed novel approach aims to optimize the structure of an information space by prioritizing ease of navigation and information accessibility. Our research incorporates Ecological Momentary Assessment records, gathered through individuals' mobile devices, alongside Electronic Health Records. The integration of these EMA records significantly enhances the accuracy of suicidal ideation prediction, surpassing traditional EHR-based methods that solely utilize clinical data. Our findings indicate that the incorporation of EMA records significantly improves the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, from 0.82 to 0.88. We analyze the distinct aspects of ERA and EHR data, revealing dissimilar patterns in each, as identified by Random Forest feature importance and dimensionality reduction techniques. The emergence of contrasting features suggests novel aspects of suicidal ideation, encompassing symptoms and factors such as sleep patterns, social interactions, and emotional states. Our analysis indicates that the EMA aspect most closely related to suicidal ideation involves individuals' reports of depressive symptoms, sleep quality, and emotional states, as opposed to the EHR aspect, which is more heavily influenced by clinical interventions, hospitalizations, and comorbidities. This study offers a fresh perspective on predicting suicidal ideation, highlighting the significance of dynamic, real-time mental health state captures in precision psychiatry. Our method can be applied to other mental health disorder predictions, such as major depressive disorder. A comprehensive X-ray observation of the Type II supernova remnant Cassiopeia A was conducted using the Chandra telescope, yielding significant insights into its high-energy emission. Notably, polarized radiation was detected within a faint, diffuse region surrounding the northwest jet at a 4σ confidence level, with an polarization degree and angle of 35% ± 17% and 26° ± 17° respectively, at a 1σ confidence. This discovery supports the synchrotron model explaining the X-ray emission in this region. Observing the entire remnant with high spatial resolution and spectral resolution can help identify circularly polarized synchrotron radiation, thus providing essential information about magnetic field orientation and the distribution of relativistic electrons in SNR environments. Employing the Chandra instrument with the help of 12 observations totaling 800 ks of exposure time, we analyzed X-ray data with a spatial resolution of 1 arcsec to 10 arcmin. As a result, we detected synchrotron radiation in multiple regions, including a faint, diffuse area surrounding the northwest jet, and found that polarized radiation at 2.5-5 keV accounts for 20-40% of the total emission in this band. Moreover, we identified a north-south jet with Compton backscatter echoes originating from the 2003 and 2004 observations, and detected a west jet in front of a prominent proton-driven shock front, which we speculate could be a forward shock modified by a rapidly moving shock front. Additionally, we observed a mixed magnetic field structure dominated by toroidal field components in multiple regions, and found that a relativistic electron population with a spectral index of 2.1-2.3 and age of 4000-7000 years best explains the X-ray synchrotron emission in these areas, thus providing essential information about the local energy spectrum, age, and magnetic field structure. This research is based on a comprehensive X-ray analysis of Cassiopeia A, where we examine polarization, spectral, spatial, and temporal characteristics, and use the Chandra observations to uncover the remnant's complex magnetic field and particle distribution, which we find to be highly irregular and affected by the powerful magnetic field in this region. By applying lattice regularization, we can determine various thermodynamic properties, such as energy density, pressure, and sound velocity, in addition to the speed of light in the background of a fixed background field. This behavior is consistent with the hypothesis that dense matter is composed of deconfinued quarks. However, we note that our results depend on the choice of background field. We examined over 8,000 massive, edge-on disk galaxies from the SDSS dataset, focusing on two types: S and U galaxies. Our analysis revealed that U galaxies have distinct characteristics, including bluer optical colors and higher star formation rates, compared to S galaxies. U galaxies, particularly those with more extreme warping, exhibited higher star formation rates. Contrary to expectations, U galaxies in groups and clusters do not show a correlation with the tidal force exerted by their nearest neighbor. However, U galaxies are more common in groups and clusters and share similarities with 'jellyfish' galaxies formed through ram-pressure stripping (RPS). This led us to suggest that RPS could be a potential mechanism explaining the presence of U galaxies in groups and clusters. Additionally, U galaxies in the local universe have a mass range similar to S galaxies, but those with higher masses are more common in groups and clusters. This implies that warping is more common in more densely packed environments and may be influenced by group/cluster environment, possibly through a shared halo effect. Further research is needed to determine the physical connection between a galaxy's disk and its surrounding halo. Three-dimensional topological insulators can be identified by a magnetoelectric coefficient with a quantized value, but it remains unclear how their properties behave when time-reversal symmetry is broken.  We investigate a model of a 3D topological insulator slab placed on a 2D substrate with weak disorder, and find that the surface of this insulator exhibits gapped states with no electronic transport due to strong disorder. However, very thin insulator layers exhibit quantized magnetoelectric properties despite being much thinner than the electronic mean free path. Moreover, our results suggest that the total magnetoelectric coefficient of the insulator is split into two components: one originating from the bulk and the other from the edges.  Due to excessive edge disorder, these edge states become imperceptible, and the magnetoelectric coefficient is largely produced by the bulk.  Conversely, our model also highlights the importance of considering all degrees of freedom, including those from edges, in the study of 2D systems with non-trivial topology.  Finally, our research indicates that the magnetoelectric coefficient can be used to diagnose insulator layers even when the layer thickness equals the mean free path or the layer thickness.  Our work paves the way for the exploration of magnetoelectric properties in thin films, opening up new avenues for the study and potential utilization of thin film systems.  Ultimately, the findings presented here can be extended for use in the analysis of various time-reversal symmetry-breaking systems, including those formed from heavy-fermion semiconductors and the surfaces of topological insulators. In systems featuring delayed nonlinearity, we observe chaotic diffusion as a typical trait, where it is found that modulating the time delay periodically leads to a significant enhancement of the diffusion coefficient by several orders of magnitude, especially when the modulation's average value equals the time delay. This diffusive behavior can be predicted through analytical calculations. Furthermore, we discovered that this diffusion can be optimized by adjusting the delay modulation period in accordance with the system's natural frequency, resulting in a substantial increase of the diffusion coefficient by up to 150 times, with this optimization achieving its maximum effectiveness when the average delay equals the time delay. This research offers a novel approach for enhancing diffusion in complex systems and potentially expands the scope of diffusive processes. Additionally, we propose a new concept of delay modulation to optimize chaotic diffusion, which may find applications in various fields involving nonlinear dynamics. It is worth noting that this study was conducted numerically and, as a result, is limited by the constraint of non-resonant conditions; however, further investigations based on analytical methods could help in understanding the resonance phenomena and extending the findings to nearly resonant cases. Based on these potential developments, we believe that this delay modulation strategy has significant potential for improving chaotic diffusion and could contribute meaningfully to nonlinear dynamics research. Finally, we outline several promising avenues for applying this concept in various fields involving nonlinear dynamics.

Discussions among developers encompass a variety of interactions, including in-person conversations and online comments, which are rich in context and can inform software development.  Understanding the thoughts shared during these interactions is essential to learning from them; therefore, we must extract and make sense of the content.  While conversations are often verbal and transitory, advancements in natural language processing technology allow us to capture and analyze the thoughts shared via online comments with greater accuracy.  By recognizing the value of these interactions for improving software, we can refer to the practice of examining and learning from them as "design mining."  In this paper, we describe our current progress in fully automating the process of discovering and interpreting the content of online comments within the GitHub repository of the DDD4T framework.  Our results show the potential of design mining to supply design options, convey stakeholders' opinions, and remind developers of past recommendations, all without requiring human involvement.  However, our findings also highlight challenges related to accurately recognizing design-related comments, effectively summarizing the opinions of multiple contributors, and differentiating between constructive and unconstructive feedback.  Addressing these challenges could enhance the effectiveness of design mining as a beneficial practice in software development.  Our implementation of design mining is unique to the GitHub repository of the DDD4T framework and awaits further evaluation to determine its general applicability to other design repositories.  In the near future, we aim to expand our research to other areas, such as improving the quality of open source projects by analyzing the content of issue reports.  Ultimately, we hope to contribute design-related improvements to software projects by design mining.  Our design mining process consists of three stages: preliminary examination, comment classification, and opinion summary.  In the preliminary examination, we manually assess the design repository on GitHub to determine whether it is suitable for design mining.  In the comment classification, we employ a machine learning algorithm using a dataset of labeled comments to classify online comments as design-related or otherwise.  In the opinion summary, we apply a natural language processing algorithm to extract the content of online comments within the GitHub repository of the DDD4T framework and summarize the opinions of multiple contributors. A proposed model explains the existence of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter.
Dark energy and dark matter stem from a false vacuum state's random energy fluctuations, characterized by large-scale negative and short-scale positive pressures, respectively, representing incoherent and coherent aspects of the fluctuations.
Gravity arises from the coherent fluctuations within the coherent field of the Higgs-like field associated with the ground state of the fluctuations.
Conversely, the adiabatic fluctuations corresponding to the perturbations of radiation contribute to the formation of structure through the overdensities acting as primordial perturbations.
It is suggested that the residual effects of the adiabatic fluctuations could give rise to primordial primordial black holes as a possible source of dark matter. 
Furthermore, the connection between the coherent field and the Higgs field implies that primordial black holes may decay into particles comprising the dark matter that formed them. 
Additionally, the potential for particle decay into dark energy due to the pressure of the coherent fluctuations is explored. 
Lastly, possible avenues for experimental verification are discussed, including the creation of primordial black holes in high-energy particle collisions and the creation of dark energy and dark matter from the decay of the coherent fluctuations themselves. 
Ultimately, the objective of this model is to offer an alternative to the standard cosmological model for the origins of gravity, dark energy, and dark matter.

We are introducing a new concept called weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within a commutative ring with identity, which serves as an extension to the existing notion of weakly prime ideals. A prime ideal $I$ in a ring $R$ is said to be weakly $1$-absorbing if for every three non-unit elements $a,b,$ and $c$ in $R$ where their product is non-zero and within $I$, it holds that either the product is completely contained within $I$ or at least two factors are explicitly contained within $I$. Our research will delve into the properties of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals, including the characterization of such ideals in rings that are (M,N)-chain free. We will specifically examine the case of a ring being $(M,5)$-chain free, allowing us to derive multiple theorems in this context. To facilitate our analysis, the properties of strongly $\eta$-clean rings will also be explored. Furthermore, we will provide illustrative examples to substantiate our theoretical claims. Lastly, our findings will be generalized to the context of non-commutative rings with a Samuelian ring structure. The key properties of a Samuelian ring will be re-characterized and additional examples provided to substantiate our claims. Our research aims to contribute to the existing literature on these types of rings as well as provide novel insights into the characteristics of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing a photonic device to precisely replicate a reference spectrum's replication pattern. As a result, concurrent identification of multiple substances becomes possible without the need for simultaneous illumination with various light sources. We outlined a general approach applicable to distinct photonic platforms and illustrated its effectiveness using a silicon photonic platform, allowing for non-contact, room-temperature analysis of multiple gas species. Our research showcases the potential of photonic technology for innovative spectroscopy applications. Nonetheless, our example involving gas detection also highlights limitations associated with conventional spectroscopy based on a NMR-like approach, primarily related to specificity and sensitivity concerns. Meanwhile, our template-based correlator design offers enhanced accuracy and robustness against noise interference. Moreover, this approach may be modified to accommodate various photonic platforms, specific to the target samples, thus increasing specificity without compromising spectral resolution. The template spectrum can be derived from computational simulations of interacton between light and the sample, or from a pre-characterized library of spectra. Moreover, this concept is not limited to spectroscopy but may also be applied in imaging and sensing applications, where a predetermined pattern is cross-correlated with a sample's natural signal to obtain valuable information. Our research has successfully demonstrated the capability of photonic technology to fundamentally transform conventional spectroscopy and sensing methods into cutting-edge technologies. This work was supported by the Strategic Research Grant and the Research Grant Scheme of the Research Office at the Hong Kong Polytechnic University. Additionally, our work benefited from collaboration with the Singapore Photonics Centre and the Nano Foundry and Photonic Manufacturing Research Centre at the Nanyang Technological University. Finally, the research was further enhanced by the support of the State Key Laboratory of Transduction Technology.

In the last few years, various machine learning models have emerged with the aim of tackling polypharmacy side effects, predicting medication interactions, and identifying ineffective medications. This paper takes a comparative approach, gathering key studies on these topics and analyzing their performance benchmarks, employed machine learning methods, and tested datasets. Our investigation highlights that "real-world proof" using external validation datasets and more diverse evaluation criteria, such as metric appropriateness and reproducibility, is needed to strengthen the trustworthiness of the models. Furthermore, we examine potential areas for improvement and suggest future research directions. To aid researchers, we create a comprehensive database of the collected studies, providing easy access to data via a public repository. This database aims to facilitate knowledge accumulation and boost the reliability of evaluation methods. Ultimately, we hope this survey and the associated repository inspire better research and inform future advancements in the application of machine learning to addressing polypharmacy-related challenges.

Imitation learning aims to eliminate the time-consuming task of creating optimal reward functions for agent training.  While imitation learning bypasses this step, the agent's behavior is not necessarily optimal; in fact, optimally-designed policies often require expert examples to be suboptimal.  Our research focuses on introducing a marginal reward to an imitation learning objective, such that the resulting optimal policy maximally captures the expert's behavior while achieving a better outcome.  Our marginal reward is based on a variational free energy term and can be optimized using supervised backpropagation; experiments in both discrete and continuous domains confirm the effectiveness of this method, achieving better performance than plain imitation learning and comparable results to more complex reward-design approaches.  Notably, our marginal reward can also be applied to tasks with image-based observations, thanks to our simplified variational inference model for action-space representations.  The resulting representations are efficient, easy to interpret, and can be used even in the absence of expert data.  Our research offers a practical solution for designing more optimal policies using imitation learning, and introduces a new variational inference model for action spaces that can be utilized in other research areas, such as representation learning and state representation design.  Additionally, our research provides a new variational inference model called Alpha- Variational Action Space (AVAS) that can be used for action-space representation in both discrete and continuous domains; AVAS successfully captures the structure of the action space in several experiments, and is more efficient than prior approaches such as Action Embedding and retrospective variational action space while achieving comparable performance in IL-only training settings.  Notably, our research also finds that the representations learned by AVAS can be used to improve performance in IL-only training settings by leveraging the learned latent variables to reweight expert trajectories using a supervised loss; this finding is confirmed in multiple experiments and highlights the practical value of the learned representations in real-world applications.  Furthermore, our research discovers that the representations learned by AVAS can be used to improve the transferability of the learned policy to new tasks by leveraging the learned latent variables to identify relevant expert trajectories in multiple experiments; this practical value is particularly valuable in real-world applications where resources are limited and prior knowledge can be leveraged to improve performance. A major uncertainty in determining the initial mass function (IMF) of the first stars relates to the unknown process by which secondary protostars form from the fragments of a collapsing gas cloud. In typical star-forming environments on the main branch, a developing star or protostar amplifies its surrounding magnetic field through differential rotation, creating a local, dense disk around it. However, this process relies on a disk already existing and a protostar being present within it, effectively preventing a new star from forming this way early on. Research has recently explored an alternative scenario in which a growing protostar or star amplifies the surrounding magnetic field through convective differential rotation, leading to the merger of magnetic islands and the creation of a disk around it, both in theoretical and observational studies. We investigate the formation of secondary protostars in a cosmological setting by advancing the original model that explained the formation of stellar systems, and demonstrate its application within a cosmological framework. This new understanding implies that stars or protostars with masses greater than approximately 10 solar masses could form quickly after the initial cosmic collapse, at a time equivalent to around 100 years after the Big Bang. Conversely, lower-mass stars, including those like the Sun, would require an extended period of time to form during the early phase of cosmic reionization. Moreover, we find that mass accumulation leading to the formation of massive (greater than 100 solar masses) stars, which are known as O or Wolf-Rayet stars, would occur over an extended period of time, potentially limiting the rate at which these stars form through the collapse of cosmic clouds. This research has significant implications for understanding various phenomena observed during the early phase of cosmic reionization, including the relative abundance of massive and lower-mass stars based on their spectral characteristics. Specifically, we find that these results could explain why we observe relatively few lower-mass stars in the ultraviolet spectrum yet numerous massive stars in the X-ray spectrum within these early cosmic environments. Finally, according to our calculations, the overall star formation rate within these early cosmic clouds could be limited by the rate at which cosmic metallicity increases due to ejection from existing stars, rather than simply fragmentation of the clouds. Association rule analysis is a widely used technique in Data Mining. This method involves partial implications between binary variables, which can be constrained by parameters such as confidence and support levels. We delve into the concept of redundancy among association rules from a theoretical perspective. Each transaction in a dataset can be viewed as a logical statement, and we investigate the idea that a partial implication can be derived from one or more earlier statements. We develop a framework for reducing the complexity of partial implications by introducing a new relation, denoted as \uceille{R}, which subsumes the set \ecaille{R} representing association rules. Furthermore, we demonstrate that \uceille{R} is composed of two components: a subset of \ecaille{R} representing redundant partial implications and another subset representing new, irredundant implications. We propose an algorithm to eliminate redundancy from association rules using \uceille{R} and provide experimental results for comparison with existing methods. We assess the efficiency of \uceille{R} in relation to association rule mining tasks via a parameter variation study. Lastingly, we explore potential applications of \uceille{R} in enhancing association rule analysis. To our knowledge, \uceille{R} offers a groundbreaking approach to tackling redundancy in association rule mining. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 2000 and 2014 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovers that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowers the odds of re-arrest and re-conviction, according to data from the North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation and the North Carolina Administrative Office of the Courts.  The data further show that receiving mental health treatment reduces the likelihood of future crimes by about 25% and lowers the chances of re-incarceration by around 35%.  The research also reveals disparities in the justice system related to race, with the benefits of mental health treatment varying among different groups: receiving mental health treatment lowers the odds of re-arrest among African Americans but raises the odds among whites, and while it reduces re-incarceration among both groups, the reduction is greater for Africans Americans (a 43% decrease versus a 29% decrease among whites).  The research suggests that the justice system is not uniformly effective in reducing recidivism, as the differences in the effectiveness of mental health treatment among different groups suggest inherent disparities within the system, as these disparities persist even when focusing on those who are not charged with new crimes (the "recidivism" analysis also includes future charges that are pending at the time of the data collection period). This research delves into a multi-aspect verification technique that integrates voice, language, and speech content for identifying individuals. To advance state-of-the-art performance, we suggest a multi-task network architecture that processes each modality separately before combining the feature vectors via a non-linear fusion method. The efficiency of this system is enhanced by exploiting the shared underlying characteristics present in the modalities. Experiments conducted on a dataset comprising multiple modalities yield a superior performance compared to single-modality and bi-modal systems, and comparable results to the current best performing systems. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that our trimodal system is capable of adapting to different data distributions more effectively. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. We also investigate the bias and consistency of these estimators and establish asymptotic normal distributions for the estimators using the Central Limit Theorem. Our results are applied to five specific parametric families: the normal, lognormal, Weibull, and Cauchy distributions. A simulation comparison highlights the efficiency of the GMLE in terms of minimized variance. Our work also contributes to the expansion of the Kiefer and Wolfowitz result to a more extensive range of applications. Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem.
This paper introduces a reliable framework that integrates data collection and
utilization under its control. The dependency relationship between utility and privacy
is taken into consideration, allowing the framework to balance these factors.
The framework incorporates a versatile set of privacy parameters, enabling the
adjustment of utility or privacy according to specific needs. To measure privacy,
the One-Sided Differential Privacy approach is used, ensuring that the addition of
new data does not decrease accuracy. The framework's reliability is demonstrated
through an accurate analysis of its reliability-utility tradeoff. Its effectiveness
is showcased in two real-world scenarios, specifically in the classification of
abnormal records detection and the prediction of skin diseases from skin images. 
The results show that the proposed framework yields significant improvements in
data utility without compromising privacy. The framework's potential for providing
dependable privacy and utility is also explored in various data publishing
situations. The integration of this framework with existing publishing methods
enables the enhancement of existing privacy mechanisms while ensuring the
dependability of privacy and utility. For instance, the integration with
k-Anonymization yields substantial OSDP improvements with minimal decrease in
utility. The combination of reliability and utility achieved by the proposed
framework surpasses that of conventional data publishing methods. The code for

The gas within protoplanetary disks exists in a uniform state around thousands of astronomical units, spanning from outer space to the inner regions near the host star. This uniform layer contains vast amounts of unseen material that played a pivotal role in the birth of planets within our solar system and exoplanets throughout the universe. A recent study using data from the Molecules with LAMBERT (M-WILDS) survey discovered two gas substructures in the protoplanetary disk surrounding the young star HD 97050. This disk is characterized by a pair of gas filaments that form at approximately 14 and 20 astronomical units from the host star. Observations indicate that the gas substructures in the HD 97050 disk exhibit properties of high-density spots that span across wide areas, rather than being the result of planet formation or magnetic winds as previously theorized for other disks. A potential explanation for the gas substructures in the HD 97050 disk involves the concept of electron impact ionization caused by X-ray emission from the host star. A numerical simulation based on this phenomenon reveals that the gas substructures can form and retain their current state due to the combination of radiation-driven gas flow and gas depletion caused by photoionization. This breakthrough research may lead to a new understanding of how gas substructures form and evolve in protoplanetary disks, and as such, the authors suggest further observational and analytical studies into the problem are warranted. A future study is planned that will utilize data from the Next Generation Athletic Trainer (NGAT) to gather new and critical observations of the gas substructures in the HD 97050 disk. Additionally, the authors plan to conduct a global analysis of the gas substructures in protoplanetary disks using data from the M-WILDS survey and other relevant studies in the field. This research will contribute to a broader comprehension of the gas substructures in protoplanetary disks, and as such, the authors are confident of receiving critical funding for this proposed study. A critical review of existing literature in the field reveals that the proposed study is original and deserves support. A potential alternative to this research by one of the authors is also proposed that involves studying the gas substructures in protoplanetary disks using data from the M-WILDS survey and other relevant studies in the field. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an integrated approach of flowcharts and modular code snippets, our tool empowers users to perform intricate data correlation and analysis, while maintaining high computational performance and efficiency. ETA's capabilities are further showcased through the demonstration of its application in the analysis of time-stamped data from two distinct sources: laser spectroscopy and particle detectors. With its innovative approach and user-friendly interface, ETA has the potential to revolutionize the analysis of time-stamped data in a wide range of fields. Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial distribution within the Milky Way, movement patterns, and the evidence of their physical connection. Our findings indicate that stellar strings are not stable, cohesive entities but rather groups of stars dispersing throughout the galaxy, and we discuss the possible origins of these structures as a result of the breaking apart of stellar clusters caused by galactic dynamics. Our research also highlights potential issues with the methods used to identify these structures, particularly the reliance on mathematical patterns in an anisotropic data set, and suggests alternative approaches for the detection of physically connected stellar groups in the galaxy. Our proposed outfit generator, called SGG, is an unconditional generator that creates high-quality, visually appealing outfit images. The system comprises three neural networks: an encoder, a middle generator, and a decoder. The first module is a modified U-Net that converges during pre-training with the target distribution of outfit images. The middle generator is a random vector generator that is learned alongside the decoder, which is a conventional U-Net, trained to map this generator output directly into an outfit image. We demonstrate SGG's effectiveness using the Fashion Outfit dataset and show via qualitative and quantitative analysis that it outperforms or surpasses or is on a par with existing fashion generators in terms of inversion, identity preservation and overall aesthetic compatibility. Notably, the output of SGG is more compatible with fashion norms when measured against the VGG scores metric. Notably, the output of SGG is more compatible with fashion norms, with the added benefit that its middle generator can be utilized to create compatible outfit configurations from individual garment images. The potential extensions of SGG are also explored in the study. The framework of quantum resource theory provides a flexible and adaptable method for examining diverse physical phenomena through the perspective of their underlying quantum states. This theoretical framework can be applied broadly due to its general and abstract nature. Within the realm of quantum resource theory, different types of resources are categorized into 'non-classical resources' and 'cloning resources'. Non-classical resources are those that cannot be created back into a classical state through local operations and projection measurements, while cloning resources are those that allow for creating multiple copies of the same state with the aid of additional information about the system. Our focus lies on exploring the characteristics of non-classical resources and cloning resources in the context of one-parameter families of quantum states. By utilizing the method of inverse projection, we are able to broaden the set of non-classical resources and demonstrate that any one-parameter family of quantum states that can be classified as non-classical resources is also capable of being classified as cloning resources. This discovery serves as a key indicator of the interconnectedness between non-classical resources and cloning resources. Our study further delves into the relationship between non-classical resources and cloning resources in the context of quadratic functions, and ultimately explores the potential for non-classical resources to be preserved under Markov evolution. This research is supported by multiple examples, including a description of the non-classical resources present in a system containing a pair of two-level systems interacting with a common one-dimensional reservoir, and a description of the non-classical resources present in a system containing a pair of two-level systems interacting with a shared one-dimensional reservoir and individual one-level systems. Our findings serve to expand our understanding of the characteristics of non-classical resources and cloning resources, and shed new light on the properties of one-parameter families of quantum states. Our analysis is also found to be relevant and applicable to recent experiments involving the preparation of non-classical states through the use of laser pulses and radiative decays. We select polynomial tempered distributions as the symbol class for this calculus. We then establish a key differential property and elucidate its mapping in relation to the commutant of a polynomial shift semigroup. As a concrete demonstration of its utility, we examine the function of a countable set of second derivative operators. Additionally, we identify a set of operators that corresponds to the compactness of the associated differential expression, and we demonstrate that these operators form a countable set. Finally, we provide evidence of an isomorphism between the $C^*$-algebra formed by the function of a countable set of differential operators and the algebra of polynomial functions on the positive half-axis. In conclusion, the function of a countable set of Laplace operators can be Brownian motion on a metric graph only if the graph is compact. Similarly, the function of a countable set of higher derivative operators on a graph or group can be expressed as iterated Brownian motion only if the graph or group is compact. Alternatively, this can be restated as the positive result that the iterated Brownian motion on a compact graph or group is equivalent to the function of the square of the Laplace operators and all higher derivative operators. Similarly, the function of the double Laplace vector bundle's finite rank projection operators can be expressed as iterated Brownian motion only if the source and target graphs are compact. A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a liquid substrate holding a particle raft by dipping a needle into it, the needle creates an obstacle that causes the raft to buckle due to capillary forces. X-ray tomography reveals that the breakdown of the raft occurs both at its edges and in the interior, forming intricate patterns. Simulations based on the elastic properties of the raft and the force exerted by the needle on the fluid allow us to accurately predict the observed failure mechanisms. Moreover, the influence of fluid dynamic forces can be excluded by performing experiments with a fluidless substrate, resulting in significantly different failure patterns. A parameter that characterizes the stiffness of the raft in relation to the force applied by the needle also effectively explains the differences in failure patterns observed in various experiments, further highlighting the importance of non-equilibrium dynamics in material breakdown. Moreover, by analyzing the statistical properties of the raft's volume, we gain a deeper understanding of the concept of fragility. Since the phenomenon of breakdown by buckling by a localized force is highly controllable, it has great potential for the development of materials with unique properties. Additionally, the intricate structure resulting from this type of failure could be exploited for the creation of highly porous materials with properties that are difficult to achieve through other methods, such as 3D laser printing. An important aspect in this context is the preservation of the material's mechanical properties, as the fabrication of similar structures by 3D printing often results in a loss of stability and the inability to withstand localized forces. By combining X-ray tomography with simulations based on the elastic properties of the material and the force exerted by the needle on the fluid, we are able to accurately determine the size distribution of pores in such structures, demonstrating the great potential of this type of material processing. As an example, we use this method to create materials with tailored pore sizes ranging from a few micrometers to over a hundred micrometers. Moreover, by analyzing the statistical properties of the raft's volume, we are able to explore the relationship between the material's fragility index and the stiffness of the raft in relation to the force applied, as well as the size distribution of pores in such structures, thereby contributing to our understanding of the dynamics of non-equilibrium material breakdown. One of these structures, featuring a buffer layer made from low-strain GaN, resulted in compressive strain strains affecting the valence band structure in a manner favorable for hole injection. Conversely, the strain in another structure, grown with strain relaxation from GaN, resulted in strain that was mostly tensile and less beneficial for device application due to its altered band structure. We present a novel module called Temporal Difference Estimator (TDE), an advanced model-free controller designed for robots navigating in complex marine environments. By integrating Gaussian Process (GP) regression into the Temporal Difference learning framework, our TDE module enables robots to efficiently learn control policies that optimize rewards while adapting to uncertain underwater settings. The incorporation of GP regression allows the model to automatically account for uncertainties and nonlinear relationships encountered in the marine environment. In our experiments, the proposed TDE module was implemented on an autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) and evaluated using simulation-based scenarios, resulting in successful policy optimization and adaptive learning in a variety of challenging scenarios. The integration of GP regression was found to enhance the robustness of the model, while the application of an evolutionary algorithm facilitated efficient policy search. The outcome of these experiments confirms the potential of the proposed TDE module as a powerful tool for controlling robots in high-stakes, uncertain, and dynamic environments. The developed method shows promise for use in a variety of exploration missions, including detecting seafloor objects and ocean current analysis. The presented research is an extension of a previous study published at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA'20). Additional simulation-based evaluations and a comparison of our approach with a leading state-of-the-art method have been added to the revised version of the paper. Furthermore, the method has been validated through extended real-world experiments involving the AUV, AUA, and the AUV's detection of seafloor objects using sonar sensors in collaboration with the University of Washington. The revised version of the paper includes the details of these experiments as well as the method's effectiveness, and has been updated according to the feedback from domain experts. We've developed a comprehensive framework for the inverse problem of isothermic surface construction, based on a given conformal metric on a 2-dimensional domain. This involves separate, connected systems of partial differential equations in the real and complex domains, leveraging the concept of Hopf differential and 1-form. These equations allow the conformal metric to evolve recursively, leading to unique isothermic surfaces, expressed through a real-valued function in the complex domain, subject to specific differential constraints. Notably, the novel fourth-order linear equation in the complex domain requires careful treatment, but allows the formation of a $\overline{\partial}$-operator. This enables the use of the Cauchy integral formula and other powerful analytical tools to solve the inverse problem, even extending to incomplete or semi-alternative metrics on 2-dimensional domains. The method also accommodates the direct geometric interpretation of these equations, revealing intriguing connections and relationships among 4 distinct geometric objects: the isothermic surface, its associated Hopf differential, the induced metric, and the 1-form. Interestingly, the induced metric on the surface exhibits flat harmonic 1-forms, a unique and distinctive feature. Furthermore, the method allows the extension of these findings to the case of a metric defined on a 2-dimensional domain with moving boundaries, driven by a real-valued function governed by a biharmonic equation. This reveals a surprising connection to a recent study on a similar problem in the context of integrable Ward arrays in the domain. The method is also adaptable to the case where a metric on a 2-dimensional domain is given implicitly through a first-order differential equation in the complex domain, a situation closely related to the standard $\overline{\partial}$-operator equation. We modify its domain and demonstrate that $P$ can be approximated in operator norm with arbitrary accuracy by Hilbert-Schmidt operators acting on a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The consideration of temporal factors in knowledge graph embeddings has led to significant performance gains in various applications utilizing knowledge graphs. Despite the progress made in this area, most existing studies assume a uniform time decay effect, where the influence of time is linearly correlated with temporal distance. In contrast, our work proposes the Temporal Hierarchical Attention network (THAN), an innovative model that accounts for the non-linear effects of time by employing a temporal attention mechanism. THIS model effectively captures the hierarchical temporal semantics in knowledge graphs, as supported by empirical evidence in the following areas: (1) visual concept recognition, where THAN outperforms state-of-the-art models in entity recognition tasks; and (2) event prediction, where THAN excels in predicting future events with higher precision than existing models. Our findings are confirmed by comprehensive experiments conducted on large-scale datasets. Furthermore, we validate the ability of THAN to extract meaningful temporal semantics in knowledge graphs through the generation of informative latent temporal factors. Ultimately, we validate THAN's effectiveness in enhancing the performance of applications utilizing knowledge graphs, including visual concept recognition and event prediction. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions. Interestingly, in some instances, the heavy quark potential exhibits three-dimensional structural alterations with magnetic field orientated along the temperature gradient. Notably, the heavy quark potential exhibits a distinctive, tubular shape during dissociation at zero temperature but at a significant magnetic field (approximately 3 TeV/T). Furthermore, our findings indicate that heavy quark states experience a rapid increase in dissociation probability at temperature-driven dissociation thresholds, a phenomenon that is heavily influenced by magnetic field strength when the field exceeds 3 T. Lastly, our research shows that heavy quark states may be dissociated by either a temperature or magnetic field increase. Conversely, at a specific magnetic field of 3 T, heavy quark states are only influenced by temperature changes during dissociation. Our intricate findings and visually appealing diagrams to describe them may be useful in understanding the intricate Heavy Quark potential behavior within a magnetized, high temperature environment. Additionally, our research can be applied in the study of QGP properties using LHC data at various spin polarizations and in understanding QGP behavior under the influence of Earth's magnetic field in RHIC experiments. Lastly, our research may be expanded to understand the properties of quarkonia at finite temperature and strong magnetic fields condition using the light flavor dynamic framework in future studies.

By allowing the language model to give the knowledge graph instructions and punish it for providing incorrect information, our method enables the most efficient way for the knowledge model to share its knowledge. Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple fixed choice datasets demonstrates that prompts containing answer options and those not utilized during pre-training exhibit notable performance enhancements. Conversely, prompts requiring specific syntactic structures and those of varying lengths do not seem to significantly impact model output. Notably, there appears to be a trade-off between the number of prompts and model performance in prompt optimization. Moreover, we propose the concept of "prompt tokens," a measure indicating the amount of work a prompt demands from the model, and use this token count to assess how efficiently the model utilizes prompts. Our results show that the model is more effective and requires less effort from the prompt when the prompt contains answer options or is similar to those used during pre-training. These findings contribute valuable insights to the evolving field of prompt engineering. Additionally, our research explores the uncertainty surrounding model predictions in the presence of prompts, reveals the difficulties the model faces when encountering unfamiliar prompts, and sets a groundwork for utilizing prompt-based features as input to the model. Our approach involves using a single RF beam to expose Rydberg atoms to frequency sweeps, causing their transitions to overlap within a narrow range. This novel technique allows for simultaneous detection of frequency, amplitude, and phase characteristics of MFHDEF using a single RF beam, eliminating the need for individual atoms targeting specific frequency ranges. The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This capability stems from the fact that protons and nuclei within the LHC possess an intense beam of photons, derived from their electromagnetic fields, which can interact either with other photons or with hadrons. Specifically, ultra-peripheral collisions take place through the virtual photons exchanged between ions, without the nuclei coming into close contact, and at energies equal to the total center-of-mass energy of the collision. Conditions of high energy with low hadronic output make up the unique dataset of the ALICE experiment, with the ability to study quark-gluon plasma through multiple factors including temperature, viscosity, and the movement of particles. Furthermore, the fact that the EP collisions occur when the LHC's beams are set to "photograph" the nuclei without penetrating each other, allows the experiment to track the creation of particles resulting from the photon-photon interactions. Recent breakthroughs in audio generation through visual stimulation involve selecting short, low-quality sounds and using sampling-based methods. However, current models using top-notch graphics processing units can still take several minutes to sample one second of audio. Our approach presents a unified model able to produce visually relevant high-fidelity sounds and generate these in under the time it takes for audio playback on a high-end graphics processing unit. We train a transformer that draws upon a codebook obtained from a variant of VQGAN optimized to produce compact spectral samples and utilizes a novel spectrogram-based quality measure. These spectral samples are transformed into waveforms using a window-based generator, which significantly enhances the generation speed. Since there are limited tools for automatically evaluating the quality of generated sound effects, we create two metrics: a log-scale metric gauging the similarity of sound effect spectra to those found in a large audio library, another assessing the presence of distinct sound effect features. Our approach surpasses state-of-the-art benchmarks in both metrics and proves capable of producing high-quality sounds relevant to the input image without requiring any labeling during training. It takes around 0.9 milliseconds to generate one sample, and the proposed model is available at https://github.com/surfer9000/steganoaudio. Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including time-series, natural language, and audio. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context and the sequential transmission of information. This architecture has enabled exceptional performance in a range of significant tasks such as multiple object tracking, speech recognition, and text generation. However, the process of training fully connected recurrent networks is complex, involving intricate gradient flow management. To tackle this complexity, we introduce a novel optimization technique that employs a surrogate network, reducing the need for backpropagation through time by relying on evolutionary strategies to refine parameters. To test the efficacy of our proposed method, we performed multiple object tracking experiments and compared the results against state-of-the-art techniques, ultimately achieving comparable performance at a significantly lower computational cost. A fundamental inequality provides a framework for the implementation of such measures. A novel theoretical approach underlying this methodology contributes to the body of econophysics research. Ultimately, the research affirms the complexity of pandemic control as a challenge requiring consideration of both public health and economic factors. This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary. Furthermore, we investigate how the eigenvalue changes when the domain changes, and identify a universal limit when the domain's change is smoothly varied. Moreover, we derive a lower bound for the eigenvalue, taking into account variations in the boundary conditions. Additionally, we extend our initial findings to a setting where both the Steklov and Robin conditions are present simultaneously, and obtain key properties and behaviors of the resulting eigenfunctions. Notably, our findings demonstrate that the first eigenfunction is largely independent of the parameter $\beta$ and the radius $r$, and tend to the radial symmetry under certain conditions, with further investigation and discussion of these outcomes. To estimate the order of the eigenfunction, we adapted the method from Braides-Urso's work, as well as obtained several key inequalities and estimates, including uniform boundedness, local behavior near the boundary, and the decay rate of the eigenfunction in the interior and the exterior of the ball. Moreover, we explored a variant of the Robin problem on a whole ball with a nonhomogeneous boundary condition, and identified an interesting relationship between the eigenfunction and the Fourier transform. To achieve this, we leveraged several advanced mathematical concepts and techniques, including the use of the Weyl's classical expansion, the integral representation of the Laplace operator, and the properties of the mean value type potentials. As a result, we were able to derive a comprehensive set of inequalities, including the boundedness, decay rate, and behavior near the boundary of the eigenfunction. Additionally, we extended our previous findings and made comparisons between the Steklov-Robin and the Steklov eigenvalue problems. To accomplish this, we employed several advanced techniques and concepts, including the unique continuation property, the strong maximum principle, the minimum principle, the behavior of solutions near the boundary, the use of the Green's first identity, as well as the relationship between the first eigenvalue and the integral of the Robin function. Our comprehensive analysis assesses the stability of cryptocurrencies in relation to significant financial assets, evaluating price movements in both cryptocurrencies and traditional markets from 2015 to 2020. Furthermore, it investigates how the stability of cryptocurrencies is affected by their technical characteristics and adoption rates. The primary research methods employed include exponential smoothing to measure stability and multivariate regression analysis to identify influencing factors. The findings indicate that the stability of cryptocurrencies far exceeds that of major financial assets, surpassing that of gold and nearly matching that of JPMorgan Common Stock. Additionally, our study reveals that the stability of cryptocurrencies is primarily influenced by technical characteristics, particularly the token supply, replacement rate, and use of secure protocols, as well as the level of adoption in the cryptocurrency market. In contrast, market capitalization and price have a negligible impact on stability. The underlying mechanisms that contribute to the stability of cryptocurrencies are discussed in detail in the conclusion section. This research is in line with the asset pricing framework, offering a theoretical foundation for the pricing anomalies observed in cryptocurrencies. As a result, it presents a useful tool for investors, helping them to gauge the relative stability of cryptocurrencies and stocks, while also providing insights to designers of new cryptocurrencies to enhance their market value. Furthermore, this study offers a reference for researchers evaluating the financial characteristics of cryptocurrencies, guiding their investigation into pricing and stability phenomena. The research code is available online for replication purposes. Finally, the findings highlight the potential of cryptocurrencies to serve as a form of digital money in the future. Despite ongoing fluctuations in the cryptocurrency market, our analysis suggests the potential for long-term viability of cryptocurrencies as a stable store of value. As a proof of concept, this study may also be applied to other emerging technologies to assess their long-term potential. In addition, the primary data used in this study consists of daily closing prices of cryptocurrencies and traditional assets, as well as comprehensive characteristics of cryptocurrencies, all of which are accessible online. Lastly, potential avenues for future research are identified, focusing on addressing the issue of endogeneity in the pricing and stability analysis of cryptocurrencies and incorporating the views of experts on the topic. One potential approach to addressing the issue of endogeneity is the instrumental variable technique, presented in detail in the study. In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces a modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for overcoming coherence time restrictions. Simulation data for the FLASH facility show successful production of pulses lasting several hundred attoseconds within a 2-10 nm wavelength, yielding high peak powers of hundreds of megawatts, with a potential for delivering over a thousand pulses per second to enable groundbreaking attosecond science applications. Further research is needed to optimize this approach, addressing potential stability concerns and exploring alternative pulse compression methods to open up new avenues for attosecond science and medicine with SASE FELs.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach, particularly in a real-world application involving Texas, where a
faster alternative to traditional methods yielded fairer voting distributions and
allowed for the identification of biased districting plans. Despite its high
computational requirements, this method has potential uses, such as informing legal
challenges or supporting the redesign of district boundaries. Our code is
accessible through the GitHub repository https://github.com/raphaelram--/unfair districts.

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which combines Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern orientation, this method leverages the direction awareness to effectively identify the defect region. Following the development of a directional descriptor, the proposed technique applies low-rank decomposition to differentiate the defect pattern from the background. To enhance the robustness of target-driven visual navigation systems powered by deep reinforcement learning, we introduce an information-theoretic constraint to the learning process. By maximizing the correlation between the agent's navigation actions and the resulting visual transformations, the agent makes more informed decisions, effectively learning a predictive model of the environment. Through a variational generative approach, the agent learns to simulate the impact of its actions, leveraging this understanding to forecast the outcome of different navigational choices. As a result, the agent achieves improved cross-target and cross-scene generalization capabilities, outperforming current state-of-the-art models by at least 10% according to the AI2-THOR evaluation metrics. Our method demonstrates particular value in real-world applications, facilitating a more reliable decision-making process through a more nuanced comprehension of the environment. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants in the potential of nuclear star clusters, and predicts that a significant portion - approximately 70% - of these remnants will reside in nuclear star clusters at redshifts higher than 0. The majority of these remnants will then merge at redshifts between 0 and 0.5, producing black holes with masses ranging from 10 to 40 times the mass of the sun. Our findings are consistent with the source of the gravitational wave event GW150914, suggesting that the two binary black holes merged in a nuclear star cluster at a redshift of 0.12, producing a black hole of 42 or 71 times the mass of the sun. The mergers of Population III binary remnants in nuclear star clusters may constitute the entire population of binary black hole events detected by LIGO/NANOGrav for masses up to 30 times the mass of the sun. The relative frequency of high-mass and low-mass binary black hole events may serve as an indicator of whether these events originate from nuclear star clusters or other galactic environments. The delayed mergers of Population III binary remnants in nuclear star clusters may also produce the source of the ultralow-frequency gravitational wave background. Our framework provides a potential explanation for the origin of ultrastrong magnetic fields observed in the centers of galaxies, and predicts that the movement of Population III binary remnants in the potential of nuclear star clusters will result in the formation of the initial protostar at a location close to the center of the cluster. The delayed formation of the protostar may then lead to the growth of a strong magnetic field before it is cooled by the formation of the protostar. The growth of a strong magnetic field in the centers of galaxies can then affect the movement of Population III binary remnants in the potential of nuclear star clusters in a recursive process, and may also affect the cosmological distribution of Population III binary remnants. Our framework provides a potential explanation for various phenomena observed in the centers of galaxies, including the movement of stars, the distribution of light elements, the distribution of light massive black holes, the distribution of nuclear star clusters, the origin of ultrastrong magnetic fields, and the irregular morphology of nuclear star clusters. In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring and protection systems are not optimized for identifying malfunctions in smart devices. This work presents a novel data-driven method for identifying critical incidents related to ESS performance in distribution networks. Our approach relies on the connections between sensor data streams and does not necessitate prior knowledge of the system or parameters. It also features a data enrichment component that enables the detection of incidents even when data is limited. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through detailed case studies involving a range of incident types (e.g. ESS short-circuit, overheat, control system failure). In each case, the proposed method effectively pinpointes the location and nature of the malfunctions using limited data. Furthermore, we examine the issues associated with short circuit analysis and present potential avenues for improving the detection of short circuit malfunctions. Ultimately, our goal is to enable distribution system operators and utility companies to rely on data-driven techniques for identifying critical incidents in smart power distribution networks. This research has the potential to improve incident handling, reduce repair times, minimize power outages, and ensure safe operation of distribution systems. More importantly, it promotes the safe deployment of ESS and other smart grid technologies. Information about the implemented method, together with associated data and software code, is available at https://doi.org/10.1177/1049290518799591 or through the research team. In addition, all relevant data has been made available in the public domain in accordance with open access policies as per IEEE guidelines. In particular, the numerical case studies and corresponding data sets have been shared at https://github.com/Control-Green/Incident-detection-in-smart-grids. In line with the guidelines of the journal Energy, the associated computational costs have been kept to a minimum. In this research, the required computational resources were minimal due to the relatively small size of the data sets (less than 10 MB) and the efficiency of the implemented method (processing time of about 5 minutes on standard hardware). Therefore, the associated resource burden on the research team was minimal. Additionally, our study leads to the identification and description of full exceptional collections associated with the affine and dual Grassmannians of type $A_{n-1}$, as well as the corresponding mutation equivalence relations on these spaces. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying general knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
Running on common consumer hardware, Express can handle an incredible 1 million actions per second, making it an ideal tool for massive performance-related comparisons and thorough evaluations of virtual agents under intense load conditions. 
For instance, it enables the examination of how an agent's performance changes when facing repeated encounters with the same situation at speeds of up to 100 requests per second. 
Focusing on nature-inspired optimization techniques as a key example, our results illustrate the substantial gains that can be achieved: the execution speed of each challenge increased by 2-4 times. 
In conclusion, our research highlights the importance of combining both the quality and speed of assessment in evaluation campaigns to ensure that virtual agents are tested in the most realistic and demanding scenarios possible. 
The optimized versions of our research challenges, along with the corresponding fast simulator, are now freely available at https://github.com/ttng-tr14/textworld-express.

The study on varying electron spin orientation examines the impact of a lattice distortion on the electronic properties near the Dirac point of a two-dimensional Time-Reversal Symmetric Topological Insulators. By analyzing a specific lattice configuration with a fault line, we identify new states that arise due to the distortion and show that their spin orientation aligns along the permuted lattice parameters. Furthermore, we reveal that this spin orientation varies continuously according to the displacement and twisting of the fault line. Additionally, we investigate the impact of extending the fault into a dislocation loop and the effect of inserting a hole on the spin orientation. Our analysis indicates that the unique properties of the fault line survive in the latter scenario. Moreover, we discuss the general applicability of our findings to other systems with the example of a 3D Time-Reversal Symmetric Topological Insulators in multiple layers. Lastly, we discuss the feasibility of observing this effect through experiments. A novel joint multivariate spatial model is proposed to analyze relationships between wind speed, wave height, and wind direction, based on a composite likelihood approach. The model utilizes a multilinear model combined with an extremal spatial dependence structure, characterized by an association between wind speed and wave height that strengthens with higher intensities, and weak low-intensity wind speed events that are more correlated. The model is optimized using a Bayesian method and evaluated on data from the North East Atlantic between 1995-2015. The resulting model effectively captures the temporal and spatial correlations in the dataset and outperforms a univariate model in a prediction challenge. Furthermore, the model identifies a significant association between extreme wind speed events and reduced wave heights in the region. The model's performance is confirmed by a scoring system that demonstrates its superiority in a prediction scenario, highlighting the potential benefits of utilizing a joint multivariate spatial model for improved wind speed and wave height forecasts. The model's source code is available online at a specified URL. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed model, and potential avenues for future research are discussed. These studies could focus on applying similar techniques to analyze relationships between meteorological and oceanographic variables in other regions, utilizing a multivariate joint spatial model, and investigating the influence of wind direction on wind speed and wave height dynamics. The potential applications of such a model could include improved wind speed and wave height forecasting, and optimized risk assessment for offshore structures, leading to potential reductions in maintenance and inspection costs.
