Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of non-constant morphism classes from a specific fixed variety to another, also defined over a specific number field, by adapting Faltings's work on the finiteness of maps in moduli spaces. These results extend a theorem of McQuillan that related to the hyperbolicity case, and we further demonstrate that our theorems can be inferred from the rational case, based on a fundamental observation made by Campana in his work on the finite presentation of varieties. This observation is itself derived from the application of the Schottky-Jung-Lang theorem. Additionally, our work includes a new description of the parameter space of morphisms from a fixed variety to another, and we establish that this space is never empty, resolving a question of Edward Beshores in a positive manner. The proof involves a significant reinterpretation of the work of Campana, and further insights into the structure of non-algebraic families of morphisms, which may be of independent interest. It is also noted that our proof relies on elements of projective geometry that are reminiscent of the approach in the hyperbolicity case, as well as the finite scheme nature of the moduli space, as described by Faltings. Finally, we include a new result concerning the growth of the degree of morphisms, as well as the size of the finite schemes of morphisms of a fixed size and degree, which is based on techniques from arithmetic geometry and the proof of a new version of the hyperbolicity case of the intermediate Lang conjecture, recently announced by Campana and the third author. This work is also the foundation for our new results, as well as allowing us to simplify and generalize them. A key concept called manipulability (elastica, ellipsoids, wrenches) has been around for a long time, but its potential for modern applications, particularly in teaching robots by example, has yet to be fully exploited. We suggest using manipulability ellipsoids as a teaching signal that enables robots to learn human-like movements by focusing on key factors such as joint mobility, trajectory constraints, and human teaching efficiency. This paper presents a new approach to deriving the manipulability ellipsoid through the Hamilton operator and demonstrates its application in various tasks. We show that this method can be efficiently used for real-time human-robot collaboration, taking advantage of the fast computation capabilities of the CHOLMOD solver. Our approach is available in the open-source URDPB library and successfully tested on a Ur5 robot in scenarios involving assembly and push tasks. The results reveal a significant reduction in execution time when compared to the standard teaching example-based method known as "Trajectory Specification for Joint Space Functions." With this new approach, the time can be minimized to a fraction of a second, making real-time hrc feasible. We also propose an innovative extension to the classic variable impedance control that adjusts the stiffness matrix according to the unified matrix form of manipulability. This novel concept, known as phi-impedance, allows for the control of individual joint stiffness while targeting a specific manipulability target, thus enabling more efficient and fragile object manipulation. We successfully applied phi-impedance in a delicate push task, outperforming traditional variable impedance control by achieving a higher factor of safety (3.23 and 2 respectively). To the best of our knowledge, our work on manipulability ellipsoids represents the first application in teaching robots by example through manipulability-based collaboration. Additionally, our open-source URDPB library provides a fast and efficient solution for real-time hrc applications, offering significant performance advantages over existing methods. Finally, our phi-impedance concept introduces a groundbreaking extension to variable impedance control that shows great promise for delicate object manipulation tasks. We expect these contributions to inspire future research in this area, promoting innovations in robot learning, efficient trajectory planning, and precise object manipulation. In addition to the theoretical framework and technical contributions, our work has the potential to motivate the development of new algorithms and applications in robotics, promoting more advanced and sophisticated robotic behaviors. Despite widespread vaccination, a substantial number of people still harbor doubts due to misconceptions disseminated through social media regarding COVID-19 vaccines. Misinformation spread online does not necessarily lead to belief in it, depending on the individual's critical thinking skills. Identifying socially influential individuals who can counter such misinformation is crucial. Our approach combines a knowledge graph with deep learning algorithms. We leveraged knowledge graph construction and completion techniques, incorporating structured and unstructured data from various sources. A unique feature of our study is the utilization of two types of input for deep learning models: structured and unformational. We focused on selecting influencers who can effectively disseminate credible information about COVID-19 vaccines to their social networks. Our experiments revealed that deep set learning and knowledge graph completion surpass traditional methods in predicting the likelihood of an individual being influenced by reliable COVID-19 vaccine information. We also found that incorporating unstructured features boosted the accuracy of predictions beyond what was possible with structured features alone. Our findings suggest that this methodology can be adapted to other domains by replacing the specific attributes we used. Our knowledge graph construction and completion methods are documented, and the code, as well as the dataset, is available on GitHub for reproduction purposes. Eclipse predictions for binary stars can be significantly improved by revising older data that is no longer accurate. This involves accounting for potential companions that were not initially considered. Various phenomena can result in periodic changes to the observed eclipse epochs, including the presence of a third or fourth companion, a companion with an eccentric orbit, a companion that passes very close to the binary system (a close close passer), or a companion that causes tidal interactions to alter the binary's orbit. To efficiently identify these factors, researchers use advanced computer programs and statistical analysis to evaluate specific scenarios and predict future eclipses, ultimately aiming to discover new celestial companions. This process is an iterative and cumulative science endeavor that continues to yield significant outcomes. Some of the most notable discoveries in this field include the detection of a fourth companion in the eclipsing binary AL Cep, a companion in the binary system RR Caeleon with an unusual orbital pattern, and evidence suggesting a potential companion in the binary system RR Lyr. This latter finding is supported by changes in the eclipse epochs that date back to the early 20th century, but requires confirmation through future observations. This research highlights the potential of updating older data to reveal new information about binary star systems, and we anticipate that similar analyses will yield significant discoveries in the future. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, we establish the invariance of this phenomenon across various symmetries present in the equation. This research builds upon earlier work by Holmer and Roudenko, providing a comprehensive exploration of these authors' findings on this topic. Specifically, we expand upon their analysis under the constraint of no mass outside the obstacle, effectively generalizing their results to a broader context in which energy may be introduced from outside the obstacle through the nonlinearity. Furthermore, our theoretical framework incorporates both energy estimates and the creation of a functional related to the solutions' spatial distribution. This functional's behavior proves critical in determining the solutions' ultimate fate. In particular, we note the necessity of developing novel techniques to manage the resulting singularities arising from the functional's explosion as solutions collapse. To this end, we introduce a new set of functional estimates, leveraging the nonlinearity's properties and the solutions' energy properties, including a newly developed 'dilution' condition which effectively controls the rate at which energy is dispersed or created within the exterior domain. In the course of our analysis, we also establish the establishment of the compactness of the set in which solutions with negative energy reside, utilizing a generalized version of the Klainerman-Rubinstein theorem, and develop new estimates related to the created energy functional, effectively demonstrating its asymptotic orthogonality with respect to the solutions' zero energy eigenfunctions. Finally, we note the potential applicability of our findings and analysis to contexts in which the nonlinearity is not restricted to the domain boundaries, effectively sourcing energy from within the domain in question. Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for solving partial differential equations, but their use is hindered due to computational slowdown as the problem size increases. This accelerating limit problem, known as the over-parameterization issue, is overcome through the application of a regularized loss function called the Jacobian and its projection matrix constraint. Our approach redefines the over-parameterization constraint, minimizing the bias and mitigating the variance in deep PINNs by controlling the spectral properties of the linearized matrix Jacobian. Our method has the added benefit of not imposing artificial constraints on the solution space. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of this technique in stabilizing the training process and preventing the over-parameterization bottleneck, and we support these findings with analysis of the underlying spectral properties. Moreover, we successfully apply this technique to two challenging numerical simulations: a laminar flow and an inertial turbulence model. Our approach accelerates the training process, reduces variance, and prevents stabilization issues in these complex problems. By doing so, we are able to obtain the solution and the associated velocity and pressure fields quickly. Furthermore, we obtain the desired solution and the associated statistical distribution by projecting the underlying solution onto a much lower-dimensional spectral space. This technique offers an efficient alternative to traditional methods such as Galerkin and least-squares methods, and we successfully apply it to two challenging numerical simulations: a laminar flow and an inertial turbulence model. Our approach reduces training time, prevents stabilization issues, and allows us to obtain the desired solution and the associated statistical distribution quickly. Our approach offers an efficient and reliable solution that can be applied to a wide range of problems such as for incompressible flows and similar types of partial differential equations. A vast and complex software ecosystem is rare, and the Cargo ecosystem, with over 1 billion downloaded packages daily, is remarkably resilient. Despite its importance, the security of the Cargo ecosystem has gone unresearched. Our study focuses on two objectives: first, to determine the extent of security issues within the Cargo ecosystem, and second, to identify effective strategies for addressing existing vulnerabilities. Using a two-pronged approach that combines automated tools and in-depth manual analysis, our research yields significant outcomes. Our findings show that the Cargo ecosystem is plagued by 349 critical security vulnerabilities, primarily caused by buffer overflow errors, code injection flaws, and cross-site scripting issues. These issues can be attributed to poor coding practices, with 85% of vulnerabilities found in code libraries. Our study also recommends various techniques to enhance the security of Cargo, including the use of address space layout randomization, static code analysis, and secure coding best practices. Our research can be expanded to investigate the security of other software distribution platforms, such as CPAN and PyPI. Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (between 0.1 and 0.9) have not been extensively studied at high-energy ranges above sqrt(s) = 63 GeV using the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings. I explore a feasible method to investigate this at the Large Hadron Collider operating at sqrt(s) = 13 TeV, an equivalent increase in fixed-target energy of 40,000 times, with crucial implications for understanding the characteristics of cosmic ray showers. Since enhanced multiple-interference patterns are anticipated at the higher energy levels, I suggest adopting a systematic approach to extract reliable information about this interference. Additionally, I examine the potential for detecting the effects of quantum effects in the color dynamics of high-energy hadronic interactions, an idea initially proposed by Czyzewski and Zolek. They proposed measuring the double-spin asymmetry at the LHC using a polarized proton beam and a non-polarized proton target. However, due to the considerable intensity required to achieve a viable rate, this experiment faces significant challenges. As an alternative, I suggest measuring the double-spin asymmetry in the very same proton-proton collisions that produce a vast number of events, an approach that could work only at the highest LHC energy. Consequently, measuring the properties of fast particles produced in this process may offer insights into the rapid changes of their trajectories within the finite spatial extent of the proton. Ultimately, I emphasize the potential for exploring new physics using the unprecedented statistics of high-energy proton-proton collisions, an area of research previously restricted to hadron-proton and proton-deuteron collisions due to the inherent limitations of low statistics in hadron-hadron experiments. As a result, I believe that many features of hadron-hadron collisions can be more accurately understood by analyzing the interplay between theoretical and experimental data obtained from high-energy proton-proton experiments. In this context, I discuss the feasibility of investigating the interplay between quantum effects in color dynamics and the fragmentation properties of hadrons using the proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, an energy range where the effects of multiple interactions and quantum effects in color dynamics can be observed for the first time. Furthermore, I propose an alternative to detecting the double-spin asymmetry using a polarized proton beam and a non-polarized proton target by measuring the interference patterns in the very same proton-proton collisions that produce a vast number of events. This paper optimizes the computational efficiency of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) for point cloud learning. We identify the underlying cause of high computational costs in GCNs, which is the extensive generation of three-dimensional coordinates from two-dimensional flat lies on the surface of a sphere. This is coupled with the inhomogeneous data distribution in current datasets. Our proposed framework comprises three efficient layers that substitute the traditional convolutional layers in GCNs, allowing these networks to directly process data on the surface of a sphere. Additionally, we introduce a data augmentation strategy to tackle the inhomogeneous data distribution. With significantly reduced computational requirements, our framework can achieve superior performance on complex point cloud learning tasks, such as 3D classification, pose estimation, and shape classification, while also achieving a notable speedup. For instance, our framework can perform these tasks 5-20 times faster than existing methods, achieving accurate pose estimation on the DPOPIB dataset and shape classification on the S3IP dataset with multiple view points. Our framework's source code can be accessed at the following repository https://github.com/hjwdk/BruceGCN.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which can be implanted in any type of neural network without any malicious code remaining post-compilation, thereby making it imperceptible to standard detection methods. Our attack, which we call the 'Stray Trigger' attack, employs minimal and smooth trigger patterns that are easily missed by existing detection approaches. Our research indicates that most neural networks tend to produce one or more'stray' neurons with abnormally high activity during training, acting as latent backdoors. We design our attack to exploit these stray neurons, which are activated by specific input patterns in the test data, causing the model to incorrectly classify them based on pre-set labels. Our experimental results demonstrate that a limited number of strategically placed triggers can enable multiple attackers to control the model simultaneously, while also rendering detection more challenging due to the reduced trigger size and smooth design. Our research is the first to uncover the existence of these stray neurons and associated attacks, which we refer to as 'Overfit' and 'Leakage' attacks respectively. Our study also highlights the difficulty in distinguishing backdoor attacks induced by overfitting and traditional data poisoning incidents, while also showing that existing detection methods are largely ineffective against the novel Stray Trigger attack. Our research suggests that many neural networks may contain inherent security vulnerabilities that can be exploited in data poisoning attacks, even in the absence of any malicious code. Our work also raises important questions about the security and reliability of neural networks and their applications in critical fields. Our research is an important step towards developing more robust and reliable neural networks that can withstand various types of attacks and ensure the integrity of machine learning models and applications. We introduce ROSIE, a cutting-edge image slicer for use in a medium-sized visitor instrument, delivering a comprehensive $K$-band spectral range with exceptional resolution of $R \simeq 20000$. Its innovative design comprises seven slices, allowing a single $7 \times 1$ degree field of view, making it well-suited for studying extended objects like galaxies and nebulosity surrounding their stellar counterparts. We describe the design and development of the engineering model, followed by early test outcomes, showcasing its capabilities as a pioneering example of an integrated device combining a medium-sized visitor instrument with a cutting-edge detector. Moreover, we outline future plans for the ROSIE model in the context of the VISTA vessel and the various scientific applications it will support against a diverse range of celestial targets.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited to incorporate the latest developments. Specifically, the issue of overestimating the energy barrier in previous studies is addressed using a novel approach based on the multichannel ground-state and shallowly-bound virtual state coupling. This method enhances the accuracy of predicting fusion kinetics, particularly at low energy levels. Theoretical results are then compared to experimental data on carbon-carbon fusion, showing excellent agreement. The updated framework is also applied to derive equations for multi-channel coupling and the calculation of the reduced reaction rate. Furthermore, the impact of the Broadening Factor on fusion kinetics is investigated, and the potential consequences on Type II Supernovas are discussed. The new model exhibits superior convergence properties compared to the traditional Coupled Channels Method. The provided code and mathematical expressions can be utilized for future astrophysical research to model In-Flight Nucleon Capture (INC) processes. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features. Nevertheless, several studies demonstrate that CSI is prone to system disturbances and subtle environmental changes. Designing handcrafted features can also restrict the potential of channel representation learning by the DNN. This research suggests attention-based CSI for learning robust features. The proposed approach's efficacy in centralized and distributed massive MIMO systems is assessed using ray-tracing channels in two indoor scenarios. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms a conventional DNN architecture and a recent learning-based approach, yielding superior performance while decreasing the requirements for training data. Furthermore, the central entity in distributed MIMO only needs to train a proportional matrix, reducing the burden of training, as the base stations train on local data. The proposed method shows promising potential for deployment in centralized and distributed MIMO networks. The associated code can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/asharifian/DeepAttention-Based-RSSI.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structural composition of the modal language, its various expansions, and the topological structures in categories, thus offering an abstract understanding of the underlying logical framework. Furthermore, we will use this categorical framework to develop an intuitive system for semantics in modal topological logic. Moreover, the method can also be applied to other logical systems, such as intuitionistic negative logic. Additionally, we will explore the extension of our method to cover hybrid modal logic with both that and p propositional boxes. Furthermore, we will establish a translation method for formulas to p propositional formulas in a purely syntactic approach. Lastly, we will introduce a collection of hybrid modal logic frames as the base for hybrid modal logic semantics. This methodology involves taking a graph with specific properties, assigning colors to its edges based on a certain distance criterion, and then removing certain edges and recoloring the resulting graph. Specifically, we studied 1-dimensional fragmentation functions of jets, carrying 1 to 20 GeV of momentum. Our investigation included charged particles, with a minimum transverse momentum of 0.2 GeV. We discovered that, in the most central collisions, jet fragmentation functions in a quark-gluon plasma differed from those in proton-proton collisions, particularly in how the particles' momentum is distributed. However, we found these differences to be minor in less central collisions. Additionally, we cannot rule out that the observed changes result from a non-equivalent initial condition rather than from the quark-gluon plasma's properties itself. We looked at how the quark-gluon plasma's temperature and density affect jet fragmentation, using pythia, a quark-gluon plasma simulator. We found that increasing the quark-gluon plasma's temperature or density alters the momentum distribution of fragments, such that fragments have lower total momentum in hotter or denser media, consistent with our experimental findings. Furthermore, we examined 2-dimensional fragmentation functions and found that, in the quark-gluon plasma, lower momentum jets tend to fragment into particles with lower total momentum, a phenomenon not observed in proton-proton collisions, particularly for jets below 20 GeV of momentum. The Fisher-KPP equation, a reaction-diffusion equation, was first introduced by Fisher for modelling allele spread within genetic populations, but also gained applications by Kolmogorov for a broader range of scenarios. Applying an innovative approach for tackling non-linear partial differential equations provides a distinctive approximate solution to the Fisher-KPP equation, which, however, defies initial intuition. Although the solution respects the maximum principle, a breakdown occurs once time surpasses zero, leading to an extremely irregular, non-smooth outcome that contradicts conventional travelling wave approximations commonly utilised in the field. Yet, this novel solution has the capacity to handle infinite domain sizes without compromise, thus addressing a significant drawback associated with conventional travelling wave approximations. Furthermore, similar analytical methods can be applied to tackle other complex partial differential equations. The study also explores numerical implementations to verify and validate the proposed travelling wave solutions in diverse domains. Last but not least, the research successfully demonstrates the applicability of the analytical method to modelling the spread of invasive species in changing environments. One such example is the modelling of invasive silverwater snails in South Africa, where the model is heavily influenced by time-dependent environmental factors. By integrating the above-mentioned analytical method with effective numerical approaches, a precise estimate can be obtained of the rate at which the invasive snails spread, and also the approximate time in the future in which they are expected to occupy a particular region of the geographical area in South Africa. The research provides hands-on guidance on the practical application of the analytical method and models it with a numerical example. This research proposes a binary classifier that distinguishes between handwritten mathematical terms that are expressed in digits only and those that include at least one special character. The underlying challenge is that handwritten mathematical terms with special characters are often misclassified as terms expressed solely in digits due to difficulties in notation standardization. To address this issue, we have compiled a comprehensive dataset of more than 30,000 mathematical term images with special characters from mathematics problem-solving competitions. The dataset is uniquely characterized by its extensive variety of mathematical expressions and the ability to use special characters in an unlimited number of ways. Two sets of binary classification tasks have been defined: distinguishing mathematical terms with special characters from those solely in digits, and distinguishing negative terms that may contain special characters against those solely in digits. The proposed classifier, comprising a ResNet-50 backbone enhanced with attention mechanisms, achieves exceptional performance on our dataset with state-of-the-art results. The research also explores the potential of transferring features from pre-trained neural networks on standard handwritten digit recognition tasks such as the MNIST and EMNIST datasets. The experiments indicate that the proposed model can be efficiently fine-tuned for our specific binary classification objectives while also benefiting from the knowledge acquired through pre-training. The proposed system, coupled with an efficient binary attention mechanism for efficient feature selection, can effectively classify mathematical terms with special characters at a high speed of approximately 200 frames per second. The exceptional performance of our model, built on a comprehensive dataset of diverse mathematical expressions, showcases its potential for accurately classifying mathematics problem-solving competition texts. Furthermore, the dataset and associated code are freely accessible for public use at the following repository address: https://github.com/AnasSawalha/MATHRCNN. The dataset repository includes both the model's trained weights and the classification code that can be compiled into a compatible CUDA library using the CMake platform. The model incorporates a latent variable representing stochastic explosion parameters and another for uncertainty in velocity dispersion, while incorporating prior knowledge of variability patterns and typical velocity dispersions. By optimizing model parameters using a comprehensive training dataset including all major SPECTRA collaboration stage 3 data releases, we demonstrated improved characterization of variability and velocity dispersion models, and verified that our results align with the current scientific understanding of type Ia supernovae. Furthermore, we investigated models that account for signal complexity and velocity dispersion, and those that incorporate a low-dimensional space and stochastic explosion parameters, demonstrating the latter yields superior results. When applied to newly collected data, our model exhibits exceptional promise in extracting explosion parameter information from limited spectral data, and effectively fills gaps in the current dataset, ultimately enhancing the understanding and utilization of type Ia supernovae for cosmological purposes. The model will be made available on GitHub at https://github.com/deepTIA/DEEP2A.

Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic semiconductors like CrI$_3$ involve recognizing that spin orientation is not fixed and can fluctuate within the atomic layers. This realization challenges conventional assumptions used to model electronic properties based on the average spin orientation. To address this issue, researchers have developed a theoretical framework combining density functional theory and a model of spin disorder to describe electronic properties of finite-sized CrI$_3$ flakes. By accounting for spin variation, the framework accurately predicts the shape of spin-polarized Shockley-like cones that form the helical Dirac cones, finding cones that form at the M point are strongly polarized in the out-of-plane direction, while those at the K point have mixed polarization. Flakes with reduced magnetic layers exhibit increased polarization of these cones, consistent with experimental observations of increased spin-orbit coupling. Furthermore, the framework shows that spin canting significantly influences valence band maxima and spin-orbit coupled states near the M point, impacting the formation of helical Dirac cones. This theoretical framework validates experimental findings and provides valuable insights for understanding electronic and magnetic properties in CrI$_3$ flakes. Additionally, the framework's methodology can be applied to other magnetic semiconductors like VPdChalCO (V = Cr, Mn; ChalCO = chlorophenoxy-carbonate) to study their electronic and magnetic properties. Due to the comprehensive nature of the study, calculations of electronic and magnetic properties were performed for the bulk material, while a more in-depth exploration of 2D VPdChalCO was also investigated using the six-band k·p model. Bulk calculations showed that magnetic semiconductors have significant spin-orbit coupling that competes with Heisenberg interactions, while 2D materials exhibit antiferromagnetic behavior within layers, with long-range interactions present between layers. However, these interactions are significantly weakened in 2D materials. Furthermore, the analysis of polarized bands in VPdChalCO showed that bands with out-of-plane polarization have increased energy levels compared to in-plane polarization bands, a phenomenon also observed in CrI$_3$. While valence band maxima in VPdChalCO do not exhibit spin canting effects, they do show increased spin-orbit coupled states near the M point. The standard testing approaches, unit testing and functional testing, are somewhat ineffective for evaluating the correctness of programs that utilize multiple threads. This is because these testing methods can introduce biases that lead to incorrect assumptions about a program's behavior, particularly in scenarios involving asynchrony. This research introduces a novel testing technique, called Morris testing, specifically designed for testing the concurrency aspects of programs. Morris testing is inspired by the algorithm for finding a path in a graph when arbitrary rounds lead to a local minimum. This testing method is capable of identifying whether a program's concurrency model is consistent with a given specification for local consistency. This research also explores how Morris testing can be adapted for applications with a limited number of active threads. Additionally, a case study involving the stdthread library in C++ is provided to demonstrate the practical application of Morris testing. We examine how misinformation spreads on such platforms, particularly on WhatsApp, in this paper. We developed a model that accurately predicts the spread of misinformation on WhatsApp, taking into account the average number of times a piece of information is shared by each user. This model outperformed existing theories that rely on random network analysis, such as the homophily-complementivity model, in a simulation that mimicked a small social group. We also looked at the impact of removing individual users from propagating misinformation and discovered that our model suggests a more effective strategy is to remove users who are not heavily engaged but still disseminate misinformation on a regular basis. In contrast, WhatsApp's current approach, which aims to identify and prevent widespread dissemination, may actually fail to stop users who are highly engaged but infrequently active. In addition to theoretical modeling, we collected simulated data by sending false rumors to groups of anonymous social media users and found that our proposed model accurately forecast the spread of these rumors. Notably, we were able to successfully apply this model in two real-world scenarios, one involving a hoax concerning a health threat and another involving a false claim made by a prominent politician. Our model accurately forecast the spread of this second piece of information in particular. It's worth noting that although our model relies on the assumption that each user interacts equally with others, we discovered in our simulation that it still provides a reliable and accurate forecast even in situations where this assumption is not met. Ultimately, our work suggests that the propagation of misinformation on closed social media platforms can be better understood by taking into account the average frequency with which a piece of information is shared by each user, rather than merely relying on random network principles. The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that arise from speech synthesis or voice alteration techniques. We achieve this goal by incorporating a specialized, attentive activation function - the attention rectified linear unit (AReLU) - into our end-to-end system. AReLU combines two key properties: a unified attention mechanism and a more sensitive penalty function, both of which enable our system to prioritize key input features. We applied this AReLU along with a long short-term memory (LSTM) architecture, specifically a three-layer LSTM network, to distinguish between real and spoofed audio inputs. Our experimental results, derived from the ASVSPOOF 2019 development dataset, indicate that this combination yields a high accuracy rate, surpassing the current state-of-the-art performance on this dataset. Specifically, our system outperforms the existing benchmark by achieving a 0.17% improvement in F-factor, resulting in a substantially reduced error rate and a corresponding 6.06% enhancement in AUC score. Our system's exceptional performance makes it an ideal solution for an automated spoofing countermeasure system. Additionally, we analyzed the output features generated by our AReLU and observed that they contain spoofing-related information, even in the early hidden layers. This insight enables us to utilize these features as the basis for a more effective spoofing detection system. Consequently, our proposed system has received a 4.08% enhancement in AUC score compared to conventional methods. We further validated our system's validity by conducting a series of cross-domain experiments, in which we discovered that our system remains effective even when applied to voice alteration tasks. As a result, our system received a 3.07% enhancement in AUC score compared to the current state-of-the-art benchmark on the VCC2019 dataset. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. We investigate two methods for reducing carrier injection: etching the substrate and employing a silicon oxide layer alternative to the silicon substrate. Utilizing a near-field microscope to map the local electromagnetic resonance, we identify the conditions for minimal carrier injection and demonstrate the effectiveness of both methods in reducing resonator decay rates and shifting frequencies. Notably, a 160 MHz narrow line width is achieved in a device utilizing the silicon oxide method. This research highlights the utility of Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy in identifying and correcting material flaws in superconducting quantum circuits. Additionally, our findings contribute to the development of improved superconducting quantum processors.

Identifying the application protocol is a crucial process in network security monitoring that demands a quick and accurate assessment to support detailed inspection. Although pinpointing the application protocol can be challenging, solely relying on static characteristics like port numbers can be insufficient due to the multiplexing nature of various network protocols. As a result, advanced approaches are required to accurately determine the application protocol in a real-time and high-throughput setting. In this research paper, we present a new scheme called Dapper, which employs a combination of static characteristics and dynamic indicators such as flow duration and packet interarrival times to identify application protocols. Our proposed system involves a two-stage processing method, which first employs a fast classification engine to filter out unlikely protocols from a pre-determined shortlist and subsequently uses a more detailed analysis to pinpoint the application protocol. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of Dapper in accurately determining the application protocol under real-world conditions. Moreover, Dapper achieves a substantial reduction in false positives while maintaining a low processing latency of less than 10 microseconds. Additionally, Dapper's improved design enables accurate calculations of protocol probability of interest in less than 10 milliseconds, which is essential for real-time network security analysis. Our study highlights the benefits of Dapper over existing approaches in both accuracy and performance, making it a cutting-edge solution for application layer protocol identification. By applying a vertical electric field, it's feasible to manipulate both electrons and magnons within a two-dimensional fermionic systems, allowing these particles to be treated as a combined entity - a magnon-electron hybrid. We've found that a relatively weak electric field can induce an unusual phenomenon where magnons acquire electrical conductivity in response, a response far exceeding that of electrons. This leads to the discovery of a novel process called'magnon injection,' where a controlled flow of magnons is injected into the system due to magnon-electron resonance. This new discovery presents an excellent opportunity to utilize magnon injection as a means of delivering precise amounts of information using magnons to overcome the fundamental scalability barriers in quantum computing. Our research offers a comprehensive understanding of how magnons and electrons interact under the influence of a gate and provides a mathematical framework for describing this interaction. Additionally, we've identified a critical parameter known as the injection rate, which determines the feasibility of magnon injection, along with a quantum phase transition occurring at a specific point of injection threshold when the two-dimensional fermionic systems transform into a three-dimensional type-I ferromagnetic system. Furthermore, applying a moderate magnetic field causes the magnon injection to cease, while a controlled flow of magnons can be achieved through the adjustment of either the gate voltage or the magnetic field to a specific critical value, creating a promising possibility of magnon injection being used as a means of delivering magnon-based information and implementing magnon-tronics. Federated learning offers a way to train AI models without centralizing user data. A novel federated learning paradigm is presented, which enables a client to employ multiple models for different tasks while simultaneously performing federated training. By allowing a client to conduct federated learning on multiple networks simultaneously, the client can achieve better performance and increase the likelihood of successful network entry. Our approach combines the advantages of having broad model capabilities and efficient federated training, making it suitable for scenarios with limited network connectivity or data privacy concerns. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the standard federated learning approach, particularly in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The code is available at https://github.com/SDuongITR/FedKT.

This study analyzes data from an online monitoring system of U.S. local news to explore connections between COVID coverage, regional case and death rates, and characteristics of news outlets and their audiences.

We examined nearly 300,000 articles from 2020, collected by the Harvard Shorenstein Center's COVID-19 News Archive, which were monitored from March to October of that year by the G glass archive news monitoring system.

Our findings show that COVID-related news coverage varied significantly across U.S. cities, with some outlets prioritizing pandemic stories over others.

We discovered a notable time-dependent correlation between local news coverage and national COVID death rates, though this link weakened as the pandemic lasted longer.

Our results also indicate that local pandemic coverage was influenced by the severity of COVID in that area, with areas hardest hit by COVID receiving less media attention to the phenomenon.

Furthermore, local news coverage of the pandemic was largely determined by the characteristics of the audience rather than the qualities of the news outlet.

We found no significant link between the severity of COVID in an area and the characteristics of the news outlet, its staff, or its coverage style.

Our study suggests that local news can effectively reflect the local pandemic landscape, though this reflection may be delayed by months, and is primarily influenced by the local audience's preferences rather than the news outlet itself. 

This research highlights the benefits of using automated online news monitoring to track the dynamic connection between local pandemic conditions and national COVID death rates, as well as the factors influencing local pandemic coverage. 

These findings can inform public health communication strategies that take into account the unique characteristics of local news and its audience. 

In addition, this research can aid the development of targeted advertising campaigns that tie back to local COVID metrics. 

Lastly, this research can support initiatives aimed at reshaping local news coverage by engaging with local news outlets and their audiences.

The fundamental ability to count is a prime example of humans' innate capacity for abstract thinking. In this ability, there's typically a notable turning point where children rapidly grasp and master counting techniques. To replicate this cognitive milestone, we developed an AI system using reinforcement learning. The agent's task is to arrange dots in a random order while aiming to predict their total quantity. We implemented a unique training approach that introduces an abrupt challenge, simulating the challenge of a child being asked to count 'all of these' dots suddenly in front of them. By mirroring the human brain's developmental process, the AI surpassed human performance in counting skills and achieved high accuracy across various counting challenges. Moreover, the AI demonstrated an understanding of one-to-one correspondence, allowing it to accurately count objects of diverse shapes even after they'd been removed from a larger group. When compared to previous AI systems capable of counting, our model showed significantly improved results, particularly in handling less common scenarios and unknown quantities. This work presents FLVoogd, a refined federated learning technique that allows servers and clients to cooperatively prevent Byzantine attacks while maintaining user anonymity. Specifically, servers utilize the Voogd protocol, incorporating distance-based quantization, to effectively conceal their model updates. Meanwhile, clients leverage trusted execution environments to securely develop and update their models in secret, using homomorphic encryption to protect this process. Crucially, servers are unable to exploit this encryption to gather sensitive information. Furthermore, clients regularly wipe their local models to prevent malicious exploitation, should they successfully subvert the learning process. In our experiments, FLVoogd demonstrated superior resilience against Byzantine attacks and impressive performance, particularly in resource-constrained settings. Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are emerging due to rising computing capabilities and data abundance. However, such networks necessitate an extensive amount of computational power during training. The limitation is even more pronounced when training models on mobile or embedded devices. Existing approaches typically focus on developing efficient models through quantization, pruning, or low-precision training. This typically involves either reducing the precision of calculations or discarding unnecessary weights. The issue with these methods is that they necessitate a time-consuming and resource-intensive process called knowledge distillation. Knowledge distillation involves training a smaller model to mimic the behavior of a larger one, but accurate scaling of this method becomes impractical for large, wide, and deep networks due to the need for a larger, often model-sized, quantization parameter tensor. The problem becomes even more complex when working with mixed-precision training, as the need for an enormous tensor for a large, wide, and deep neural network can cause memory shortages during training. The problem is further exacerbated in GPU-based training due to memory limitations. A potential solution to this problem is ClickTrain, a knowledge distillation framework designed to train efficient, wide, and deep neural networks. ClickTrain incorporates an innovative scheme where a larger, smaller, or equally-sized tensor can be trained efficiently using a novel 'click-training' method. This involves training a smaller model to mimic the behavior of a larger one, but with a larger tensor size, without the need for an even larger tensor. The need for an enormous tensor size is actually an artifact of previous methods and can be completely avoided. As such, ClickTrain can train models more efficiently, especially when resources are limited during training, by effectively eliminating the need for an enormous tensor size. Experimental results show the efficacy of ClickTrain; it can train models up to 8 times faster, especially when compared to traditional knowledge distillation methods, by efficiently training a smaller model to mimic the behavior of a larger one, even when resources are limited. The ClickTrain code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ashishbirla/ClickTrain. The pre-trained models are available at: https://github.com/ashishbirla/ClickTrain/tree/master/models. This hypothesis, first introduced by Urrutia-Talero and colleagues in 2016, claimed that sub-Neptune-sized planets tend to develop into giant planets when their orbital radii fall within a specific'sweet spot'. This research aims to verify the Urrutia-Talero hypothesis through an analysis of the Saturn radius distribution. Utilizing the exoplanet catalog compiled by the Exoplanet Archive, the team calculated a saturation radius for Saturn-sized planets and investigated the variations in this radius based on different orbital distances. While their results initially appeared to support the Urrutia-Talero hypothesis, showing a peak in Saturn saturation radius within the 'Habitable Zone' and decreasing gradients both inward and outward from this area, further investigation revealed this pattern could be attributed to the decreasing density of known exoplanets within the 'Habitable Zone' and the associated bias. Consequently, the evidence does not conclusively support the Urrutia-Talero hypothesis at this time. Sequential decision-making in a constrained environment is referred to as a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). CMDPs are applicable to a broad range of situations, including two-planner games utilized in various operations management problems, where the primary objective is to determine an optimal decision-making strategy at each step that satisfies predefined constraints. The typical approach to solving CMDPs involves finding a policy that optimizes the objective function and adheres to the constraints, which can be computationally intensive and sometimes impractical due to the complexity of the constraints. An alternative method utilizing reinforcement learning (RL) is explored to solve CMDPs, where an agent learns from its environment to make constrained decisions. The existing RL frameworks for CMDPs are primarily centered on optimizing the objective function, with limited consideration for constraints. The focus of this research is on an emerging RL framework that incorporates the constraint information into the reward function as a penalty term. We devise an innovative penalty term structure as a non-smooth function, which can effectively represent various types of convex and concave constraints encountered in real-world applications, including their combination. The non-smooth penalty term structure has a continuous derivative, except at the constraint violation points, where the derivative jumps abruptly, facilitating the utilization of penalty term structure for two-planner games. An advantage of this approach is that the penalty term can be easily modified to adjust the strictness of the constraints. The efficacy of this approach is confirmed through numerical simulations applied to a production planning problem with a restricted output capacity due to a limited market demand. The results show that the proposed method can solve this complex problem efficiently, which would be difficult to solve using conventional methods. Furthermore, the proposed method allows for the incorporation of strict output constraints, reducing overproduction and addressing the issue of non-anticipative constraints in two-planner games. The approach has a promising potential for solving a broad range of CMDPs effectively. The research contributes to the existing literature on sequential decision-making in a constrained environment by incorporating the constraint information into the reward function as a penalty term, facilitating the utilization of two RL frameworks, and verifying the non-smooth nature of the penalty term. The results of this research can be applied to various problems such as production planning with an output constraint, transportation planning with a route constraint, and scheduling with a time constraint. Many handwritten mathematical symbol recognition systems have been developed over the years, but the challenge of accurately segmenting complex mathematical expressions, particularly those handwritten, remains a significant issue. To address this problem, a novel approach is presented for decomposing complex handwritten mathematical expressions into individual symbols. This method relies on a graph-based representation of mathematical expressions, allowing the application of graph partitioning algorithms to divide the expression into its constituent symbols. To tailor these algorithms to the task of handwritten mathematical symbol recognition, a novel scoring function is proposed that leverages knowledge about the visual appearance and statistical frequency of handwritten mathematical symbols. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, extensive experiments were conducted using two datasets, one comprising handwritten mathematical expressions and the other consisting of rendered mathematical expressions. The results demonstrate the ability of this approach to successfully decompose complex expressions with high accuracy, particularly for the case of rendered mathematical expressions. Further work is suggested to refine the technique and its potential applications in the recognition of handwritten mathematical expressions in education and assessment. Our research involves the application of the contact process to random regular graphs and numerical analysis of the system's steady-state. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge. Adverse weather conditions, such as heavy rain or fog, can hinder sensor functionality, such as visibility in the infrared or stereo vision. We introduce a novel approach using lidar point clouds to establish a consistent coordinate system without relying on pre-trained models or assumptions about sensor calibration. Our method utilizes a temporal baseline from a series of lidar scans to calculate the rotation and translation transformation between the initial and final frames. Evaluations within simulated and real-world settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our technique in navigating through unknown environments, even in the absence of visible sensor data. We further combine our navigation method with motion planning to achieve seamless movement to target locations. Our proposed navigation method is included in a public github repository along with the generated frames database. Our approach scored first place in the 7DQN challenge, where participants were evaluated on their lidar-based navigation capabilities within a variety of indoor environments. Additionally, let $V_{2n}(q)$ be the free left module of its counterpart ${^2T_n(q)}$. Studies have proven that the submodules of $V_{2n}(q)$ can be directly mapped to points in affine planes of order $q$ in $S_{2n}(q)$, establishing a connection between projective plane points and cyclic non-free submodules of $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$. Specifically, we demonstrate that these affine plane points correspond to the isomorphism types of certain cyclic non-free cyclic submodules of $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$. We show that the number of these affine plane points is equal to the count of isomorphism types of certain cyclic non-free cyclic submodules of $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$. Moreover, we derive a formula for the number of these isomorphism types and confirm that it matches the known value of affine plane points $q^{n-1} + q^{n-2} + \ldots + q + 1$. Finally, we explore a generalization of our findings to arbitrary left modules of $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$. Specifically, we establish a connection between the module's division rings and the field's extension in affine planes. We illustrate our hypothesis through its application to the module $V_{2n}(q) \oplus V_{2n}(q)$. Our analysis also reveals that the module's rank in its division ring corresponds to the affine plane's order, enabling us to derive formulas for the module's dimensions in certain situations. Moreover, we investigate the connection between the module's direct sum indecomposability and the affine plane's block size. Lastly, we examine our generalized findings' applicability to the Desarguesian plane $S_n(q)$. Specifically, we investigate the module's direct sum indecomposability in this case and derive a formula for the count of isomorphism types of certain cyclic non-free cyclic submodules of $\mathcal{R}_n(q)$. Moreover, we explore the connection between the module's division rings and the field's extension in spherical codes. This approach integrates optimism principles with Bayesian posterior expectations, enabling the determination of an optimal action by identifying the treatment that yields the most optimistic outcome. However, our modified method is found to occasionally yield suboptimal results in complex situations, prompting the development of a more robust variant that Bayesian optimism Q-learning. This new method relies on Monte Carlo sampling to estimate the posterior expectation, leveraging the historical experience reward estimates, and is proven to converge asymptotically to the optimal regime. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the efficacy of both methods in real-world applications. Specifically, while the standard optimism-based method outperforms the standard Q-learning by reducing the likelihood of poor outcomes, the Bayesian optimism-based method surpasses its classical counterpart in likelihood reductions, thereby confirming its superior decision-making capabilities. Finally, potential future applications and research directions are explored. In a flat band superconductor, bosonic modes can freely propagate whereas unpaired electrons are fixed in place. This unique property allows for the creation of exotic bosonic condensates without restricting electron motion. Our research focuses on a flat band superconductor with p-wave symmetry, where three distinct bosonic modes exist: nodal, antinodal, and flat band modes. By applying strain, these modes can couple to the strain field, giving rise to soft modes that simplify the analysis of bosonic effective action. We discover that effective interactions among bosonic modes become apparent when electrons are gapped, and these interactions have concrete implications for the analysis of bosonic effective action. Through strain modulation, these effective interactions can be precisely controlled, potentially enabling the observation of bosonic condensates at higher temperatures. Moreover, the application of strain allows for the separate modulation of nodal and antinodal bosonic modes, paving the way for experimental exploration and potentially yielding evidence of Majorana mode behavior within this system. By exploring the effects of scalar potentials, it is also demonstrated that bosonic fragility can be robust against certain types of perturbations. Finally, potential experimental indicators of bosonic fragility are discussed. Notably, a strong indication of bosonic condensate presence may come from the observation of a magnetic susceptibility increase at a critical temperature, as evidenced in superconducting materials like twisted trilayer graphene under strain modulation. Moreover, the presence of bosonic condensates can be verified by measuring the ratio of bosonic and quasiparticle tunnelling conductances. Moreover, the application of local tunneling spectroscopy could provide spatially-resolved evidence of bosonic condensate presence, as theory suggests a notable conductance discrepancy between bosonic and quasiparticle tunnelling at a critical temperature. The Gaussian distribution is uniquely determined by the distribution of a linear combination and a power function of independent identically distributed random variables. We identify the a-adic solenoids for which this relationship holds, effectively proving a theorem analogous to the generalized Polya theorem. This proof relies on solving a functional equation for a specific class of functions associated with the character group of the a-adic solenoid. The solution reveals that the characteristic function of a Gaussian distribution is distinct among characteristic functions of the form $\tau^{n} \circ \rho_{a}$, where $\tau^{n}$ is a composition of the shift operator $\tau$ exactly $n$ times and $\rho_{a}$ is a translation by $a$. We also show that this distinctness implies the existence of a specific $S$-arithmetic function, which we term $P$, such that its image under the shift operator $\tau$ is essentially a finite set. This key finding allows us to explore other statistical properties of the standard Gaussian distribution on solenoids. Specifically, our method may be adapted to establish a broader class of 'Gaussian-type' distributions on solenoids, characterized by a distinctness property analogous to that of characteristic functions. Moreover, at a more general level, our approach may be applied to identify 'Gaussian-type' distributions on groups characterized by unique functional equations involving transformations of random variables. Ultimately, our study of the Gaussian distribution on solenoids may be seen as an inversion of the classical problem of defining a Gaussian distribution through a functional equation. In this inverted context, the distinctness property of characteristic functions serves as the defining criterion for what we term a 'Gaussian-type' distribution. Additionally, in groups other than solenoids, we propose a more general concept, 'Gaussian-type' distribution, which we illustrate with specific examples in abelian groups. In particular, in torus groups, we identify a 'Gaussian-type' distribution as one that is circulant and has a distinctness property analogous to that of characteristic functions. Conversely, any circulant distribution on a torus group, characterized by a distinctness property analogous to that of characteristic functions, is shown to be solenoidal. Furthermore, our method may be extended to identify a broader class of 'Gaussian-type' distributions on groups, characterized by functional equations involving transformations of random variables, thus providing new perspectives on this topic. Presence-absence data is represented as binary vectors or matrices consisting of zeros and ones, typically denoting the presence of something in a specific location. These data types commonly appear in research contexts such as ecological studies examining species distributions and are also applied in the analysis of networks by representing the presence of connections between nodes as ones and the absence as zeros. Clustering nodes based on the absence data can be achieved by interpreting the zero patterns as the result of a latent multivariate distribution, specifically a proximal multivariate Poisson distribution, whose parameters are learned from the data using the alternating direction method of multipliers algorithm. A multivariate logistic model is proposed to model the variation along the latent dimensions, allowing for the prediction of future zero patterns. These predictions can then be utilized for network prediction tasks such as estimating the probability of connections between unseen nodes or predicting the presence of connections in the future. A comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method is conducted through simulations and real-data examples, including studies of species distributions and drug interactions networks. The results indicate that the proposed method compares favorably to existing approaches, producing more accurate predictions in many cases. A public Python implementation is provided under the name SAM for statistical analysis of multivariate data, accessible at https://github.com/aliadm1/SAM. Two additional applications are discussed for enhancing the basic model: a method for learning varying dimensional structures from the data and a model for predicting the dynamics of changing network configurations over time. A theoretical proof has also been developed for establishing the convergence of the ADMM algorithm during its optimization process. This proof utilizes an evolving Q-function approach, previously reported in the context of reinforcement learning, to demonstrate the convergence of the algorithm, specifically showing that the iterates remain in a convex region and ultimately converge to the optimal solution. Furthermore, this proof can be modified to apply to solving any optimization problem involving the alternating direction method of multipliers algorithm, by utilizing a uniformly convex and smooth objective function, along with the monotonic decrease property. The existing literature lacks a formal proof of the convergence of the ADMM algorithm for solving the proximal multivariate Poisson regression model. An important aspect of this proof is the establishment of a bounded iterates result, which is crucial for enhancing the basic model in various ways, as demonstrated through real-data examples. Additionally, this proof can be extended to solve optimization problems involving non-differentiable objectives, utilizing the majorization-minimization principle, by introducing a smoothly quaderative lower bound for any non-differentiable convex function. In recent years, salient object detection using deep neural networks has received significant attention, but dealing networks that demand enormous computational power for accurate prediction can be very challenging, especially on mobile and edge devices. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel framework for salient object detection that uses a cross-attention context extraction module in a lightweight network design. By incorporating a cross-attention mechanism within a single layer, our network is able to learn complex context information without expanding its depth or width, making it extremely efficient. By doing so, our method achieves a balance between high quality prediction and low computational requirements, outperforming other lightweight networks in terms of both qualitative and quantitative performance while requiring significantly less computational resources. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/IndigoTeam/CACEN.git. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this balance, as our method produces state-of-the-art results on various datasets while being substantially more efficient than other state-of-the-art approaches. Notably, our framework achieves a significant gain of 5.44% in mAOE and 3.44 in mSCE with only a moderate increase of 0.08 in MS, making it an extremely effective approach. The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. A pre-trained transformer model, specifically the BERT, was used to develop a universal model that could process English tweets, and this model was then fine-tuned to identify offensive content, and subsequently used to determine the categories of hate speech. An additional model, based on the same BERT architecture but fine-tuned using Lagrangean Dual Optimization Method, was used to handle non-English tweets. Our results indicate that the BERT-based model outperforms the baseline models, and with further optimization using LDOM, we were able to successfully detect hate speech in four additional languages, and maintain high accuracy in the top-3 accurate predictions for the English task. Ultimately, we successfully ranked 5th and 14th in the English and multi-language tasks, respectively. In this paper, we provide an in-depth analysis of the BERT model and its limitations when applied to natural language processing tasks. In particular, we discuss the challenges of applying a pre-trained model to a new dataset, and the importance of further optimization when working with limited data. Additionally, we highlight the advantages and disadvantages of using the Lagrangean Dual Optimization Method to introduce an economic incentive for optimizing model performance. In the context of this study, we used LDOM to model a hypothetical scenario where a hypothetical researcher named Alex would use the proposed method to improve his model's performance, and demonstrate how this method could be applied to various offline data. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). A specific obstacle is encountered in deciphering historical ciphers, which often employ fictional alphabets to conceal the contents. To overcome this problem, we propose a novel approach that relies on a sequential Max-2-Sentential Machine (seqMax2-SM) trained on mere sentences. Two additional tasks are integrated into the training, each focusing on a single sentence at a time. We apply these models to the decipherment of two historical ciphers from the 17th and 18th centuries, using a method that synthesizes missing data from dictionaries and language models. The results indicate that our proposed approach yields superior outcomes, with significant improvements exceeding 5% in recognition accuracy. Notably, we successfully deciphered one of the ciphers using this method, which was previously unsolved; our findings are verified to align with the established textual evidence. Furthermore, we make available a specially created dataset consisting of 1,650 pages, comprising 520,000 tokens, extracted from 160 scanned images of the two ciphers. This dataset is unique among HTR resources, with the majority of its documents originating from the 17th and 18th centuries. We also provide a public repository containing the code, data, and additional materials for the benefit of the HTR community. In particular, our research is intended to stimulate further analysis on the previously mentioned ciphers at 1015.uk-nlp09 and 1015.uk-nlp10. We hope that these studies, coupled with our findings and the newly created dataset, will contribute to a better comprehension of these significant historical documents. They have gone unresolved for over a decade, despite our best efforts, and we are hopeful that our results will inspire future investigations. We are confident that our proposed approach will yield even more impressive outcomes in the future, with the potential to unlock the secrets of these two historical ciphers, as well as the third cipher at 1015.uk-nlp11, which has also remained unsolved. We anticipate achieving a breakthrough in the near future. In conclusion, our research marks the first instance of applying seqMax2-SM models in the context of HTR with limited resources. We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an exploration of one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This guide, composed by academics from the University of Bristol's Physics Department, offers a flexible and self-contained outcome to complement university teaching. The student is encouraged to delve into the characteristics of the Su-Schrieffer-Hegger model, where they can discover the origins of its topological features, calculate essential physical properties, and determine the properties of bulk and edge modes in various situations. Key topics covered include the origins of the topological phase, methods for detecting topological properties, interacting versions of the model, and extensions to the 2D case through the Rashba effect. A set of challenging questions is provided to aid in understanding the subject. This educational material is designed to introduce students to the concepts of one-dimensional and two-dimensional topological superconductors, using the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model as the primary tool for exploration. The topics covered are critical in the fields of condensed matter physics, superconductivity, and quantum information, and are expected to benefit students preparing for the National Physics Olympiad. The material is flexible and can be completed by students in 20-50 hours. Following the successful use of this guide in the 2021 National Physics Olympiad Qualifying Exam, the problems presented here are now part of the official curriculum. The instructional notes were created by Y. X. Pan, Z. Wang, and X. L. Wang from the University of Bristol's Physics Department, in collaboration with the Physics Olympiad Office. They are presented here in a revised and improved format, provided by Professor C. J. Pacheco. The original version was first published online in January 2022. The current version has been updated in July 2022 to correct errors and incorporate feedback from the community. The updates include revised problem solutions (Chapter 7) and an expanded reference list with new entries (Chapter 8). The instructional material is dedicated to Professor John Bardeen and his collaborators, in recognition of their pioneering work on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model and associated topological phase. The updated version is also dedicated to Professor Bernd T. Meyer, in appreciation of his contributions to condensed matter physics and his influence on the community. Consequently, this characterizes compactness of the composition operator with a continuous symbol (limited to its closure) on the Bergman space of the polydisc. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been limited to applications employing transposed sparse matrix-matrix operations. Researchers have recently introduced new techniques, dubbed Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), allowing a broader range of applications to take advantage of GPU parallelism. SMMO enables efficient execution of operations on multiple data objects using a single, distinct instruction type, despite differing operand sizes. This concept expands the realm of SMMO applications significantly, with numerous dense linear solvers and sparse matrix-free linear solvers, including the conjugate gradient solver, fitting within this category. Our study focuses on optimizing BLAS Level 2 routines, specifically dot products and vector scalings, by adapting them to run in parallel on a single GPU SM using SMMO principles. We introduce novel hybrid SMMO strategies, incorporating multiple data objects of varying lengths, to maximize performance and achieve a substantial speedup when compared to standard, sequence-based approaches. Our experiments demonstrate the potential for significant performance gains, with the dot product outperforming its baseline by almost five times for large problem sizes, and the vector scaling reaching nearly twice the performance under the same conditions. This groundbreaking SMMO-based implementation will undoubtedly pave the way for the widespread adoption of more complex algorithms within high-performance computing environments. Moreover, our findings highlight the considerable potential for further performance enhancements by exploring alternative SMMO configurations and algorithmic variants. Lastly, our research indicates that the key to optimal performance lies in an in-depth analysis of the respective problem sizes and their implied data object lengths. This insight will likely inspire future innovations in the field. Our source code is available online for public use at https://github.com/pcardon2/HSMMO. We introduce family universal U(1)X models incorporating three right-handed neutrinos, by defining U(1)X as a composite of SO(10) U(1)Y and U(1)χ gauge symmetries. To incorporate quantum gravity effects, we propose the introduction of a Dirac fermion χ as a dark matter candidate that is odd under gauged Z2 symmetry post U(1)X breaking, leading to a natural realization of Dark Matter (DM) with minimal lattice cross section even at small DM masses. The potential for Dark Matter in these models can be explored through direct and indirect searches, particularly through Dark Matter annihilations in Dark Matter dominated halos, where we demonstrate new opportunities for observation. This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. Initially, the authors establish a lower bound of Ω(ε^(-1)log n / log ε^(-1)) for the competitive ratio of any online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm for points in 1-dimension, proving it to be tight. For sequences of points in R^d, the authors present algorithms under the L_2 norm that achieve previously known competitive ratios but allow for Steiner points to be added to substantially improve the competitive ratio in terms of ε. However, the authors also prove that eliminating the dependence on n in dimensions d ≥ 2 is not possible, while providing improved lower bounds under the L_1 norm: Ω(ε^(-2)/log ε^(-1)) in the plane and Ω(ε^(-d)) in R^d for d ≥ 3. These findings offer the first known competitive ratio lower bounds for online Euclidean spanners. Moreover, the authors present nearly optimal expected competitive ratios for the offline version of these problems. Additionally, the paper explores the feasibility of adding Steiner points to optimize the competitive ratio, presenting both upper and lower bounds under different norms, ultimately leading to a fully automated algorithm design. These findings contribute to previous research in this domain [1, 2, 3] and also relate to previous work on spanners [4, 5, 6]. All the provided results are based on Euclidean distances, although they can easily be applied to weighted graphs with edge weights in the range [1,∞]. Furthermore, the paper employs a novel approach to analyze the competitive ratio, avoiding the concentration of the competitive ratio, and instead, considers the expected competitive ratio, providing tighter bounds than previous research. Lastly, the paper presents simple and efficient algorithms for providing constant-factor approximations to the optimal competitive ratio, providing insights into these problems and their potential applications.
